#5606. Healthcare purchasers must weigh hospital quality alongside their prices, Leapfrog says

Healthcare purchasers must weigh hospital quality alongside their prices, Leapfrog says" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Patient safety watchdog The Leapfrog Group released its latest collection of hospital safety grades hand-in-hand with calls for policymakers and stakeholders to consider, or directly tie, patient safety reporting with price transparency.

The twice-yearly release brought top marks for 900 out of a total 2,366 graded hospitals, and the lowest “F” score for just three. There were 774 hospitals that earned a “B” grade, 655 a “C” grade, and 35 a “D” grade.

No grades were assigned to another 447 hospitals, a decision the group made after a judge’s ruling in a lawsuit involving the scores it would assign to facilities that did not voluntarily submit their quality data to Leapfrog’s survey (Leapfrog appealed that decision in September). Leapfrog’s decision not to score these has generally shifted its letter grade distribution upward, and the organization has said it is reviewing a potential methodology change for upcoming gradings to incorporate non-submitting hospitals.

Still, “a record number of hospitals are choosing to publicly report their safety and quality performance, and we applaud them for holding themselves accountable to their patients,” Leapfrog President and CEO Leah Binder said in a statement.

At the state level, Connecticut maintained its claim on the largest portion of hospitals earning an “A” grade (64.3% of its total), followed by Utah, New Jersey and South Carolina. Leapfrog also called out Rhode Island and Maine for jumping up the rankings—from eighteenth to seventh for the former, and from seventeenth to eighth for the latter. No hospitals were given an “A” grade in five states: Iowa, North Dakota, South Dakota, Vermont and Wyoming.

A hospital’s assigned grade is calculated by reviewing recent data on up to 22 patient safety measures, including a 10-part Medicare composite of reported patient safety and adverse events. Safety scores for specific hospitals can be searched on the group’s website.

Leapfrog and Binder, in a news release outlining its latest scores, made the case that its grades and similar independent measures warrant a seat at the table in a transparency conversation primarily focused on hospital costs.

“Progress on price transparency is important, but there’s no good price for bad care,” Binder said. “We are calling on the Trump Administration and Congress to ensure price transparency is integrated with patient safety and quality transparency.”

The group backed its calls by pointing to a recent analysis (PDF) conducted by the Purchaser Business Group on Health (PBGH) that reviewed employer claims, federal price transparency data, and quality and safety measures including Leapfrog’s. It “found little to no correlation between negotiated prices and standardized quality measures,” as hospitals that received high safety grades often charged cheaper prices than those in the same market with lower grades.

Leapfrog and Elizabeth Mitchell, president and CEO of PBGH, said the analysis—currently being expanded for practical usage by healthcare purchasers—is an example of how a more wholistic view of prices and care delivery should be considered when weighing a hospital.

“Employers have an appropriate duty to pay a fair price for high-quality care, and they can’t meet it by looking at price alone,” Mitchell said in the release from Leapfrog. “When we put the data together, some of the most expensive hospitals were not the safest. Our members want to buy high-quality, safe care that is fairly priced. That shouldn’t be too much to ask.”

#5605. Opinion: STAT+: I’m a cardiologist. I’m a little puzzled about the blockbuster new study on deprescribing statins

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Khetpal is a preventive cardiologist and assistant professor of medicine at the Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine. He writes The Workup, a STAT column about cardiology.

At the American Heart Association’s recent annual meeting, the overarching theme coming from the center stage, bathed in Pantone red, was one of high-profile neutral findings.

As I listened to the results of the STREAM trial — which found that older adults without a history of heart attacks or strokes who stopped taking statins didn’t have significantly different outcomes from those who continued taking them — I jotted down that the study continued the theme.

But as the Kaplan-Meier curves were cast onto the screen, something felt off: The curves diverged, rather than stayed together. Theoretically, this scenario can happen in noninferiority studies, where researchers are testing whether an intervention offers similar outcomes compared with a standard. De-prescribing statins in this group, by the expectations set by researchers at the beginning of STREAM, was technically noninferior, but nevertheless, still inferior. The patients randomized to stop taking their statin did worse compared with those who continued. Even the trial’s data safety monitoring board suggested that patients who have stopped their statins should talk to their doctors about resuming their medications.

#5604. Walking and weight training may not be enough to keep your bones strong

The type of exercise you do may be more important for your bones than how long you spend doing it. Researchers at Semmelweis University have found that intense physical activity involving sudden bursts of movement, quick changes in direction, and sharp turns appears especially effective at stimulating new bone formation.

The findings, published in Sports Medicine - Open, suggest that certain fast-paced sports may provide greater benefits for bone metabolism than walking or conventional strength training. The research could help scientists develop more effective exercise recommendations for preserving bone health and reducing the risk of osteoporosis.

Why Exercise Intensity Matters for Bone Health

To investigate how different forms of exercise affect bones, the Semmelweis University team reviewed 24 clinical studies involving 1,238 healthy adults.

Instead of relying on bone mineral density measurements, which can take considerable time to reveal changes, the researchers examined blood markers associated with the production of new bone tissue. These biological indicators can reveal how bones respond to exercise within a matter of weeks, allowing scientists to detect changes much sooner.

"What makes our study unique is that we examined not only the type of exercise - whether endurance, resistance, or combined training - but also exercise intensity, frequency, and duration. Our goal was to determine which forms of exercise stimulate bone metabolism most effectively and which appear to be less beneficial from this perspective," said Dr. Péter Ferdinandy, Vice-Rector for Science and Innovations at Semmelweis University and senior author of the study.

Football and Handball Show Surprising Bone Benefits

The strongest responses were associated with vigorous sports that repeatedly require players to accelerate, change direction, turn, and make powerful movements.

Recreational football and handball stood out in particular. These activities were linked to increases of up to 45-46 percent in blood markers associated with bone formation, suggesting that they may provide a particularly strong stimulus for the body's bone-building processes.

More conventional activities generally produced smaller responses. Walking, step aerobics, and standard resistance workouts performed in the gym were less effective at stimulating the measured indicators of bone formation.

The findings were especially unexpected for resistance training, which is commonly recommended as a way to support skeletal health.

"The most surprising finding was that resistance training did not produce a significant effect on markers of bone metabolism, even though several professional guidelines recommend this type of exercise for maintaining bone health. Likewise, low- or moderate-intensity endurance exercise, such as walking or jogging, showed no meaningful long-term effect," explained Viktória Barna, PhD student at Semmelweis University and first author of the study.

Why Walking and Weight Training Still Matter

The results do not suggest that walking, jogging, or other less demanding activities should be abandoned. These forms of exercise continue to offer important health benefits, even if they do not stimulate the measured bone-building processes as strongly as more intense sports.

Rather, the research indicates that maintaining healthy bones may require greater mechanical stimulation than many everyday activities provide. Movements that place more substantial forces on the skeleton appear to produce a stronger response in the biological processes involved in forming new bone.

However, the researchers stress that people should not suddenly begin strenuous exercise without preparing appropriately.

This is especially important for individuals with cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, or metabolic conditions, as well as those who already have osteoporosis. Anyone in these groups who is considering a new activity or a more physically demanding exercise routine should first speak with their treating physician, general practitioner, or a sports medicine specialist. Medical guidance can help determine whether the activity and its intensity are suitable for their health and physical capabilities.

Could High-Intensity Exercise Help Prevent Osteoporosis?

The findings offer a new perspective on how exercise could be used to maintain bone health as people age. While the analysis focused on markers of bone metabolism rather than direct changes in bone density, the results suggest that vigorous activity may encourage early biological changes that support bone formation.

"According to the World Health Organization, regular physical activity offers numerous health benefits. However, our findings suggest that low-intensity exercise alone is not sufficient to stimulate bone metabolism. High-intensity exercise may trigger early beneficial changes in bone formation, potentially helping to slow bone loss and support healthy aging," summarized Dr. Nóra Sydó, clinical specialist and co-author of the study.

The researchers believe that understanding which movements most effectively stimulate bone formation could lead to better exercise programs designed to preserve skeletal strength and help prevent osteoporosis.

For now, the findings highlight an important distinction: staying physically active is beneficial for overall health, but keeping bones healthy over the long term may depend not only on how much people move, but also on how powerfully and dynamically they move.

Materials provided by Semmelweis University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5602. Florida court tosses Tampa General Hospital's suit against Eli Lilly over 340B discounts

Florida court tosses Tampa General Hospital's suit against Eli Lilly over 340B discounts" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

A Florida federal court has tossed Tampa General Hospital's lawsuit against Eli Lilly over the 340B drug discount program.

Florida's Middle District court dismissed the case on a motion from the drugmaker on Wednesday. If Tampa General Hospital wants to file an amended complaint, it must do so within 30 days.

The hospital initially sued the pharmaceutical company over a policy it implemented that requires providers to submit claims-level data on pharmacy and medical dispensing if they participate in 340B. Lilly said it would pull back discounts for providers that did not comply with the requirement and has done so for several organizations, drawing ire from the industry.

Tampa General said the decision is "unconscionable and immoral" in the initial complaint, filed in July.

However, the district court argued that Supreme Court precedent holds that organizations like hospitals do not have the private right to sue if they have been charged beyond the threshold, based on a 2011 decision. SCOTUS said that the right to sue was not outlined by Congress, so it is not an avenue available to these organizations.

"The Court made clear that there is simply no private remedy to superintend the pricing and provision of these discounted drugs," per the order.

"To permit this suit would be to encourage piecemeal litigation and defeat the [Supreme] Court’s insistence on maintaining the Congressional plan 'harmoniously and on a uniform, nationwide basis,'" according to the document.

Eli Lilly cheered the decision in a statement.

"Today’s decision is an important step toward a more transparent 340B program," a Lilly spokesperson said. "Lilly’s claims data requirement asks hospitals for basic information—information they already give insurers every day—to prevent unlawful duplicate discounts."

"Decades of HRSA guidance and two federal appeals courts confirm that Lilly can lawfully require this information," the drugmaker said. "More than 3,200 hospitals and clinics already share it with Lilly, and we hope Tampa General Hospital will join them."

Tampa General Hospital has sued Eli Lilly and Company over the drugmaker’s “unconscionable and immoral” rescindment of discounted pricing under the 340B program.

The complaint, filed last week for the U.S. District Court in the Middle District of Florida, is early legal fallout from a policy Lilly implemented earlier this year that requires providers participating in the federal subsidy program to submit claims-level data for all pharmacy and medical dispensations. The company threatened to pull the discounts for those that didn’t comply and made good on its threat for a subset of hospitals last month, sparking outrage among provider groups.

Tampa General, a nearly 1,000-bed disproportionate share hospital, confirmed in the legal complaint that it was among those cut off. It is now spending 25% to 50% more on average for Lilly products, “many of which it must purchase because of Lilly’s status as the market’s only supplier of a given drug product.”

Tampa General’s lawsuit frequently describes Lilly in such terms, framing the drugmaker as holding significant monopoly power and wielding it in violation of the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act. It also often draws contrast to the 340B program’s intent to support the margins of safety-net hospitals providing care to vulnerable patients, against Lilly’s current status as the largest pharmaceutical company in the world by market cap.

A spokesperson for Lilly, in a statement given to Fierce Healthcare, described the lawsuit as “just another part of the broader hospital campaign to fight transparency and hide the fraud, waste and abuse that plague the 340B program.”

Tampa General asked the court to order an immediate end to Lilly’s policy and to award damages for the higher prices to which the hospital was subjected. It contends Lilly’s alleged failure to comply with 340B pricing requirements and decision to continue marketing its products as 340B-discounted are unfair trade practices under the Florida statute.

“The most valuable pharmaceutical company in the world is engaged in a campaign to transfer dollars earmarked for charitable purposes into its own pocket,” the complaint reads. “The direct and inevitable result of Lilly’s actions is reduced healthcare for poor people. Its actions shock the conscience and are self-evidently unconscionable.”

Tampa General, similar to the hospital associations that have protested Lilly’s policy, contends that the claims data it requires imposes substantial administrative burden on 340B providers. Even “hospitals who have caved to Lilly’s new demands” have effectively had the prices for their covered outpatient drugs increased due to those administrative costs, it wrote in the complaint.

Lilly and other drugmakers who have signaled similar plans have said they need claims data to spot instances in which a drug purchase is improperly granted multiple discounts under overlapping programs. The company has also disputed that the burden of its policy is as substantial as hospitals say.

“The claims data Lilly requires hospitals to share is information they already collect and send to insurers regularly,” the Lilly spokesperson said of the lawsuit’s claims. “Refusing to share that same data with Lilly shows that hospitals are more concerned with hiding rampant abuse in the program than improving its integrity. Lilly will keep working to ensure this program serves vulnerable patients instead of hospitals and their for-profit partners.”

The 340B program has proven to be a magnet for industry and policy conflict, particularly in recent years as its scale has ballooned. The divide is most evident in the ongoing clash over a pilot rebate program that the Trump administration attempted to launch at the top of the year but was forced to restart after the hospital industry’s legal pushback.

340B providers also received a shock this past week when the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services floated a significant reduction in its 340B reimbursement to 33.4% below average sales price in its annual proposed rule on hospital outpatient payments.

#5601. Colorectal cancer is rising again after 20 years, and scientists don't know why

Colorectal cancer rates are climbing again in the United States after more than two decades of decline, and the troubling increase is affecting far more than younger adults. New research published in NEJM Evidence reveals that the disease is becoming more common across nearly every age group under 70, raising concerns about a growing public health challenge.

Colorectal cancer is already the second leading cause of cancer deaths in the United States and the leading cause among adults younger than 50. Although rising cases in younger people have attracted widespread attention, the latest findings show that the problem extends into older generations. Researchers warn that a continued increase could place additional pressure on the healthcare system as more patients require cancer treatment and long-term care after diagnosis.

Colorectal Cancer Rates Reverse Decades of Decline

To investigate the changing pattern, Caitlin Murphy, PhD, MPH, Professor of Pediatrics and Public Health Sciences at the University of Chicago, and her colleagues examined the latest colorectal cancer incidence data from the National Cancer Institute. Their analysis tracked changes in diagnoses from 2000 through 2023.

The results revealed a significant reversal. In 2000, the age-adjusted colorectal cancer incidence rate was 55.2 cases per 100,000 people. By 2022, that figure had dropped to 36.7. However, the rate increased to 38.3 in 2023, marking the first overall rise after more than two decades of falling rates.

"This is the first time that we have seen an increase in the overall rate since in more than 20 years," Murphy said. She emphasized that the long-standing downward trend had been a major feature of colorectal cancer statistics for decades. The new analysis indicates that rates are now increasing in every age group through ages 65 to 69.

Murphy, an epidemiologist who specializes in colorectal cancer patterns, had anticipated that the increase initially observed in younger adults would eventually become apparent among older people. She attributes this expected progression to a phenomenon called the "birth cohort effect."

This effect describes how people born during the same general period can share risk patterns that become more apparent as they grow older. In this case, individuals born in the 1960s and subsequent decades appear to face an elevated risk of colorectal cancer as they enter middle age and later life.

"I think of a birth cohort effect as the interaction of age and time," Murphy explained. "As people born around the same time move through time and age together, we're going to see more colorectal cancers being diagnosed."

A Sharp Increase Among Adults Ages 45 to 49

One of the most striking findings involved people between 45 and 49 years old. From 2019 through 2023, colorectal cancer incidence in this group increased by 12.76% annually, the largest rise recorded among the age groups examined.

Researchers believe much of this particular increase can be explained by changes in cancer screening recommendations. National guidelines lowered the recommended starting age for routine colorectal cancer screening from 50 to 45, allowing more people to be tested and more previously undetected cancers to be identified.

"That means that screening is doing as we intend it to do -- it's catching cancer earlier," Murphy said.

But increased screening cannot account for the broader pattern. Colorectal cancer rates are also rising among adults ages 65 to 69, while the decline has stalled among those ages 70 to 74. Both populations have historically experienced substantial benefits from screening, and approximately 80% of people in these age groups are current with recommended testing.

These findings are particularly concerning because they suggest that additional, unidentified risk factors could be counteracting some of the progress achieved through decades of cancer screening.

The research team also investigated whether disruptions during the COVID-19 pandemic might have distorted the results. Cancer screenings and diagnoses were affected during the pandemic, potentially changing when cases were detected. However, the upward trend remained even after the researchers removed data from 2020 and 2021. Screening activity had also largely recovered to its earlier levels by January 2021, making pandemic-related disruptions an unlikely explanation for the increase recorded in 2023.

"These results motivate us to understand reasons for this rise, so risk factors can be identified and possibly reduced," said Sonia Kupfer, MD, director of the Gastrointestinal Cancer Risk and Prevention Clinic at UChicago Medicine.

Why Colorectal Cancer Is Rising Across Generations

The growing number of colorectal cancer diagnoses among younger Americans has become a major health concern. American Cancer Society data show that incidence among adults ages 20 to 49 increased by approximately 3% per year between 2013 and 2022.

This increase in colorectal cancer among people younger than 50, often referred to as early-onset colorectal cancer, has drawn considerable public and scientific attention. The latest study suggests that understanding why younger adults are developing the disease more frequently could also help explain what is happening in older populations.

"There are many unique challenges when you're diagnosed with cancer at a young age, so it's important that we shine a spotlight on that problem," Murphy said. "But in terms of understanding the root cause, I think our study shows that we can consider that whatever might be causing colorectal cancer in younger people is now also causing it to increase in older people as well."

The underlying causes remain uncertain, but researchers are investigating whether exposure to chemicals in the environment could play a role.

Murphy and her colleagues are working with Xin Hu, PhD, a toxicologist at Emory University, to examine this possibility. Their approach involves analyzing small blood samples for evidence of thousands of environmental chemical exposures simultaneously. By identifying which substances are associated with potential risks, the team hopes to narrow the list of chemicals that deserve more detailed investigation.

The researchers then plan to collaborate with Kupfer to explore how these chemicals affect colon tissue. To do so, they will use organoids, laboratory-grown models that reproduce important features of the colon. These miniature tissue systems allow scientists to study biological responses in a controlled environment and could help uncover how certain exposures contribute to colorectal cancer.

Why Colorectal Cancer Screening Remains Critical

With cancer rates increasing across a broad range of ages, the researchers emphasize the need to keep tracking national cancer statistics as new registry information becomes available each year.

Murphy cautions that the consequences could become substantial if the current pattern continues. As large numbers of Americans born in more recent decades grow older, rising incidence rates could translate into many additional cancer diagnoses. That would increase demand for medical treatment and services supporting people who survive colorectal cancer.

While scientists work to understand the factors behind the increase, screening remains one of the most effective ways to find colorectal cancer early and reduce the risk of dying from the disease.

Current national recommendations advise adults at average risk to begin regular colorectal cancer screening at age 45 and continue through age 75. For people younger than 45 or older than 75, screening decisions should be tailored to individual circumstances, including family medical history, symptoms, and other health conditions.

Colonoscopy continues to be considered the gold standard for colorectal cancer screening, but patients also have additional testing options. These include newer blood-based screening tests and stool tests that can be completed at home.

"There are several ways to do screening that should be discussed with a clinician, so people know what the different screening tests are intended for and how often these need to be repeated," Kupfer added.

She also stressed that people younger than 45 should not ignore possible warning signs simply because they have not reached the age recommended for routine screening. Those without known genetic or family history risk factors should still seek medical attention if they notice blood in their stool, persistent changes in bowel habits, or unexplained weight loss.

The research, titled "Colorectal cancer among U.S. adults, 2000-2023," received financial support from the National Institutes of Health and the Eli and Edythe Broad Center of Regenerative Medicine and Stem Cell Research Ablon Scholars Program.

Along with Murphy, the study's authors include Folasade P. May of the University of California Los Angeles, Xin Hu of Emory University in Atlanta, and Samir Gupta of the University of California San Diego.

The University of Chicago's medical and biological sciences programs are also continuing to expand their work in cancer research and patient care. In April 2027, UChicago Medicine is scheduled to open the AbbVie Foundation Cancer Pavilion, which will be Chicago's first freestanding cancer pavilion. The facility is intended to bring together advanced diagnostic services, new cancer treatments, research that translates laboratory discoveries into clinical care, and comprehensive support for patients and the surrounding community.

#5599. Google Cloud brings AI agents to the supercomputing bottleneck

High-performance computing, or HPC, is merging with artificial intelligence faster than many research teams can adapt. Compute capacity is hard to get, and workloads now run across clouds and on-premises clusters. The metric that matters is shifting from peak performance to time to discovery.

That shift is on full display as supercomputing and AI converge at SC26 in Chicago. Researchers need more compute than any single site can provide, and cloud providers are now pitching AI agents as the layer that ties scattered resources together, according to Annie Ma-Weaver (pictured, left), head of high-performance computing product at Google Cloud, a unit of Google LLC.

“We are powering that flexibility. and we understand that researchers really need access to compute, but they don’t necessarily wanna learn all the nitty-gritty of how to tie that compute together, how to get it orchestrated across all their different clusters,” Ma-Weaver said.

Ma-Weaver and Megan Gawlik (right), high-performance computing product manager at Google Cloud, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how AI agents are simplifying access to distributed computing resources, changing simulation and weather forecasting and raising questions about researchers’ reliance on AI-generated results. (* Disclosure below.)

Google Cloud builds its agentic HPC strategy on three pillars: purpose-built hardware, open-source orchestration such as Slurm and Kubernetes, and collaborative AI agents, Ma-Weaver explained. The company laid out the approach in its SC26 announcements. Agents now help scientists comb through research literature, debug code and generate hypotheses in minutes instead of weeks, according to Gawlik.

“You’re able to go explore more scenarios and you might be using that same time to just go sanity test that hypothesis that’s coming out,” Gawlik said. “I think it’s not only a speed thing, but I think it’s an accuracy thing that you’re able to really get from that additional speed.”

Simulation is changing as well. Engineers used to run simulations across an entire parameter space. Now they can use AI up front to decide which candidates are worth testing, Ma-Weaver noted.

“What we’re seeing, for example, with computer-aided engineering, is that you can actually identify ahead of time which are non-essential parameters and you don’t run the simulation, thereby reducing the total simulation time,” she said. “We also find that if you’re doing design and you have initial prototypes, you can generate new, novel and creative prototypes.”

The gains are already reaching weather forecasting in production. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s forecasting platform has heavy, tightly coupled workloads and once ran only on-premises, but it now runs on Google Cloud, Ma-Weaver explained. The National Hurricane Center also used Google’s WeatherNext model to predict the path and intensity of Hurricane Melissa in October 2025, Gawlik noted. But the growing reliance on AI-generated results also carries a risk for younger researchers, who may lean on machine output instead of developing critical-thinking skills, she added.

“AI is still not perfect,” Gawlik said. “I think even though there’s an output, we call it AI slop. It could still be slop.”

#5597. Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide

A new study from the University of Eastern Finland has identified an intriguing relationship between the types of protein men consume and their testosterone levels. Researchers found that men who ate more animal protein tended to have lower testosterone concentrations in their blood, while those who consumed more plant protein generally had higher levels.

The findings, published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition, suggest that protein sources may be associated with male hormone levels in different ways. However, the researchers caution that the differences were relatively small and that the results do not establish whether protein intake directly influences testosterone.

Testosterone is an essential male sex hormone that helps maintain muscle mass, bone health, and sexual function. Although age, excess body weight, and lifestyle habits are known to influence testosterone levels, scientists have conducted relatively little research into how diet, especially protein consumption, might be associated with this hormone.

Study of More Than 2,500 Men Reveals Contrasting Protein Patterns

To investigate the relationship, researchers analyzed information from 2,546 men between the ages of 42 and 60 who lived in eastern Finland. The participants were part of the ongoing Kuopio Ischaemic Heart Disease Risk Factor Study, a research project conducted at the University of Eastern Finland.

Between 1984 and 1989, the men recorded everything they ate over four days, allowing researchers to evaluate their dietary habits and protein sources. Blood samples were also collected to measure total testosterone and sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), a protein that helps regulate the amount of testosterone circulating in the bloodstream.

The researchers then divided the participants into four groups based on their protein consumption. A clear contrast emerged when they compared the men with the highest and lowest intakes of animal and plant protein.

Men who consumed the most animal protein had average total testosterone concentrations 1.2 nmol/l lower than those who consumed the least. Plant protein showed the opposite pattern, with men in the highest intake group having testosterone concentrations 1.1 nmol/l higher than those in the lowest group.

Similar relationships were observed for SHBG concentrations. The associations remained after the researchers accounted for age, body mass index, and several other factors related to diet, lifestyle, and health.

Dairy and Plant Proteins Show Different Testosterone Links

A closer examination of individual protein sources revealed additional differences. Higher consumption of protein from dairy products was associated with lower concentrations of both total testosterone and SHBG.

Meanwhile, men who obtained more plant protein from vegetables and sources other than cereal products tended to have higher total testosterone concentrations.

Meat protein showed a somewhat different relationship. Although greater meat protein intake was linked to lower SHBG concentrations, researchers did not find a corresponding association with total testosterone levels.

These distinctions suggest that the relationship between dietary protein and male hormones may vary depending on where the protein comes from, rather than simply how much protein a person consumes.

Despite the contrasting patterns, the researchers emphasize that the observed testosterone differences were modest. It is also unknown whether changes of this size have any meaningful consequences for health.

"Although the observed differences in testosterone concentrations were statistically significant, they were relatively small. Based on this study, it is not possible to infer whether these differences have implications for health," says Doctoral Researcher Miika Wynne-Ellis from the University of Eastern Finland.

An important limitation is that the research was cross-sectional, meaning dietary intake and hormone measurements were examined without tracking how changes in protein consumption affected testosterone over time. As a result, the findings cannot establish a cause-and-effect relationship.

Other dietary characteristics or metabolic factors could help explain the associations. The researchers also cannot determine whether eating different types of protein influences testosterone production or changes how the hormone functions in the body.

For now, the findings highlight an interesting connection between protein sources and testosterone levels, while leaving open the question of whether changing protein choices could have any direct effect on male hormone health.

#5596. Cigna Group Foundation making $31.5M in grants available to community organizations in 10 states

Cigna Group Foundation making $31.5M in grants available to community organizations in 10 states" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Cigna is making $31.5 million in grant funding available over the next three years to nonprofits in 10 states that are aiming to tackle several key community health priorities.

The company said that funds will be made available through its philanthropic arm, the Cigna Group Foundation, with applications open now through Dec. 18. Cigna said in an announcement that it's looking for organizations tackling youth mental health, veteran wellness and the impact of complex health needs on patients and their caregivers.

Cigna said the program seeks to deepen the company's community health strategy to address critical challenges.

The company first launched a new approach to community health and engagement in 2024, and since then has deployed more than $30 million in funding to 190 nonprofit organizations. Projects backed by these grants have reached at least 321,000 people, Cigna said.

"Over the past several years, we’ve seen the tangible impact we can make when we invest in strong nonprofit partners and come together to help communities achieve better health and vitality," said Melissa Skottegaard, board chair of The Cigna Group Foundation, in the announcement. "We’re building on what’s working, bringing together funding, collaboration and the skills of our employee volunteers to address some of the most pressing health challenges facing communities across the street and around the world."

Cigna will allot $10.5 million to each of the three focus areas under the initiative, per the announcement. Youth mental health, for example, has been a leading topic at the company for some time, and the company said it will also continue to build on its partnership with the Boys and Girls Clubs of America in this area.

In that partnership, Cigna has helped build out trauma-informed care services to 90% of clubs, reaching 11,000 employees. The company said that these efforts have supported 1,600 youths, and that its workforce has contributed more than 2,000 hours to local clubs.

Eligible organizations can apply for two-year, $250,000 grants to support programs in the three categories. The funds will be available to groups in Arizona, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Missouri, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Tennessee and Texas, per the announcement.

Cigna said its foundation will also continue to support community health through its Health Equity Impact Fund.

"Community organizations can be a powerful source of support for people navigating complex health conditions,” said Matt Perlberg, president of Evernorth Pharmacy & Care Delivery and board member of the Cigna Group Foundation, in the announcement. “By helping patients and caregivers connect with resources and overcome barriers to care, these organizations can provide important support alongside essential medical treatment, helping people navigate their health and care journey.”

Tons of news coming from the nation’s capitol as Democrats set their agenda for next year, but it’s worth highlighting what else happened yesterday.

Epic officials publicly addressed whether their business practices choke innovation, as detailed in a STAT investigation. What did they say? Scroll down.

After the White House pulled its nomination of Heidi Overton for commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration on Tuesday evening, the future of the agency that oversees $4.1 trillion worth of food, tobacco, and medical products is extremely unsettled.

The agency’s current acting commissioner, Kyle Diamantas, has reportedly said he’s uninterested in taking the role permanently, and even indicated he doesn’t want to stay at the FDA past the new year. Meanwhile, it is very unlikely that Congress has enough time to install another nominee before January, meaning that Senate Democrats will have final say over the next commissioner.

Who in the White House tanked Overton’s nomination? Who will replace her? Some people have suggested Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas, or even a little-known guy named Marty Makary. (The former FDA head did not respond to request for comment.)

Where does this leave the agency? STAT’s Margaret Manto breaks it down.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) is feeling optimistic about the first stage of his plan to vastly expand health coverage in the U.S. He predicted at a Wednesday press conference that Democrats will pass legislation lowering the Medicare eligibility age while President Trump is still in office, and that Trump might not veto it.

Sanders would like Congress to lower the Medicare eligibility age from 65 to 55, expand coverage to include dental, vision, and hearing care, and guarantee free Medicaid coverage to children until age 19.

And he pushed back on the assumption that Trump would veto such a bill. “I am not absolutely certain that Trump would not sign it,” he said.

The health committee does not have jurisdiction over Medicare, but Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), who is expected to lead the committee that does, said he is on board with Sanders’ plan. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) also supports the “Medicare for More” and “Medikids” proposals, an indication the party’s liberal and moderate wings are quickly moving toward common ground on a health care agenda.

Sanders also offered insights into the health care investigations he might undertake, including of health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and the insurance and pharma industries.

“Taking a hard look at the way the insurance industry runs, how they distort health care. Taking a hard look at the pharmaceutical industry as to why we pay by far the highest prices in the world for prescription drugs. Those are areas that need investigation,” he said. — John Wilkerson

Less than two months before he leaves office, Bill Cassidy took a stand.

The Republican senator from Louisiana rejected Jim O’Neill as the nominee to lead the National Science Foundation, cancelling the vote to confirm him over doubts about his willingness to stand up for scientific integrity.

The high-ranking health official had previously served at the Department  of Health and Human Services and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention under health secretary Kennedy. But O’Neill “did not do enough to stand up for science and against irresponsible decisions and statements” from Kennedy in those roles, Cassidy said at a meeting of his committee.

More from my STAT colleagues on Cassidy’s bold move as his time in the Senate runs out.

At a panel discussion at HLTH, a health technology conference in Las Vegas, Epic’s executives for the first time responded directly to a STAT investigation that found the company is undercutting competition by selectively withholding data access needed by rival application developers.

Officials at Epic, the largest maker of electronic health records, defended against allegations of anticompetitive conduct and said they are seeking to build a more open ecosystem amid a deluge of requests for integration coming from third-party software vendors. They also said the company would make it easier for companies to use AI to read data stored in the company’s platforms.

Lots more juicy details from this panel, moderated by Brittany Trang. Read more.

In the wake of the midterm elections, leaders of the Make America Healthy Again movement have said that their candidates were up against opponents with massive funding advantages.

But filings show that the movement’s political arm had more than $10 million to spend during this election cycle. Instead of directing those funds to promising candidates, it funneled millions to allies, associated organizations, and pundits.

One notable example: The PAC spent less than $50,000 on a California House race it called “the most direct ideological confrontation between the movement and its institutional opposition anywhere on the 2026 ballot.” It spent more money this cycle at Mastro’s Steakhouse D.C., a white-tablecloth spot that offers $110 porterhouse steaks. Another great story from our DC team.

Later this morning, a little-known but influential panel that recommends which preventive services must be covered by insurance will meet for the first time in more than a year, writes STAT’s Chelsea Cirruzzo.

The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force will review recommendations related to cervical cancer, perinatal depression, and unhealthy alcohol use in teens and adults, all of which have not been updated in at least five years, and have been awaiting finalization since last year, when Kennedy canceled the group’s meetings and overhauled its membership.

Read more from Chelsea Cirruzzo about the meeting and some of the new members’ conflict of interests.

#5594. Study of 750,000 pregnancies reveals a surprising twist about Ozempic and Wegovy

A major study involving more than 750,000 pregnancies has uncovered an important difference in the potential pregnancy risks of popular weight loss medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy. Women who unintentionally used these drugs shortly before or during early pregnancy were more likely to give birth prematurely, but only when the medications had been prescribed to treat existing diabetes.

Among women taking the same medications for weight management, researchers found no significant association with premature birth or other pregnancy complications examined in the study.

The findings suggest that diabetes itself, rather than the medications, may be responsible for the increased risk of early delivery. The research was published in Human Reproduction Open, a leading journal in reproductive medicine.

The medications examined included semaglutide (brand names: Ozempic, Wegovy) and liraglutide (Saxenda). Both belong to a widely used group of drugs known as GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs). Originally developed to manage type 2 diabetes, these medications also suppress appetite, making them effective treatments for weight loss. However, their safety during pregnancy has not been established.

Why Ozempic and Similar Drugs Raise Pregnancy Concerns

Professor Henriette Svarre Nielsen, who led the research at the Department of Gynecology and Obstetrics at Copenhagen University Hospital Hvidovre in Hvidovre, Denmark, explained that the rapid rise in GLP-1 prescriptions has created an urgent need for better information about pregnancy exposure.

"GLP-1 RA treatment has, within the last few years, become the medication with the sharpest increase in prescriptions worldwide. Current guidance suggests the treatment should be stopped eight weeks prior to planning a pregnancy. However, this is based on early-phase model organism studies, and not real-world evidence. Nonetheless, because of its widespread adoption, inadvertent exposure in early pregnancy is inevitable, and there is hardly any evidence to guide clinical counseling when it happens."

To investigate these concerns, researchers examined whether accidental exposure to GLP-1 medications around conception was associated with complications during pregnancy. They focused on preterm birth (birth before 37 weeks), pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, delivering a baby that was unusually large for its gestational age, stillbirth, and placental problems.

Study Examines More Than 750,000 Pregnancies

The research team used Denmark's nationwide health registries to examine 756,636 pregnancies involving a single baby among 480,231 women. All pregnancies resulted in deliveries between October 1, 2009, and December 31, 2023.

The researchers classified a pregnancy as having possible accidental exposure to GLP-1 medications if the woman filled a prescription for semaglutide or liraglutide during the eight weeks before or after the first day of her last menstrual period.

This 16-week period included the time when a woman might not yet realize she was pregnant, as well as the early stages of fetal development when major organs begin to form.

Of the pregnancies included in the study, 529 involved prescription records indicating exposure to GLP-1 medications during this period.

To make the comparisons more reliable, the researchers accounted for several characteristics that could influence pregnancy outcomes. These included maternal age, body mass index (BMI), smoking habits, location, education, and whether the woman already had diabetes. They also considered the month and year of pregnancy to account for possible seasonal patterns and changes over time.

Diabetes May Be the Key to Premature Birth Risk

The results revealed a striking distinction between women prescribed GLP-1 drugs for diabetes and those using them for weight loss.

Dr. Kathrine Hviid, the study's first author and a PhD student in the same department, said the findings could help shape future research and improve medical guidance for women who unknowingly use these drugs during early pregnancy.

"We made some extremely important findings that have implications for future studies, such as randomized controlled trials of GLP-1 RA usage in pregnancy, and for clinical counseling.

"We found that these medications were associated with an increased risk of preterm birth, but the risk was only present when the medication was used for diabetes treatment, and not for weight management. This suggests that the underlying condition of diabetes, rather than the medication, may be driving this association."

At first, women with GLP-1 prescriptions appeared to experience several pregnancy complications more frequently than those without exposure. However, most of these associations were no longer statistically significant once the researchers accounted for other factors that could affect pregnancy outcomes.

The remaining significant association involved premature birth among women who had been prescribed liraglutide or semaglutide to manage diabetes.

Compared with women who had not been exposed to these medications, the adjusted odds of premature delivery were 70% higher among women taking liraglutide for diabetes and 84% higher among those taking semaglutide for diabetes.

The researchers' accompanying announcement also reported estimated increases of approximately 11% for semaglutide and 9% for liraglutide among women with pre-existing diabetes.

Crucially, the same elevated risk of premature birth was not observed when the medications were prescribed specifically for weight management.

This difference suggests that the underlying medical condition may play a larger role in pregnancy outcomes than exposure to the medications themselves.

What the Findings Mean for Women Taking GLP-1 Drugs

According to Professor Nielsen, future investigations must distinguish between women taking GLP-1 medications for diabetes and those using them for weight control. Combining these groups could obscure important differences in their underlying health and pregnancy risks.

"Future studies must take account of the reason a woman has been prescribed these medications, as the risks differ between women using GLP-1 RAs for diabetes versus weight management. This is one of the first studies to examine GLP-1 RA exposure in early pregnancy according to the reason for prescription. As more evidence accumulates, these findings will guide clinical counseling for women inadvertently exposed to GLP-1 RAs in early pregnancy. In Denmark, about 70% of people who use weight loss medications are women and so it is inevitable that some may take it without realizing they are pregnant."

Although the results provide useful new information, Nielsen emphasized that additional research is necessary before changing existing medical recommendations.

In particular, the findings do not justify abandoning current guidance to discontinue GLP-1 medications before a planned pregnancy. They also do not provide enough evidence to establish new clinical counseling recommendations based on why the drugs were prescribed.

Important Limitations of the Pregnancy Study

One of the investigation's greatest strengths was its size, with health records covering more than three-quarters of a million pregnancies.

However, the study was observational, meaning it could identify associations but could not determine whether GLP-1 medications directly caused premature births. Other factors, including the effects of diabetes itself, may help explain the results.

Another limitation was that the researchers relied on prescription records. Although they could determine whether a woman had filled a prescription, they could not confirm whether she had actually taken the medication.

The researchers nevertheless believe that most women who purchased the drugs were likely to have used them because of their substantial cost.

In Denmark, patients generally contribute toward the cost of GLP-1 injections, although government subsidies are available for diabetes treatment. For example, a 1mg injection of Wegovy or Ozempic (semaglutide) costs approximately €180 and €114, respectively, with the diabetes subsidy reflected in the lower price.

Dr. Hviid said: "Because of the high cost, we assume that compliance is very high among the women prescribed GLP-1 RAs."

Experts Call for More Individualized Pregnancy Guidance

The findings also attracted attention from researchers outside Denmark.

In an invited commentary published alongside the study, Drs. Yeyi Zhu and Monique Hedderson of Kaiser Permanente Northern California and the Center for Upstream Prevention of Adiposity and Diabetes Mellitus in Pleasanton, California, described the results as important additions to the growing research on GLP-1 medications and reproductive health.

They wrote that the findings "complement and extend an emerging evidence base on the reproductive safety of GLP-1 RAs."

The researchers also emphasized that the distinction between diabetes treatment and weight management could help doctors provide more personalized advice to women who accidentally used these medications around conception.

"For clinicians, the study by Hviid et al. (2026) may inform preconception and early pregnancy counseling. The observation that elevated preterm birth risk was confined to women treated for diabetes, and not to those using GLP-1 receptor agonists for weight management, supports more balanced, individualized discussions with patients who may have experienced inadvertent periconceptional exposure. For patients with diabetes, the study reinforces the importance of recognizing diabetes as an important risk factor for obstetric complications and prioritizing metabolic health and glycemic management before and during pregnancy."

Ultimately, the study highlights why a woman's underlying health conditions matter when evaluating the potential pregnancy risks of GLP-1 medications. While the findings offer some reassurance regarding accidental exposure among women using these drugs for weight loss, they do not establish that the medications are safe during pregnancy.

Further research will be needed to clarify the risks and determine how best to counsel women who become pregnant while using these increasingly popular treatments.

Materials provided by European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5592. The Thanksgiving Hosting Stress Test: Is Your Place Ready for the Big Day?

Hosting Thanksgiving in your first home is exciting, but it can also feel overwhelming.

“You likely want everything to look and feel ‘put together’ as soon as possible despite the fact that a fresh move-in is typically anything but,” says Kate Pechinka, founder and principal designer of Kate Kelly Interiors in Chester Springs, PA.

The pressures of living up to the warm environment you’ve either experienced growing up or seen in movies or advertisements combined with the added demands on your home’s systems don’t make things any easier.

“Suddenly, multiple people are using the bathrooms, the dishwasher and garbage disposal are running frequently, the oven is working for hours, and guests are moving through spaces that may not have been arranged for entertaining,” explains Kevin Vander Hyde, vice president of Vander Hyde Services in Grand Rapids, MI.

Here’s the good news: With a little preparation and planning, you can ensure your home is Thanksgiving-ready and alleviate a great deal of stress long before your guests arrive.

These expert tips can help you address safety concerns, secure your belongings, and prevent common hosting mishaps this Turkey Day—all while keeping your sanity and budget in check as a new homeowner.

Ensure keepsakes, special family heirlooms, and other high-value items are either put away, well protected, or displayed in a place that invites appreciation, but not direct interaction like a high mantel or glass-front china cabinet.

“Anticipate that curious guests of all ages might not be able to fight the urge to touch,” Pechinka explains.

Chances are guests will set drinks or food items down on your tables, couches, and other furniture. That’s why it’s important to shield them from accidental spills, stains, and scratches.

For pieces with inviting tabletop surfaces you don’t intend to move, Pechinka recommends  having a piece of glass cut at your local glass shop to place on the surface.

“This option can create a polished look and provide a high level of protection. It’s also cost-effective when you consider the cost to refinish or replace a piece of furniture,” says Pechinka.

No matter where you live, your home is likely filled with trip hazards like step-downs into family rooms, or area rugs that change the height of flooring surfaces. These potential hazards can create unique challenges for guests of all ages.

“To reduce their risk, improve lighting in these areas. You can also use rug tape to keep rug corners down,” Pechinka explains.

Children or nosy adults may walk into bedrooms and other rooms you might not want them to venture into.

Make sure you know how many dishes, coffee cups, and utensils you need.

“This simple check keeps you from washing dishes midparty and lets you remain fully engaged with your guests,” Pechinka adds.

Make sure the oven heats properly, the stovetop burners work, and the dishwasher completes a cycle without leaking.

“If you're preparing several dishes, plan out cooking times and oven space in advance. Avoid plugging multiple high-wattage countertop appliances into the same overloaded circuit,” says Vander Hyde.

Run the kitchen and bathroom faucets, flush the toilets, and check that sinks and tubs drain properly.

“Slow drains, low water pressure, dripping faucets, or unusual odors can be signs of a plumbing issue you should address before guests arrive,” Vander Hyde explains.

Remember that catching and resolving a small problem early on is always easier and less expensive than dealing with an unexpected and much larger repair once the holiday is over.

Resist the temptation to treat the garbage disposal like a trash can.

Avoid putting grease, cooking oil, large amounts of food, or fibrous scraps down the drain. Run cold water while operating the disposal, and feed food scraps gradually rather than trying to grind everything at once.

“Grease and food buildup are common contributors to holiday drain clogs,” says Vandrer Hyde.

With multiple guests showering, washing dishes, and using hot water, demand can increase significantly. That’s why it’s vital to ensure the water heater is operating normally.

“Watch for signs of trouble, such as inconsistent hot water, leaks, or unusual noises. If you notice any of them, it’s time to call a plumber,” Vander Hyde explains.

Before guests arrive, test the thermostat, replace a dirty air filter, and make sure vents aren't blocked by furniture or rugs.

“If the furnace is making unusual noises or struggling to maintain the temperature, arrange an inspection before the holiday,” adds Vander Hyde.

#5590. Six days, six outages: Why reliability isn’t resilience

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

A rash of major outages over the past week all seem to follow a similar script. Services go dark, Downdetector lights up, the provider posts a string of status updates, a root cause emerges a few days later, and everyone goes back to work, assuming it won’t happen again. This past week, that script was on overdrive.

None of these was a cyberattack, and as far as anyone can tell, none was related. A dormant bug, overloaded legacy routers, a bad internal update and an on-premises hardware glitch are about as different as root causes get. Some of these systems run in the public cloud, some in a company’s own data center, and some on air traffic control gear that’s decades old. That’s precisely the point. The common thread isn’t the technology. It’s that each organization had a critical dependency fail, and the business stopped with it.

That’s the lesson I want business leaders to take away. Outages aren’t rare events to be explained away after the fact. They’re a certainty to plan for, and the plan must address what happens when an entire service fails, not just a server or a data center.

I wanted to dig into what real resilience looks like, and Zscaler Inc. is an interesting case study for a specific reason. When a company deploys Zscaler, every user, branch and device connects to applications through its Zero Trust Exchange. That places Zscaler squarely in the critical path. If it goes down, users can’t reach Microsoft 365, Salesforce, internal apps or anything else, no matter how healthy those applications are. That all-or-nothing exposure has forced Zscaler to think harder than most about what happens when its service fails.

At the last Zenith Live, Zscaler’s user event, I asked Chief Executive Jay Chaudhry about this, and he explained that because of the critical nature of their offering, it can’t afford any downtime, so the company built resiliency into its service design. After all these outages, I asked to speak with Chaudhry and Chief Reliability Officer Misha Kuperman to gather lessons learned for the industry.

To be clear, Zscaler couldn’t have kept a single Microsoft mailbox online or restarted the FAA’s routers, and no one at the company claimed otherwise. But its approach to continuity for its own platform is a useful model for how any service on a company’s critical path, including software-as-a-service, should be architected. Here are my thoughts on what this means for boards and C-suite leaders:

I came from financial services, where the disaster recovery site was non-negotiable and everyone knew which services had to survive a failure. Chaudhry, who spent years at IBM Corp., made the same point.

“Most of my large customers had a production data center and a DR data center,” he told me. “If the production data center went down, they’d fail over to DR. That was standard practice. When the world moved to the cloud, they forgot about it, thinking disaster recovery was the cloud provider’s responsibility, even though it is actually a shared responsibility.”

He’s right, and the record proves it. Availability zones and multiregion designs protect against hardware failures and localized events, but they share software, control planes, configuration pipelines and often DNS. When a bad configuration or a dormant bug propagates, it spreads everywhere. That’s exactly what happened to Microsoft.

Availability architecture and resilience architecture aren’t the same thing. One keeps a service up when a component fails. The other keeps the business running when the entire service fails. Most companies have the first and assume they have the second, but as we have seen recently, that assumption is incorrect.

During the call, Chaudhry used an analogy that everyone can understand. You can own the world’s most reliable car and service it religiously, yet you still buy insurance for other risks not covered by the warranty, such as theft or a tree falling on it. Having insurance and knowing when and how to use it helps you get back on the road quickly. Zscaler has built the cyber equivalent.

In the real world, people understand it. In cyber and digital, we seem to forget and rely on service-level agreements. A 99.999% uptime commitment sounds good until you translate it into business terms. Chaudhry said some of Zscaler’s largest banking customers told the company that five nines wasn’t enough, “because we could lose hundreds of millions of dollars if you went down even for five minutes.”

Going back to my IT days, I’ve never liked SLAs because they are financial instruments, not operational ones. They tell you what credit you’ll receive after the fact, not how you’ll keep processing payments, as Chase customers learned, or how you’ll keep planes in the air, as United learned. Regulators have recognized this. The EU’s Digital Operational Resilience Act and Australia’s CPS 230 both require regulated firms to assess, test, and mitigate the risk posed by their technology providers. “Our cloud provider went down” is no longer an acceptable defense.

IT executives should stop asking, “What’s our provider’s SLA?” and start asking, “What must our business continue to do when a critical dependency fails, and have we proven we can do so?”

The instinctive response to an outage like Microsoft’s is to buy from a second provider. Chaudhry shared a story about a chief information officer whose CEO had flagged Office 365 as a business risk and told him to find an alternative. The CIO signed up for Google Workspace. When asked whether documents, links and role-based access controls would work after a switch, even in half the cases, he said he didn’t think so.

That’s the reality. Email alone is hard enough because users lose their history the moment they switch. Modern productivity suites aren’t storage anymore. Every email includes links to shared documents, permissions are tied to identity, and workflows span multiple apps. Kuperman framed the problem in terms of scale: “I can switch between Gmail and Outlook, but can 10,000 people? Will they be as productive?”

The same problem applies in security and networking, where the stakes are arguably higher. The vendor A/vendor B model requires two policy sets kept in perfect sync, two client software sets and a way to move tens of thousands of users and devices from one to the other in the middle of a crisis. Kuperman described one customer for whom it “used to take seven days to switch over and 30 days to switch back. You can’t run a business like that.”

A backup that’s never tested at full scale isn’t a backup. It’s a hope. And a backup that changes the user experience will fail exactly when it’s needed.

Another instinct is to turn off security entirely; however, when a crisis occurs, threat actors will rally and launch campaigns. During the CrowdStrike outage, phishing campaigns were mobilized almost immediately, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency had to issue warnings not to take the bait. Threat actors are present both internally and externally, so security must remain on guard during critical failures, especially when they are publicly known.

This brings me to what Zscaler has done with its Business Continuity Cloud and why I think it’s the right template for the industry. Rather than asking customers to bolt on a second vendor, Zscaler built a dedicated, per-customer environment that’s architecturally separate from its primary Zero Trust Exchange.

The design choices are important to understand. The Business Continuity Cloud runs in third-party data centers, not Zscaler’s own, on separate networks, autonomous system numbers, DNS, and cloud domains. Software and threat-intelligence updates are deliberately staggered so a bad production release can’t land in the backup at the same time. Policy and identity data sync one way into a read-only, last-known-good state. It’s offered across nine regions, enough to keep operations in-country if a nation were cut off.

“No linkage — no network, no shared routers, no switches, no shared network operations,” Chaudhry said. That’s the old production/DR discipline, rebuilt for the cloud. After watching overloaded routers ground the nation’s air traffic, “no shared routers” doesn’t sound like overkill.

There were two operational details I felt were worth noting. First, Zscaler encourages customers to continuously route synthetic or trusted-user traffic through the backup environment in peacetime, so the failover path is validated daily rather than in an annual tabletop exercise. Second, the failover is automated to optimize for a low recovery time objective or RTO, or it can be triggered by the customer, ensuring it works even if Zscaler itself is unreachable.

Zscaler says nearly 100 customers now use its service, including a global bank with more than 300,000 users, a global pharmaceutical company with more than 100,000, and a U.S. telco with more than 75,000. The company charges what Chaudhry called a nominal fee to cover the dedicated infrastructure, network and always-on capacity.

The lesson from the Microsoft outage, in particular, isn’t that customers need a second productivity suite. It’s that the primary provider should offer a fate-separated continuity environment as part of the service. Zscaler has shown it can be done for a global security cloud. I’d like to see every SaaS provider that sits in a company’s critical path, and Microsoft in particular, be pressed by large customers to offer the same.

The Microsoft outage also exposed a concentration risk that many companies have faced through enterprise licensing agreements. Microsoft said the incident affected not only Exchange and Teams but also Defender XDR, Defender for Office 365 and Intune. For many organizations, Microsoft is the productivity suite, the identity provider and the security stack. When the shared infrastructure beneath them fails, all three can fail together.

Kuperman described the minimum set of capabilities a business needs to keep operating during a disaster: people, identity, network and security, and business-critical applications. Each must work, and any one can fail. “You have to think about where your eggs are and which baskets they’re in,” he said.

I’m not arguing against platforms. But boards should understand where consolidation has created a single point of failure across identity, applications and security, and ensure those layers don’t share the same fate.

This won’t be the last major outage, and the next one may be a cyberattack, a war, or a configuration push rather than a dormant bug. Here’s what I recommend IT and business leaders do now:

The cloud delivered on its promise of agility and scale, but in the process, the industry let a hard-won discipline lapse. This past week reminded us that everything fails eventually, whether in the cloud, a data center or an air traffic control tower. When it does, an SLA credit won’t keep the business running. A real continuity plan will.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5589. Scientists discover a common sugar may help cancer cells break free and spread

A common sugar found in many foods and sweetened drinks may play an unexpected role in helping aggressive ovarian cancer spread. Researchers at The Wistar Institute have discovered that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy can release fructose, which acts as a signal that encourages nearby tumor cells to break free and spread.

The findings, published in Nature Aging, reveal a previously unknown way that cancer cells can continue influencing a tumor even after treatment has stopped them from multiplying. The discovery also raises important questions about whether dietary sugar and commonly prescribed cholesterol medications could affect how cancer progresses.

"Some cancer cells that survive chemotherapy aren't dividing anymore, but they're still biologically active," said Aidan Cole, Ph.D., a postdoctoral fellow in the lab of Katherine Aird, Ph.D., at The Wistar Institute and first author on the study. "Instead, they continue to release molecules that send signals to nearby cells. Our study is among the first to show that a nutrient -- in this case, fructose -- can act as one of those signals."

Why Ovarian Cancer Often Returns After Chemotherapy

Most patients with ovarian cancer receive platinum-based chemotherapy, a treatment that uses drugs containing platinum to damage the DNA of cancer cells and prevent them from reproducing. Although many patients initially respond well, the cancer eventually returns in most cases. It also frequently spreads throughout the abdominal cavity, the space inside the abdomen that contains organs such as the stomach, intestines, and liver.

This spread, known as metastasis, is responsible for approximately 90% of ovarian cancer deaths. Understanding what allows cancer cells to escape from their original location and establish new tumors is therefore a major priority for researchers.

Previous studies have suggested that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy may contribute to recurrence even when they are no longer actively dividing. These surviving cells can continue producing and releasing a mixture of substances that influence the behavior of surrounding cells.

To investigate this process, Cole and his colleagues developed an experiment that separated the surviving cancer cells from the molecules they released. They discovered that these released substances, even without the surviving cells themselves, were enough to significantly increase cancer spread in a preclinical model.

"As far as we know, this is the first time anyone has shown, in a preclinical model rather than just a dish, that it's the molecules these cells release -- not the cells themselves -- that drive the cancer's spread," said Cole.

A Common Sugar Emerges as a Surprising Cancer Signal

The next challenge was identifying which substances were responsible for encouraging cancer cells to spread. The researchers discovered an unexpected culprit: fructose.

Fructose is a naturally occurring sugar found in fruit, honey, and other foods. It is also a component of table sugar and high fructose corn syrup, a sweetener frequently used in soft drinks and processed foods.

The study revealed that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy could produce fructose and release it into their surroundings. Rather than simply serving as an energy source, the sugar acted as a chemical messenger that encouraged neighboring cancer cells to become more capable of spreading.

The researchers also uncovered another concerning possibility. In their preclinical experiments, consuming high amounts of fructose comparable to those found in sugary drinks could promote signals associated with cancer spread even without chemotherapy treatment.

This observation suggests that diet might influence cancer progression through a mechanism scientists had not previously recognized. Fructose consumption is particularly relevant in the United States, where high fructose corn syrup can account for approximately 8% to 20% of daily calorie intake in some individuals.

Unlike many factors that influence cancer risk and progression, dietary fructose intake can be changed. That raises the possibility that nutritional strategies might eventually become part of efforts to limit cancer spread.

However, researchers have not yet tested whether reducing fructose consumption improves outcomes in patients with ovarian cancer. The findings do not establish that eating sugar causes cancer to spread in humans, and additional research is needed before specific dietary recommendations can be made based on this mechanism.

How Fructose Helps Cancer Cells Break Free

To understand how fructose encourages cancer spread, the researchers examined what happens inside cancer cells exposed to the sugar.

They used several advanced methods to investigate the biological changes involved, including a CRISPR screen. This technique allows scientists to systematically examine genes and identify which ones influence a particular cellular process.

The experiments revealed that fructose suppresses cholesterol production in neighboring cancer cells.

Although cholesterol is often discussed in connection with heart disease, it also serves essential functions throughout the body. It is an important component of cell membranes, the thin outer layers that surround cells and help regulate how they interact with their environment.

In this case, cholesterol helps maintain the connections that hold neighboring cells together. These connections act somewhat like biological glue, making it harder for cancer cells to separate from one another.

When fructose reduces cholesterol production, those connections weaken. As a result, cancer cells can detach more easily, potentially allowing them to escape and spread to other locations.

This discovery provides a possible explanation for how a common nutrient can influence one of the most dangerous aspects of cancer.

A Surprising Connection Between Statins and Cancer Spread

The cholesterol finding also led researchers to investigate an unexpected question involving statins, medications widely prescribed to lower cholesterol.

Approximately 39 million people in the United States take statins. These drugs work by reducing the body's production of cholesterol and are commonly used to lower the risk of heart attacks and strokes.

Because fructose appeared to promote cancer spread by suppressing cholesterol production, the research team wanted to know whether statins might produce similar effects.

Their experiments showed that statins alone could weaken the connections between cancer cells, making it easier for them to separate and escape.

The finding raises questions about whether cholesterol-lowering medications could influence the effectiveness of chemotherapy in certain situations. Researchers are now investigating that possibility, but they emphasize that the results have not been demonstrated in patients and are not a reason for anyone to discontinue prescribed statins.

"We haven't tested this effect in patients yet, but it raises questions about combining cholesterol-lowering drugs with chemotherapy, especially since ovarian cancer is most common in postmenopausal women who are often already on statins," said Katherine Aird, Ph.D., professor and co-leader of the Molecular and Cellular Oncogenesis Program in the Ellen and Ronald Caplan Cancer Center at The Wistar Institute, and senior author of the study.

Could Fructose Also Help Other Cancers Spread?

Although the research focused on ovarian cancer, the scientists suspect that the same biological process could occur in other forms of the disease.

Cancers affecting organs within the abdomen and torso can also spread to nearby tissues and organs. If fructose influences the connections between cancer cells in a similar way, the discovery could have implications beyond ovarian cancer.

"We think other cancers that spread within the torso -- pancreatic, colon, liver -- could behave similarly. We can't call it universal yet, but we think the effects are not just limited to ovarian cancer," said Aird.

Aird and Cole have already begun designing additional experiments to determine whether their findings can be reproduced in pancreatic, colon, liver, and other cancers.

The research opens a new avenue for understanding how cancer spreads, particularly after chemotherapy. It also suggests that the relationship between nutrients, cholesterol production, and cancer cell behavior may be more complicated than previously understood.

While the potential implications for diet and medication remain uncertain, identifying fructose as a signal that helps cancer cells break free could eventually point researchers toward new strategies for preventing metastasis and improving cancer treatment.

Materials provided by The Wistar Institute. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
