A $29.5 million residence spanning an entire floor of the Ritz-Carlton Hotel has hit the market in New York City.

Measuring 5,724 square feet—which is nearly three times the median in its ZIP code—Residence 29 at 50 Central Park South is one of the city’s “most prestigious addresses,” according to listing agent Zina Raslan of the Gambino Group at Compass.

The five-bedroom, five-plus-bathroom dwelling is one of only a dozen permanent residences exclusive to the hotel. And while it’s accessible through a private elevator vestibule, it offers a unique perk that’s also available to Ritz-Carlton guests.

“You can order room service from your very own home,” Raslan confirmed.

With ample east- and west-facing windows found throughout the home, the skyline and Central Park views are absolutely spectacular. There are even two private terraces that look over the park—one for dining and one for lounging.

“These spaces give you a reason to really pause and enjoy the setting of New York City,” Raslan said, conjuring ideas of “morning coffee overlooking the greenery of Central Park” or “dinner outside as the lights change.”

The residence is an excellent spot for hosting, with three dining areas—a formal dining room, a casual breakfast nook, and the aforementioned outdoor space—all connected by a seamless flow from the gorgeous Calacatta marble kitchen.

A unique solarium serves as a light-flooded space to relax, separate from the rest of the home.

“You are truly in the heart of New York City. You have Central Park at your doorstep, Fifth Avenue moments away, and everything that makes New York extraordinary around you,” Raslan said.

#5547. Sovereignty is the AI story everyone mentions and few have planned for ahead of 2027

AI infrastructure economics are entering a more sober phase as enterprises move past standing up AI factories and start asking how to run them profitably. Durability, real demand and long-term value are now the tests separating lasting providers from the froth.

That shift rewards cloud providers with an operating track record rather than a single speculative wager. Vultr has extended its global cloud to AI with chips from Nvidia Corp. and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. Enterprises are now making a flight to quality toward stable, cost-efficient platforms, according to Kevin Cochrane (pictured), chief marketing officer of Vultr.

“We’re seeing now not speculative bets in the buildout of AI infrastructure. We’re seeing real bets based on proven economics, proven ROI that people are looking to achieve,” Cochrane said. “What I think is going to wind up happening is a maturation of our industry leveraging this open stack.”

Cochrane spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how AI infrastructure economics favor a global footprint and why sovereignty requirements reach well beyond national governments. (* Disclosure below.)

Vultr now operates 34 cloud data center regions, the latest a new region in Chennai, India. That footprint was built to keep cloud-native applications close to users, and inference follows the same logic, Cochrane explained. Agents make fast turns back to reasoning models, so CPUs and GPUs must sit together near the edge, he noted.

“This is kind of what Vultr was built for, which is one global platform, not isolated islands of data centers that are serving a bespoke customer. It is a true global cloud platform,” Cochrane said.

Sovereignty adds another constraint, and it reaches well beyond national governments. A global insurer tuning an open-source model for credit risk needs training clusters in each country because the underlying data cannot cross borders, Cochrane noted. Regulators are already tightening the rules, as the U.S. Commerce Department’s new curbs on remote chip access show.

“The way you have to post-train a model for credit risk in the U.K. versus Germany versus Singapore versus the United States, it’s going to be different,” Cochrane said. “It uses different data.”

#5545. Anthropic’s Backers Have Another Big Bet: Americans Staying Renters

Anthropic’s stock market debut on Thursday is expected to value the artificial intelligence company at $1.5 trillion, putting some of Wall Street’s biggest investment firms in line to cash in from its rapid rise.

In its pitch to investors, the maker of Claude offers a vision far grander than the 2,800 millionaires the IPO is expected to mint. AI, it says, could “significantly accelerate global growth and dramatically improve quality of life for people around the world.”

But some of its backers are making another bet on a future where renting dominates the housing market.

Among them are Blackstone and Brookfield, two investment giants whose portfolios extend from emerging technologies to the nation's housing stock.

“Amidst continued macroeconomic uncertainty, we believe rental housing is the number one thing you want to own,” reads a 2025 shareholder update from Blackstone Real Estate Income Trust, known as BREIT.

Under a heading touting Blackstone Real Estate’s “Best Ideas,” the fund pointed to record homeownership costs, sluggish construction, and a national shortage of 4 million to 5 million homes. It called those conditions “powerful tailwinds” for its rental housing investments.

To housing advocates, though, those tailwinds are precisely the headwinds they’re working to reverse, says Jordan Ash, housing director at the nonprofit watchdog Private Equity Stakeholder Project.

The investment thesis anticipates a future in which “there are many more people who are just going to be renters for life,” Ash tells Realtor.com®.

“The renter is not their customer,” he says of large private equity landlords. “They're accountable to their investors.”

And now, the rental market is showing signs of turning in those investors’ favor.

Median asking rents rose 0.1% in October—the first annual increase since June 2023—across the 50 largest metros, according to Realtor.com research. The increase was small, but it came as the apartment construction boom that helped hold rents down began to fade.

Meanwhile, households that might otherwise leave the rental market face a steep price for becoming homeowners.

Mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, roughly double their 3.69% level in October 2019, notes Realtor.com senior economist Jiayi Xu.

“Elevated mortgage rates are one of the key barriers to homeownership, because they significantly raise the monthly cost of buying,” she explains. Higher ownership expenses have added to the burden.

That financial hurdle is apparent in Dallas–Fort Worth, TX, where Blackstone owns rental homes through Tricon, the operator it acquired in 2024.

Across the metro, the median monthly cost of buying a starter home was $2,741 in October, compared with $1,471 to rent, according to data from Realtor.com. That means making the leap to homeownership would involve finding an additional $1,270 in the monthly budget—after also coming up with a down payment.

It's easy to understand the bet then—with a gap that wide, who would ever be able to afford the jump?

Washington has tried to make that leap easier by limiting buyers’ competition from Wall Street. Following President Donald Trump’s January executive order, Congress enacted restrictions on additional single-family home purchases by institutional investors controlling at least 350 such homes. The ban takes effect on Jan. 7, 2027, with exceptions that include qualifying build-to-rent projects.

But limiting competition from investors does not, by itself, close the monthly gap between renting and owning. And while that gap gives households a reason to keep renting, BREIT expects declining construction to give landlords more room to raise rents.

“Ultimately, lower supply should support rent growth and real estate values over time,” the fund wrote in its Nov. 4 shareholder update, which did not address the institutional investor ban.

Of course, that outcome isn’t assured. Although the multifamily construction pipeline has shrunk from its peak, it remains large by pre-pandemic standards, Xu says. Projects already underway could continue giving tenants more options.

Even so, “If new multifamily deliveries cannot keep pace with rental demand, we expect rents to rise,” she says.

But even buying a home doesn't always end the relationship with a landlord.

Ash points to Brookfield’s acquisition of YES Communities, an operator of manufactured-home communities where residents can own their houses while paying rent for the land beneath them.

Residents’ complaints about rising costs and neglected maintenance predated Brookfield’s purchase. And as the deal approached, some appealed directly to pension funds invested with the firm, seeking assurances that a new owner would improve their circumstances.

“The rent just keeps going up, but no improvements have been made,” Michigan resident Abbie Pedrotte told University of California regents, according to Ash’s reporting.

By October, those concerns had reached Congress.

In an Oct. 13 letter, Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-MI) and two colleagues pressed Brookfield about its plans. They asked whether it intended to raise home and lot rents by more than 3% annually and whether it would cooperate with residents seeking to purchase their parks. Written answers were requested by Nov. 20.

For its part, Brookfield’s published strategy calls for increasing resident homeownership and expanding tenant programs to “boost operating income and retention.” Owning the house can give a resident a stake in the community while preserving the landlord’s income from the land.

“We own the appreciating part of real estate. It’s fantastic,” Lowell Baron, CEO of Brookfield’s real estate business, told investors in September.

Some of the firms betting on continued demand for rentals are also financing a construction boom of their own.

BREIT had deployed more than $9 billion into data center developments in 2026 by its November shareholder update, helping expand the infrastructure supporting AI and cloud computing.

Blackstone has already identified a potential cost for other real estate—including homebuilding.

On its October earnings call, President Jon Gray said rising construction costs and limited new supply were being intensified by higher interest rates and “crowding out from the AI infrastructure build.”

A construction industry survey offers evidence of that competition. Among firms reporting on data center projects’ workforce effects, 58% cited increased competition for skilled workers, while 49% reported greater wage pressure, according to the 2026 AGC/NCCER Workforce Survey.

Xu cautions against treating those findings as a measure of the impact on homebuilding.

“The survey points to labor pressure where data centers are concentrated, but it does not isolate AI investment from factors like immigration enforcement and tariffs, nor does it directly measure residential construction costs,” she explains.

And to their credit, the private equity firms are also moving to help finance additional housing. Blackstone launched a homebuilder lending platform in May that it expects to support more than 50,000 new for-sale homes annually.

Buying existing homes changes ownership without adding to the housing stock, Xu explains.

“Financing new construction, by contrast, increases the stock, which is the key to expanding supply and improving affordability for both groups,” she says.

Anthropic’s backers have capital to help build the future they describe. Households waiting for a more affordable home need some of that future to include them.

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#5543. Mortgage Applications Dip as Rates Hit Three-Week High

House keys with a house shaped keychain resting on a mortgage application form

Mortgage applications dipped slightly this week, in keeping with the average 30-year mortgage rate rising to a three-week high.

The latest Market Composite Index from the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA)—its measure of mortgage loan activity volume and includes purchases and refinances—shows mortgage application activity decreasing 2.3% on a seasonally adjusted basis after last week’s 6.2% increase. On an unadjusted basis, the Index decreased 5% compared with the previous week.

This week’s decline follows weeks of fluctuations as the 30-year fixed mortgage rate still solidly remains over 7%–last week decreasing to 7.11% according to Freddie Mac but currently sitting at 7.46%, according to Mortgage News Daily. Freddie Mac’s next rate report will be released Thursday.

“Mortgage applications dipped as mortgage rates moved higher, with the 30-year fixed mortgage rate up to its highest level in three weeks at 7.35 percent,” said Joel Kan, CMB, MBA’s vice president and deputy chief economist. “Purchase applications were down 18 percent from a year ago, as renewed affordability challenges from elevated mortgage rates have pushed prospective homebuyers to the sidelines.”

MBA’s Refinance Index decreased 2% from the previous week and was 54% lower than the same week one year ago. MBA’s seasonally adjusted Purchase Index–its weekly measurement of nationwide home loan applications based on a sample of about 75% of U.S. mortgage activity–decreased 3% from one week earlier. The unadjusted Purchase Index decreased 7% compared with the previous week and was 18% lower than the same week one year ago, according to the report.

The refinance share of mortgage activity saw an increase this week–to 41.1% from 39.8% the previous week, with Kan pointing to a rise in FHA refinances as most notable.

“Overall refinance activity was down over the week, but FHA refinances increased almost 7 percent,” Kan stated. “The FHA rate was around 30 basis points below the conforming rate, which supported refinance opportunities for some homeowners.”

The FHA share of total applications increased to 16.1% from 15.5% the week prior, with MBA listing the VA share of total applications increasing to 12.8% from 12.4% the week prior. The USDA share of total applications remained unchanged at 0.5 percent from the week prior.

Kan also pointed to additional macroeconomic indicators as potentially weighing on home-purchase application activity into the new year.

“Treasury yields rose last week amid data showing inflation accelerated in October and Fed officials acknowledging that additional rate hikes may be needed in the coming months,” he said.

#5542. Lot Supply Rises for Ninth Consecutive Quarter

The supply of vacant developed lots continued to loosen in the third quarter as slower construction activity brought the national lot market further into balance, according to Zonda.

Zonda’s New Home Lot Supply Index rose to 88.5 in the third quarter, up 20.8% from a year earlier and 3.9% from the second quarter. It marked the ninth consecutive quarterly increase in the index.

The index measures the supply of single-family vacant developed lots relative to the rate at which builders absorb those lots through housing starts. Zonda rated the national market “appropriately supplied” in the third quarter.

In the second quarter, the index sat at the boundary between “slightly undersupplied” and “appropriately supplied.” The third-quarter increase placed the national market in the latter category.

“The national lot market is moving more firmly into balance,” says Sean Fergus, vice president of economic research for Zonda. “But that balance needs to be viewed in the context of today’s housing market.”

Fergus noted that affordability pressures and widespread incentives continue to challenge builders’ ability to convert demand into sales. An appropriately supplied lot market indicates that lot availability is better aligned with the current pace of construction, he said, but does not mean the industry’s longer-term land constraints and cost pressures have disappeared.

Lot supply increased year over year in every major metropolitan area tracked by Zonda except Boise, Idaho. Among the markets where supply increased, the average annual gain was 32%.

Baltimore, Portland, and Seattle posted the largest year-over-year increases in lot supply. Boise was the only market where supply tightened, with its index falling from 65.7 in the third quarter of 2025 to 51.9.

Despite the broader improvement in availability, 12 of the 30 markets tracked by Zonda remained “significantly undersupplied.” Eight markets changed supply ratings during the quarter, Zonda points out.

Zonda also reported a modest increase in the future lot pipeline. Total upcoming lots increased 1% year over year and 1.6% from the second quarter.

Upcoming lots include properties in the later stages of development that are typically expected to become vacant developed lots within 12 to 18 months.

The increase suggests additional lots are moving toward delivery, although the pipeline is expanding much more slowly than the current supply index. The divergence reflects the role of softer starts in loosening lot conditions: available lots are lasting longer as builders respond to weaker demand and elevated mortgage rates.

#5540. Metano launches with $12M to help enterprises secure AI agents

Artificial intelligence agent security startup Metano Inc. today launched with $12 million in funding to help enterprises secure AI agents across endpoints, cloud infrastructure and software-as-a-service applications.

Metano’s platform is aimed at giving enterprises consistent visibility and control over AI agents, bringing together agent discovery, context-aware threat detection and real-time enforcement in a single layer.

It’s seeking to address the issue wherein security teams face a growing and fragmented attack surface as organizations deploy AI agents across devices, coding environments, cloud infrastructure and SaaS applications. Metano argues that existing security products protect individual infrastructure layers but lack the visibility and behavioral context needed to secure autonomous agents operating across them.

Making the problem harder is that AI agents, which often run with legitimate credentials and approved tools, can make decisions and take actions dynamically. Instructions, external content and operating conditions can all change how an agent behaves, according to Metano, introducing risks that may not be apparent during initial testing.

“Traditional security tools weren’t designed for AI agents that can make decisions and change their behavior as they operate,” Chief Executive Neelima Rustagi explained.

The first part of Metano’s offering is discovery, with the platform identifying approved and unapproved AI agents, Model Context Protocol servers, skills and software packages, along with their access privileges and potential security exposure.

The second part is Hive, Metano’s real-time context graph, which connects agent tasks, identities, tools, data access and actions. By analyzing activity across an entire session, Hive identifies suspicious behavior and determines whether an agent’s actions align with its intended purpose, allowing security teams to understand why an agent’s behavior may pose a risk.

Metano also offers enforcement as the third part of its platform, placing security controls wherever agents operate. Security teams are given centrally managed policies and guardrails to stop dangerous actions as they occur, even when an agent’s activity may bypass traditional network gateways.

The platform’s detections draw on research from MARS Labs, Metano’s own AI security research team. Malicious skills, compromised software dependencies and vulnerabilities in MCP connections are among the threats the group investigates. The company says its agent detections are mapped to MITRE ATLAS and the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications.

Rustagi co-founded the company with Chief Technology Officer Ratnesh Pandey. The Metano team also brings security experience from ServiceNow Inc., Zscaler Inc., Palo Alto Networks Inc., FireEye Inc. and Microsoft Corp.

Among the companies already using the platform is data engineering firm Streamvector Inc., which does business as Sigmoid. Srivatsa Ramarao, Sigmoid’s chief information security officer, said Metano has helped Sigmoid adopt AI securely while minimizing shadow risks, allowing it to “say yes to AI across the business.”

Sierra Ventures led the seed round, with Correlation Ventures, High Alpha and 360 ONE also participating. According to Mark Fernandes, managing partner at Sierra Ventures, every platform shift in security produces a few companies that “own the new control point,” with agents representing one of the biggest disruptions he has seen.

Metano’s platform is generally available now, and the company claims security teams can begin using it in under 30 minutes. Also on offer is a free Eval Edition, which provides 30 days of real-time agent scanning so security teams can identify agent activity, risky configurations and potential exposure in their own environments. Metano has completed a SOC 2 Type 2 examination and holds ISO 27001:2022 certification, along with a listing on Okta Inc.’s Okta Integration Network.

#5539. Home Prices Hold Steady as Sales Drop and Inventory Expands

Home prices remained relatively resilient in October despite a sharp slowdown in sales and continued growth in available inventory.

The national median sale price was $383,598, down 0.4% from October 2025, according to the latest housing market analysis from Homes.com. Home sales fell 11.7% year over year while inventory increased 4.8%.

The combination gave buyers more choices even as elevated mortgage rates limited demand while sellers faced greater competition for the smaller pool of buyers prepared to purchase.

“October’s results tell a more nuanced story than the nearly flat national price number alone would suggest,” says Brad Case, chief residential economist at Homes.com. “Sales were down substantially from a year ago even as buyers had more homes to choose from, yet prices barely moved. That suggests demand remains strong, but buyers appear increasingly selective about which homes they choose to purchase.”

Single-family homes posted the smallest annual price decline among the property types tracked by Homes.com. The median price declined 0.3% from October 2025, compared with 1.4% declines for both townhomes and condominiums.

Single-family sales fell 11.2% year over year, while inventory increased 5%. Townhome sales dropped 13.5% as inventory grew 5.3%, and condo sales fell 15.1% while inventory increased 3.6%.

The figures point to a market where additional inventory has yet to translate into significant national price declines, particularly for single-family homes, Homes.com points out.

The relatively flat national median masks significant differences among major housing markets. Among the 40 largest markets tracked, 10 posted annual price gains of at least 2%, while nine recorded declines of 2% or more.

San Francisco posted the largest highlighted gain, with its median sale price rising 17.7% year over year despite a 13% decline in sales. Jacksonville prices increased 6.1% even as sales fell 14.4%. On the opposite hand, Austin recorded a 9.7% annual price decline, followed by a 4.1% decrease in Nashville.

Inventory trends also varied widely. Seattle had 22.8% more homes for sale than a year earlier, while inventory in Jacksonville was 9.8% lower.

#5538. Hosting Guests Is Reshaping What Americans Want in a Home

Hosting friends and family may be doing more than filling the house. It’s also changing the way Americans think about what they want from their homes.

A new survey commissioned by KB Home found 58% of Americans say hosting guests has made them rethink what they want in their current or future home. The research, conducted by Talker Research, surveyed 2,000 U.S. adults in October.

Gathering spaces emerged as particularly important when respondents considered what makes a home comfortable for holiday hosting and special occasions. Open living areas led the list, selected by 35% of Americans, followed by outdoor entertaining spaces at 30%.

Kitchens also figured prominently. Twenty-four percent prioritized a spacious kitchen, while 21% selected an open kitchen. Another 21% pointed to a large or dedicated dining space.

“Hosting friends and family can highlight what people love about their homes and what they wish worked better,” says Gena Kirk, vice president of corporate design at KB Home. “From spacious living areas and open floor plans to finishes that reflect personal style, a KB home works for everyday life as well as special occasions.”

Having guests over also appears to sharpen homeowners’ perceptions of their existing spaces.

Nearly one-third of hosts, 31%, said entertaining makes them think about ways to make their homes more welcoming or comfortable, and 25% said it makes them want to declutter or clean more often.

The experience isn’t always positive. While 29% of hosts said entertaining makes them feel proud of their homes, 20% said it makes them self-conscious and 24% notice things they would like to change.

Shared spaces receive much of that scrutiny before guests arrive. Among hosts, 45% said they focus most on tidying the living room, followed by bathrooms at 35% and kitchens at 31%.

For builders, the findings reinforce the continued importance of flexible gathering spaces that can serve both everyday life and larger get-togethers. They also point to the role kitchens, outdoor areas, and living rooms play not simply as individual rooms but as interconnected entertaining spaces.

Talker Research conducted the online survey for KB Home between Oct. 9 and Oct. 13 among 2,000 U.S. adults with internet access.

#5537. Anthropic’s Blockbuster IPO Set To Spark a New San Francisco Housing Frenzy: ‘Expect More All-Cash Offers’ and Bidding Wars

Real estate agents in San Francisco are bracing for further acceleration of the housing market as Anthropic makes an initial public offering at a reported valuation of $1.5 trillion.

The Bay Area has been a hot spot for newly wealthy AI trendsetters in recent years, rebuilding a market that was left hurting during the COVID-19 pandemic as tech offices emptied. With major AI companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic planting roots in San Francisco, the housing market has grown competitive, leading what some real estate agents are calling a “mansion shortage.”

Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO went live on Thursday, marking one of the largest public-market debuts in history.

The Claude developer, which will trade under the ticker ANT, initially said it planned to price shares at between $70 and $78, which would value the company at between $1.3 trillion and $1.45 trillion. Late Wednesday, The Wall Street Journal reported the company planned to debut at $83 per share, taking the valuation to $1.5 trillion.

In addition to the public offering, Anthropic is set to receive an extra $26 billion in a private placement sale of shares to several other major tech companies, including Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, and more, according to Yahoo Finance.

While employees and insiders won't see cash in hand until after a significant lockup period, the debut could give many early shareholders the confidence to move forward with real estate purchases.

“Confidence may change before purchasing power does. There are lockup periods, taxes, and individual circumstances to consider, so I wouldn’t expect everyone to start buying houses the following week,” San Francisco real estate agent and founder of Vivre Real Estate, Danielle Lazier, tells Realtor.com®. “But the anticipation has already motivated some buyers to act because they’re concerned about competing with more AI money later.”

This will not be the first IPO debut that Lazier has worked through, so she knows how the influx of confidence and wealth can push people toward real estate investments. Even tech companies that hit major milestones without going public can lead to major shifts in local spending.

“Having worked here through Google, Facebook, and other IPOs, I’ve seen how that wealth can move into housing as people diversify and make longer-term plans,” says Lazier. “OpenAI hasn’t gone public, but its private stock sales have already helped employees buy homes.”

The AI boom has already significantly reshaped the housing market in the Bay Area. Realtor.com research found that elevated down payments in the Bay Area, when compared to key comparison markets like Miami, New York City, and Austin, TX, are evidence of the impact of AI wealth.

The study captured baseline down payment numbers from 2020 to 2022, when AI hadn’t yet taken hold and mortgage rates hadn’t spiked. When mortgage rates peaked in 2023 and buyers put more money down if able, down payments within the luxury home market rose between 3 and 8 percentage points in all four metros.

In the 2024–25 period, mortgage rates had eased, but the AI boom was in full swing. Down payments in Miami, New York City, and Austin all met or dropped below their pre-rate-shock level, but buyers in the Bay Area continued to put 6.6 percentage points more down to buy a home, showing clear evidence that AI equity had found its way into pockets and into real estate.

By 2026, the median down payment in counties considered to be AI hubs, including San Francisco, Santa Clara, and San Mateo, reached 25%, while median down payment in nearby nonhub counties of Alameda, Contra Costa, and Marin remained at 20%.

When applied to the AI-hub group’s median listing price of about $1.33 million, that 5-percentage-point difference translates to $61,180 in additional down payment, according to Realtor.com data.

The influx of new wealth has been compounded by a limited number of desirable homes, making the market fiercely competitive.

“Additional purchasing power is competing for a limited resource. We have very few spacious, finished homes with practical layouts in desirable location,” says Lazier. “Having the money to renovate doesn’t mean having the time or interest to manage a San Francisco construction project.”

The stunning seven-bedroom, 6.5-bathroom home hits all the marks: a beautiful view of the San Francisco Bay, a sport court in the back, and a 2007 renovation that combines its classic architecture with functional modern living.

It also comes with a $35 million asking price.

More competitive buyers could mean more bidding wars, but not every listing should expect that, according to Cameron Walker of Clever Real Estate.

“Expect more all-cash offers, shorter time on the market, and more bidding wars,” Walker tells Realtor.com. “But a hot market doesn’t mean everyone’s house will get overbid offers. The newly rich are discerning homebuyers, so expect well-priced houses to get multiple offers and overpriced houses to languish.”

Not everyone will be going after massive estates with flashy price tags. A comfortable home close to company offices and existing connections will see high demand.

Neighborhoods such as Noe Valley, Pacific Heights, Presidio Heights, and Cole Valley are ones to watch following Anthropic’s debut, according to Walker.

#5534. Family Found Dead in Foreclosed Home Survived Months Longer Than Previously Thought

New evidence suggests that at least one member of a family found dead inside a foreclosed-upon Connecticut home survived longer than previously thought—paving the way for transfer of title to a new owner.

The bizarre case hinges upon whether the home's owners died before or after the foreclosure was recorded. If the owners were already dead at the time of the filing, the foreclosure may be deemed illegitimate, and a search for rightful heirs would begin.

Edward Marchion stumbled into the mystery in June, when he purchased 7 Stanwich Lane, a four-bedroom, three-bathroom home in Burlington, CT, in a foreclosure auction for $525,000. The 2,800-square-foot home sits on more than 2 acres and comes with a hot tub, patio, and deck, according to the listing.

A few days after placing the winning bid, Marchion finally entered the property and came across a grisly sight. The skeletal remains of the property’s previous owners, Sally Anne Cash and Paul Cash, and their adult son Brian Cash, were found inside.

Marchion then asked a judge to halt the closing on the property to determine the timeline of the Cashs’ deaths.

In a July 2 filing in the state Supreme Court, Marchion’s lawyer John C. Lewis III asked the court to delay closing until the Connecticut State Police could determine whether the Cash family died before or after the foreclosure action.

"From a title perspective, unless it can be determined that the Defendants were alive on the date the lis pendens was recorded (August 6, 2025), then the foreclosure action is defective," wrote Lewis.

Now, months later, new evidence from the family’s probate attorney and state medical examiner’s office shows that the family’s deaths likely took place long after the foreclosure paperwork was filed, paving the way for Marchion to receive title to the home.

Paul and Sally Ann Cash purchased 7 Stanwich Lane in 2019. At the time, they took out a $385,000 mortgage on the property. But court records filed by their mortgage servicer showed that the couple stopped making monthly mortgage payments in December 2024. Shellpoint Mortgage Servicing filed a notice of foreclosure on the property on Aug. 6, 2025.

When police entered the property this past June, they discovered Paul and Sally Ann in a second-floor bedroom and Brian Cash in a bedroom above the garage. All three were found in sleeping bags and wearing multiple layers of clothing.

The home was packed with clutter and garbage bags, but authorities said the only food found in the house was powdered milk.

The family was known to have been extremely reclusive and the home’s interior reflected prolonged isolation and deprivation.

The exact cause of death is still being investigated, though authorities believe that either malnutrition or hypothermia were factors.

In late October, Shellpoint attorney Christopher Throgmartin filed a petition to request that proceeds from the sale of the property to Marchion be used to pay outstanding property taxes that accrued while the investigation was taking place. His petition also requested that Marchion be able to access the property in order to winterize and secure it at is own expense.

Two days later, the surviving relatives of the Cashes signed documents waiving their rights to 7 Stanwich Lane, further paving the way for the sale to Marchion to move forward.

Then, in an affidavit filed on Nov. 10, Connecticut State Medical Examiner Dr. Mary Kate Schwerdt testified, “The condition of [Sally Ann Cash’s] internal organs, and the level of decomposition is consistent with a death that occurred after August 6, 2025.”

Dr. Melissa Pasquale, who completed the autopsy of Brian Cash, testified that he also died sometime after August 6, 2025. The Medical Examiner’s office believes that Paul Cash died first.

Mary Anne Charron, the probate lawyer appointed as estate examiner for Sally Ann and Brian Cash by the Farmington Regional Probate Court, filed an affidavit stating that “In the course of the investigation, I discovered numerous electronic devices, including multiple laptops, flash drives, hard drives, several phones, a camera, as well as thousands of writings which appear to be journal entries, many of which include dates and time of entry.”

Charron said she found entries believed to be Sally Ann’s, dated August, September, October, and November 2025. She also found outgoing text messages dated from September and October 2025. The last known phone activity Charron documented was dated Dec. 16, 2025, roughly a year after the Cashes stopped paying their mortgage.

"Based on the dates of the journal entries, text chains and screenshots on cell phones, as well as correspondence with the Medical Examiner regarding the level of decomposition of the bodies, it is apparent that Sally is the surviving spouse," Charron wrote in the court filing.

Realtor.com® reached out to Marchian’s lawyer, John C. Lewis III, for comment.

#5533. Exclusive: Fig Security partners with Elastic to show how data changes affect detection coverage

Security operations startup Fig Security Inc. today announced an integration partnership with Elastic N.V. that it says gives security teams visibility into how data changes affect their detection coverage.

The partnership sees Fig’s capabilities for mapping detection dependencies now integrating with Elastic Security, the open security operations platform from Elastic. The platform offers prebuilt integrations and detection rules to establish coverage from day one, with Fig claimed to help security operations engineers safeguard that coverage as their environments evolve.

Detection rules are dependent on data arriving in the structure they expect, including the fields and values needed to identify suspicious activity. According to Fig, those dependencies can break when changes are made in tools that the security team does not own. The resulting problem, which Fig calls drift, leaves rules active while the data feeding them is missing the information needed to catch an attack.

Once connected through a read-only application programming interface key, Fig’s Security Data Lineage feature maps an Elastic environment’s sources through pipelines, mappings and fields to the detection rules that use them. Any change to a source, pipeline or mapping is said to have Fig identify the affected detections, along with a suggested repair.

“Elastic gives security teams control over their data, and Fig gives them control over the engineering around it,” said Gal Shafir, co-founder and chief executive of Fig, who previously led global security architecture for Google Cloud Security. Teams are able to test each change against their own environment, he said, before shipping it as code.

Environments “never stop changing,” according to Jamie Hynds, director of product at Elastic, who said Fig traces those changes to the detection rules that depend on them so that SecOps teams can maintain their coverage.

Fig also works alongside Elastic’s Automatic Import and AI Agent, two features designed to help teams build new integrations and custom rules as their requirements grow. Changes tested in Fig against the organization’s own data can then be shipped as code using continuous integration and continuous delivery, with version control and one-click rollback included.

The integration is also aimed at organizations moving to Elastic Security from another security information and event management platform. After Elastic’s Automatic Migration has translated their existing detection rules, Fig checks each translated rule against the data available in Elastic ahead of cutover. Rules that need rework are flagged, with a recommended fix for each.

Founded in 2025 by Shafir, Nir Loya Dahan and Roy Haimof, Fig launched in March with $38 million in seed and Series A funding from Team8 and Ten Eleven Ventures. The company added an AI agent and software-style deployment tools to its platform in July.

The Fig and Elastic integration is available now, with demonstrations offered through Fig’s website.

#5532. How Will Amendment 3 Affect Florida Real Estate Sales? Experts Weigh in

Mortgage rates business concept of investment housing real estate interest rates 3d home appraisal. planning savings money of coins to buy a home concept for property ladder, mortgage, real estate.

(TNS)—Sweeping property tax cuts are on the horizon for some Florida homeowners following the passage of Amendment 3.

The measure will raise the statewide homestead exemption to $250,000 over the next two years. It will also place stricter limits on tax increases for all other properties.

But will it give Florida’s real estate market a leg up during tough economic times? Industry leaders are divided, with most taking a wait-and-see approach.

The total number of homes sold in the Tampa Bay metro area is down about 5.2% compared to this time last year. That’s according to the latest statistics from the Suncoast Tampa Association of Realtors.

Related: Before the election, data showed there was not a strong case for either the measure passing or failing.

Some real estate agents are urging out-of-state buyers to move before the end of the year to lock in tax savings. Anyone who moves after 2026 will have to wait five years to receive the full homestead exemption.

Corina Lessa Silva, president of the Suncoast Tampa Association of Realtors, said she’s not expecting a dramatic bump in sales over the next couple of months. You don’t have to buy a home to establish residency, she said; renting works, too.

Still, “If a big piece of that monthly payment—which is property tax—is going to be lowered…it could help more people get into homes in the long term,” Lessa Silva said.

Savings will vary widely. The nonpartisan nonprofit Florida Tax Watch estimates that by 2028, homestead property owners could save an average of $1,133 in Hillsborough County, $956 in Pinellas and $1,150 in Pasco.

For renters trying to break into the housing market, those savings probably aren’t enough to make up for the other costs of homeownership, said Lei Wedge, an assistant professor of finance at the University of South Florida’s Muma College of Business.

Freddie Mac pegs the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate at a steep 7.18%. The median price for a home in Tampa Bay is about $400,000, according to the Suncoast Tampa Association of Realtors.

“Just because your future property tax will be cheaper, it does not help you with your down payment right now,” said Wedge.

Though most of the focus has been on single-family homeowners, commercial property owners are bracing for major changes, too.

Bowen Arnold, principal of Tampa-based DDA Development, said in the past 3 or 4 years, he’s seen the taxes on commercial properties he owns shoot up more than 10% in some cases.

Under the new rules, local property appraisers cannot increase the assessed value of non-homestead properties by more than 5% per year.

But don’t expect to see a spike in commercial sales as a result, said Andrew Frey, a managing director at the commercial real estate firm JLL.

“This will be of zero benefit for the buyers, it’s just a windfall for the current owners,” he said.

The biggest question hanging in the air is how local governments will fill major funding gaps caused by these tax cuts.

One solution might be by increasing the millage rate used to calculate our tax bills. That would end up canceling out some of the savings promised to homesteaded property owners, while raising everyone else’s taxes in the process, Wedge said.

Developers could also end up shouldering greater costs if cities decide to charge higher impact fees or raise the cost of construction permits, said Arnold.

All this uncertainty could put a damper on commercial markets, said Frey. “Investors like predictability. It could cause investors to push pause for a while until these things are sorted out.”

Now, after revealing that doctors found cancer in his left kidney, the "Vanderpump Rules" alum is looking ahead to recovery following a five-hour surgery to remove the tumor.

Taylor, 47, took to Instagram on Nov. 18, to share his diagnosis, explaining that the discovery came after he was hospitalized with kidney stones in July.

A CT scan also showed a tumor on his left kidney. After a series of tests and appointments, he learned it was cancer—a revelation he had kept private for months.

"This is something I’ve kept private for the past few months because it’s been one of the scariest times of my life. Back in July, I woke up one morning in horrible pain and ended up in the hospital with kidney stones. What I thought was just a kidney stone turned into something I never imagined," he penned on his candid social media post.

He added, "My CT scan also showed a tumor on my left kidney. After many tests and appointments I found out it was cancer. I lost my father to cancer, so hearing that word just broke me. It put me in a really dark place. The hardest part was the waiting. Knowing there was a tumor growing inside me while trying to go about my life like everything was fine. It’s crazy how you can act like everything is normal when deep down you’re a mess."

The reality TV star revealed that he underwent a five-hour surgery and is awaiting the results.

"One thing this experience and the last couple years have taught me is when life gets really hard, you find out fast who’s really there for you. And believe me.. it’s been eye opening. While speaking to People about his diagnosis, Taylor told the outlet, “It’s been a really scary few months. The tumor was larger and deeper than originally expected, which made the surgery more complicated. The home has a masculine style, with natural wood accents and soft, neutral colors throughout. Taylor’s son, Cruz, whom he shares with ex-wife Brittany Cartwright, also appeared in the photos, looking at ease in the space.

Taylor said the home was made special for both of them, thanking RENWIL Decor for helping bring the rooms together.

The move followed a series of changes in Taylor’s personal life. Earlier in the year, he announced that he was moving into a new place, describing it as a “new chapter” and saying the move had gone smoothly.

By the time he shared the May photos, the house appeared furnished and lived in, with cozy touches that made it feel like a home for father and son.

Taylor’s latest update now gives that glimpse of domestic life a more emotional backdrop. He said he had kept the diagnosis to himself because the experience had been frightening.

His father, Ronald Cauchi, died from throat and esophageal cancer in 2017, and Taylor said hearing the word “cancer” brought him to a dark place.

More than anything, Taylor said, he wants to be healthy and present as Cruz grows up. He also thanked his girlfriend, Lori Krebs, for standing by him during the ordeal, saying her support had meant everything.

As he begins the next stage of recovery, Taylor said he is taking things “one day at a time.”

His new home reflects a fresh start he had been building with Cruz; the diagnosis has made his priorities clearer.

Taylor said the experience reminded him not to take his health for granted and to value the people who show up when life becomes difficult.

With the tumor removed and further results still pending, his attention is now on healing and being there for his son.

#5529. When AI Pulls the Comps, Make It Show Its Work

Happy African American real estate agent looking at some leaflets of a house for sale

RISMedia’s September 25 Newsmakers roundup, “Tech Sharpens Strategy: Staying Ahead With the Right Tools,” asked agents and executives which systems are actually helping them capture market share and demonstrate value to clients.

One answer stuck with me. Veroushka Volkert of ONE Sotheby’s International Realty described using AI to produce listing remarks and email campaigns almost instantly, and also to pull real-time comps and list-to-sale data.

Those are two very different jobs, and I think our industry is starting to treat them as one. When AI drafts listing remarks, a mistake is cheap. You read it, fix a sentence and move on. When AI hands you a comp set, or a number a client will base an offer on, a mistake is expensive, and it usually isn’t visible on the page. A paragraph that reads well and a figure that is wrong look exactly the same.

I’ve invested in rental property for more than 20 years and own 50+ units across five states. Most of my expensive lessons came from numbers that looked finished and weren’t. One offering memorandum for a Chicago six-unit described the building as fully occupied on page two. The rent roll, around page 25, showed five of the six units vacant. Nothing flags that unless someone, or something, is told to reconcile the two.

So here is a simple standard I’d suggest for any agent or broker bringing AI into conversations about value or income. Before a number goes in front of a client, you should be able to answer three questions about it. Where did it come from? A comp, a vacancy rate or a rent estimate should trace back to a source you could name out loud if the client asked. “The model said so” is not a source. A rent figure delivered as a single confident point is also less useful than a range, because markets rarely hand you one number.

Was the arithmetic actually done, or approximated? Language models are remarkable at writing and at reading documents. They are not reliable calculators. A DSCR or a cap rate that is approximately right is worthless to a lender, and a buyer who relies on it finds out at the worst possible moment. The tools worth trusting read with AI and calculate with plain math.

What did it leave out? This is the question that protects investor clients most. In most jurisdictions property taxes reset at the purchase price, so a cap rate built on the seller’s current tax bill is overstated before the buyer even closes.

Roofs, HVAC and other core systems need reserves tied to their age, not an assumption that nothing will break. Who pays the water bill can swing expenses by $500 to $1,000 per unit per year, and it is often buried deep in the documents.

An AI that only answers what you asked will share your blind spots. None of this is an argument against AI. Agents who use it well are going to look much sharper than those who don’t, especially to investor buyers who expect underwriting and not just marketing.

But the question RISMedia put to its Newsmakers was about demonstrating value, and in anything involving money, demonstrating value means showing your work. The next time a system gives you a comp or a projected return in seconds, ask it where each figure came from, and whether you can change an assumption and watch the answer move. If it can’t tell you, that’s your cue to slow down before your client does.

Disclosure: I am the founder and CEO of relea.ai, which builds underwriting software for multifamily investors and brokers. This letter is not about any one product, and the standard above applies to every tool, mine included.

Simon Asselin is the founder and CEO of relea.ai, which builds underwriting software for multifamily investors and brokers.

A Brooklyn apartment building adjacent to the site of last week's deadly building collapse is set to be demolished after city officials determined that it was unsafe to enter.

On Nov. 11, the three-story mixed-use building at 1321 Flatbush Ave. suddenly collapsed, killing eight people, including two children, and injuring 18 others.

When 1321 Flatbush collapsed, it took the adjoining wall of 1323 Flatbush Ave. with it, leaving the apartments in that building exposed to the elements. Striking images from the scene showed the perfectly undisturbed apartment interiors of 1323 Flatbush just as tenants had left them as they rushed to escape.

The collapse occurred while workers were doing excavation work at 2625 Bedford Ave., adjacent to 1321 Flatbush—a job site that had a history of safety violations, including proceeding with demolition in defiance of a stop-work order, according to the Department of Buildings.

The city has opened an investigation into the cause of the collapse and is doing sweeps of more than 160 work sites across the city associated with the construction team at 2625 Bedford Ave.

”If there is anyone or any entity operating in this city that bears responsibility for what happened, we will hold them fully accountable," New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a press conference last week.

Brooklyn District Attorney Eric Gonzalez has also opened a criminal inquiry into the collapse. No charges have been filed yet.

Displaced tenants of both buildings are staying in hotels provided by the American Red Cross through the end of November and the Department of Housing Preservation and Development has offered them additional financial support and resources.

On Wednesday, the Department of Building's forensic engineers determined that it would not be safe to allow construction workers inside of 1323 Flatbush Avenue in order to properly shore the building and stabilize it.

Instead, the DOB has recommended demolishing the existing building, and have issued an Immediate Emergency Declaration prohibiting access to the structure.

"Given the dangerous condition of the building and the imperative to make sure no one else gets hurt, ordering for the controlled safe demolition of the building is the only available option. Our entire Administration will continue to support the tenants displaced by this incredible tragedy and help the neighborhood, and our entire city, recover," Buildings Commissioner Ahmed Tigani said in a statement.

Tigani noted that "allowing workers into the building to do the necessary heavy-duty shoring needed to stabilize the buidling would put those workers at risk."

Instead, workers will install shoring at neighboring 1325 Flatbush before working to demolish the property.

Tigani cited "structural stability of the floors inside the building, as well as asbestos contamination of items remaining inside" as potentially dangerous to residents. The DOB also determined that it would not be safe for tenants to enter the buidling to retrieve their belongings.

Both 1321 Flatbush and 1323 Flatbush were built in 1930s, and had been zoned as mixed use residential buildings, with four apartments on the second and third floors and a commercial space on the ground floor.

According to HPD's database, 1321 Flatbush had 98 open violations while 1323 Flatbush had 182 open violations prior to last week's collapse.

Vacate orders for 1325 and 1327 Flatbush Avenue remain in place as of Wednesday, the DOB said.

She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. #5527. Nodal Networks raises $11.3M to solve global shipping bottlenecks

Nodal Networks Inc., a company that builds artificial intelligence decision networks to manage the world’s shipping container terminals, announced today that it has raised $11.3 million in seed funding to help port and rail hubs reduce congestion and move more cargo.

Freight networks move more than a billion shipping containers per year. They carry everything from clothing, electronics, furniture, raw materials for construction and perishable goods – the things that people rely on every day.

However, according to Sea-Intelligence Pte. Ltd., a Copenhagen-based shipping consulting and data analytics company, in September only half of the world’s container ships arrived on time and the late ones were a week behind. Oftentimes, ships can spend nearly half their time at port not working cargo.

Nodal Networks believes the solution is better management, not new infrastructure, which will be key to providing better terminal capacity.

“Watching ports through Earth-observation satellites, I started to see transport as a physical internet: Containers are the data packets, ports and rail yards are the routers, and congestion is the lag,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Paul Albert-Lebrun. “So, we went looking for the routers. We spent eight months in ports, terminals and rail yards, and even sailed the North Sea aboard a container ship, learning the work from the people who do it.”

Albert-Lebrun worked in satellite operations and later led product at Kepler Communications Inc., a space telecom company. Co-founder and Chief Commercial Officer Nic Westgate, by contrast, comes from mining engineering, approaching the problem from the opposite end.

Together, they combined their expertise in Malcom, the company’s AI-powered platform for improving terminal operations, named after Malcom McLean, a North Carolina truck driver turned entrepreneur who pioneered modern container shipping.

The AI platform combines agents with specialized forecasting models that can see, understand and predict incoming shipments, timing and offloading metrics to follow congestion, track lost productivity and make better-informed decisions about container placement, equipment allocation and loading operations. The company said it’s already deployed in terminals across three continents but did not provide details on which locations.

“There’s a lot of noise about AI in our industry right now, and I see a new company pitching terminals almost every week,” said Peter Levesque, an adviser to Nodal and former president of Ports America Inc. and CEO of CMA CGM North America LLC. “Most bring a general-purpose tool and look for somewhere to apply it, and few can answer the question every operator asks: what’s the return? Nodal got into the details, surrounded itself with the right people and kept the customer’s bottom line at the center of everything.”

Levesque added that Nodal has proven itself in terminal after terminal by showing measurable results.

According to Nodal, Malcom has already reduced truck time by one-half in one terminal after operators reassigned yard equipment. At another terminal, ship loading and unloading speeded up by 5% after the team pinpointed what kept cranes waiting for containers. In both cases, the company said Malcom helped operators identify which decisions would have the greatest impact.

The company said it would use the new funding to expand Malcom’s reach to more terminals within the groups Nodal already works with, support new customers and advance product development. It also intends to extend Malcom beyond the terminal, adding planning for shipping lines, railroads and trucking companies, becoming support for transportation networks where operators work together to exchange information.

#5526. ‘Momentum is the cure of all fear’: Mauricio and Alexia Umansky talk ‘Special Forces’

Jumping out of a helicopter into water below, rappelling down a 22-story building, enduring chemical warfare gas exposure — if you’ve never seen Special Forces: World’s Toughest Test, these are just a few of the tasks that must be completed.

It’s a reality TV show in which celebrities do physical challenges from the actual Special Forces selection process playbook. It’s like a competition show, but there are no eliminations, and no one gets voted off.

To leave, participants must voluntarily withdraw, be medically withdrawn by a DS (directing staff) due to injury or be dismissed for refusing a direct order. During the final test, the DS ejects those who fail the interrogation or selection test.

Season 5 is set in the Malaysian jungle. It features Candace Cameron Bure, Brandi Glanville, Oliver Hudson, Ruby Rose, George Santos, Bre Tiesi, Matt Barnes, and Mauricio and Alexia Umansky, among others.

At the time that this article was published, Alexia was still in the competition. Mauricio voluntarily withdrew after a rib injury sustained during a hand-to-hand fighting challenge with former NBA player Matt Barnes. Mauricio said the injury took two or three months to heal.

The following challenge involved gas, and Mauricio didn’t think his ribs could take it. He said he feared having a bad lung injury in the Malaysian jungle. Alexia agreed with the decision, saying the gas was the “most painful thing” she’d ever experienced in her life.

Inman spoke to Mauricio and Alexia midway through the season about the experience, the latest industry news and what’s next for The Agency.

What follows is the conversation, edited for length and clarity.

I think for me, 100 percent, the heat. I think I anticipated intense heat and intense humidity, but you don’t know what it’s like until you really feel it … It was so unbearably hot, and in our barracks that we slept in, there was no windows, and when you were inside, you actually couldn’t tell like what was even happening out there. But it was almost like … “Good, let me be locked in this metal box because the outside is crazy.”

Mauricio: I think for me, it was just the intensity of what a jungle really is. The first day we got there … when we were all showering and waiting to shower, there was a scorpion crawling on my leg, about to go in my boot, which I felt it and took it off just in the nick of time. Because if it went in my boot, it would have stung me, no question, right?

Alexia: It’s so hard to choose because literally every single thing was hard. Part of me wanted to say the car rides leading up to each challenge, because we didn’t know what was coming, and it was always so intense in the car. My heart would start pounding … the bottom line is the hardest part is just making sure that your mindset is correct [in] doing all these things and waking up each day and moving forward because that’s really what gets going is just moving forward and choosing to keep on going.

Mauricio: Yeah, I think Alexia nailed it. I mean, for me, it was really all about the little victories. The only way to survive is by looking at small victories, small steps … we used to say just make it to the next meal, just make it to the next day, just make it to tonight.

For me, the hardest part was leaving, was having to voluntarily withdraw. I did not want to have a medical withdrawal, so I didn’t want to go see the doctor and have them withdraw me.

Mauricio: Not one thing for me. What about you, Alexia?

Alexia: No. There’s nothing about this that’s easy.

Alexia: We loved everybody so much. I mean, we still talk all the time, and we still love each other so much. The words of affirmation we all told each other to this day are so special … But I think my first answer would have to be Candace [Cameron] Bure … she’s so strong, and we got looped together for a bunch of things because of our height similarities.

Mauricio: Well, I have to say that the person who surprised me the most was Alexia … the strength of her mind, her strength and what she did was extraordinary.

Alexia: Oh my god, yeah. Are you kidding me? All the time.

Alexia: Definitely thought it was pretty cool. It was an honor to be punched in the chest by DJ Tanner … I actually appreciated very much that she didn’t hold back because I just felt like I was treated like an equal, an individual.

Alexia: I’ve never punched anyone or anything … the second she threw the first punch, I knew she was so much stronger than me. But my goal was to just not fall down. I really didn’t want to fall down, so I was just trying to stay up the entire time. It felt like a fight went on for so long.

Alexia: I had zero plans on talking about that while we were there. Before we go into the course, they make you talk to some psychologists … they do ask you before the show, “What’s the worst thing that you’ve ever been through?”

And I remember thinking, like, “Are we gonna go there? … That would be so inappropriate. Everything’s in my power, and I’m not gonna go there” … Once I was finally in there, I understood why they asked … you’re stripped down to the very core of you, and you’re tired, and you’re pushing yourself, and you’re emotional, you’re exhausted … And Bre Tiesi, she got emotional, and [she said to me] ”I haven’t cried in years. I hate crying.”

It was really about discovering and repurposing the strength that I always felt that I had, but there was a time that I had felt that I had lost that.

And each night, as I was going to sleep, I just remember thinking to myself, “This is so rewarding, and this is so empowering, and this is so incredible for someone that has gone through what I have” … some people [feel like they] get their voice back. I always felt like I had my voice, but I feel like I got to discover a strength I always knew I had that someone had pushed me to question, and feeling that was just incredibly healing.

Alexia: No, not my parents. I had told two of my sisters before, and then, obviously, I told my dad on the course, and then, before the show aired, I ended up calling my mom and [sister] Portia to tell them because I obviously did not want that to be the first time they read it. And even though I spoke about it on the course, I’m still very, very afraid to tell them afterward, too.

Mauricio: It was extremely difficult … I was just proud of Alexia every single day, every single moment … hearing that story was just another revelation of her conquering and finally talking about something that I wish she never held back … I just wanted to reach out and just hug her. But by the same token, I also wanted to give her space and let her be her in that moment that she was sharing with everybody. So there was like a lot of stuff going through my mind.

There was anger toward this kid that did this … But [watching her let go of it] was beautiful to watch … from my perspective, it was like, “Do I reach over and become a dad and just give her a big hug, or do I let her go through this moment, psychologically speaking, of letting it all come out?”

And I was just proud of her all the way around.

In hindsight, I love that she was able to share that, get it off her chest with us, with everybody, with the world. I think it’s super powerful.

Yes, I live by a lot of different small philosophies. Certainty versus doubt. Momentum is the cure of all fears. All of these are the different things where you just have to move forward, right? In order to accomplish something, you kind of just have to move forward, right? … the moment that I went from being an agent to opening up a brokerage, you jump off the cliff; you hope the parachute catches.

To today … here we are in a really difficult real estate market. I mean, it is not fun out there right now whatsoever. Yet [The Agency is] still growing. We’re still putting money out there. We’re still doing things right. So yeah, to me that’s just a philosophy that I always live by.

Mauricio: I don’t know. We’ll just keep going. I really like that show Traitors. I would love to be on that show. That could be a fun one for me, so I’m putting that out into the universe.

Alexia: My dream would be to do a reality TV show with my family … We did Buying Beverly Hills, and we’ve done Real Housewives for like [16] years now. But we’ve never done something all of us together, just us, and I think that’ll be really cool.

Mauricio: I’m going to leave that one on the table. If anything, it’s for 2030. There’s still plenty of time to do that and make that decision. But I love LA, and I think I can help LA a lot. I think we live in an amazing city, and if the moment comes, and I’m set up in the right position in the business and I feel like I can actually win, I might do it. But I wouldn’t do it if I didn’t feel like I could actually win.

Mauricio: It’s an absolute mess, what’s going on in our in our in our industry right now, particularly with the listings. My take is, it’s quite simple. I think that there’s a lot of change that’s happening. I believe that it’s somewhere in the middle. Like I do everything.

I believe sellers should have choice, but I believe that we should be sharing those private listings amongst everybody — every agent, every brokerage firm, not just keeping it for themselves. I feel like there’s a lot happening right now in the industry where everybody’s really looking out for themselves: the MLSs, NAR, Compass.

Actually, Compass, I think, wants to collaborate, wants to share, but they’re in a big, big fight. But in the meantime, this Clear Cooperation Policy is what is allowing them to keep all the listings to themselves and not share them … The PLS is exactly what that was, and I still think that if Clear Cooperation Policy didn’t pass, it would have been an amazing business to have right now.

Mauricio: We are really positioned as the premier luxury brokerage firm outside of Compass right now. They’ve got Sotheby’s, they’ve got Christie’s, they’ve got all of those different brands, and we’re the only independent luxury brokerage firm out there right now.

So I’m excited to be in that position. Competitors make you better every single day … I’m excited in terms of where we sit, where we stand in a very difficult time; I’m not excited about the market. We really need to do some things to improve it. We’ve had three years of very, very difficult conditions, and it’s going to be very difficult for people to survive. And those that do survive will come out better.

I think we’re in a good position to survive, but we’ve got our work cut out for us over the next year, year and a half. But we’ll continue to grow. We’ll continue to expand, and I’m excited to just be a part of this industry. But man, it’s hard out there right now.

#5525. Mortgage Rates Surge Again as Stubborn Inflation Ends Brief Reprieve

Mortgage rates are rising again after four consecutive weeks of declines, as hotter-than-anticipated inflation data sets the stage for another interest rate hike, putting upward pressure on Treasury yields.

The average rate on 30-year fixed home loans jumped to 7.28% for the week ending Nov. 19, up 17 basis points from 7.11% recorded the week before, according to Freddie Mac. For perspective, rates averaged 6.26% one year ago.

"While prospective borrowers often shop around for a home, they may not always think to do the same for their mortgage, as comparing multiple rate quotes can potentially save them thousands over a loan's lifetime," says Sam Khater, Freddie Mac's chief economist.

The October Consumer Price Index (CPI) report came in above expectations last week on both the headline and core measures, all but guaranteeing that the Federal Reserve will raise its benchmark rate to curb inflation at the next Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on Dec. 8.

The looming hike, combined with the persistence of the war in Iran, pushed the 10-year Treasury yield back toward 5% this week, putting mortgage rates on an upward trajectory once again.

"The debate has shifted from whether the Fed hikes in December to how aggressively it moves," says Realtor.com® senior economist Anthony Smith. "That is a tough backdrop for mortgage rates heading into what is already a seasonally slow stretch for the housing market."

Markets are currently pricing a 93% chance of a 25-basis-point increase next month, according to the CME FedWatch tool.

Meanwhile, pending home sales fell to a record low in October, and existing home sales hit their lowest level since 2010, as the surge in mortgage rates through mid-October took its toll on buyers and sellers.

Earlier this week, the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) reported builder confidence falling to a new 14-year low, even as permit activity dropped to its lowest level since the early days of the pandemic, signaling that the supply pipeline will face continued pressure in the months ahead.

For buyers who remain active on the market, current conditions offer some meaningful advantages, including less competition from other shoppers, inventory climbing 8.6% year over year, and sellers increasingly willing to negotiate on price.

This week, the median listing price fell 2.4% from a year ago to $405,000, matching its steepest decline since early October, according to the latest Realtor.com weekly housing market update.

"The challenge is that until inflation cools enough to put mortgage rates on a durable downward path, affordability will remain the dominant constraint on the market," says Smith.

Your credit score plays a role when you apply for a mortgage. A credit score will determine whether you qualify for a mortgage and the interest rate you'll receive. The higher the credit score, the lower the interest rate you'll qualify for.

The credit score you need will vary depending on the type of loan. A score of 620 is a "fair" rating. However, people applying for a Federal Housing Administration loan might be able to get approved with a credit score of 500, which is considered a low score.

Homebuyers with credit scores of 740 or higher are typically considered to be in very good standing and can usually qualify for better rates, which can reduce monthly payments.

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5524. We keep coaching real estate agents to be salespeople. That was never the job

OPINION: Lance Pendleton argues that real estate agents are consultants, not salespeople. Learn what to ask before you pay for a coaching program.

I was the national head of agent development at Compass, and I’ve been in front of more than 30,000 agents since. I’ve also sold the thing I’m about to take apart, so keep that in mind while you read.

Here’s the usual scenario: You sign up for a coaching program. You’re excited, and you should be. Everybody wants to feel a little less alone in a job you mostly do by yourself, in your car.

You didn’t fail the program. The program failed you. How come?

The reason is simpler than anybody wants it to be. Nearly every coaching program in this business teaches professional sales skills to people who are not in sales. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators.

Nobody has ever talked a family into a house they didn’t want to live in. What we do is help people through the largest and most emotional decision of their lives with the least amount of damage. We read a room. We tell someone the truth about their kitchen, and we hold a deal together at 9 p.m. on a Sunday when the buyer’s father has opinions.

That is not selling. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators. If you can fog a mirror, you can get a license. Very few people can do those four things well, and I’ve yet to see a program that teaches them as a skill set.

This isn’t the coach’s fault. Coaches were trained the same way the rest of us were. Build the database. Reach as many people as you possibly can. Add value, and then add more of it tomorrow.

There’s a word buried in there that I think is the dumbest one in our industry, and I say that with love. Value.

We all have the same value. Every one of us can pull a comp, open a door, write an offer and get to a closing table. What almost none of us have is a point of differentiation, the thing that tells a consumer specifically what you do for them and why it ought to be you. You can follow “add value” for a decade and stay interchangeable with the other four agents the seller interviewed.

There’s a second reason the homework never gets done: Agents live in two periods of time: now and not now.

Now is the pipe that burst three hours before a closing. Now is the appraisal, the inspection, the client calling at 10:30 p.m. about something that could have been a text. Now is loud, it’s permanent, and it pays this month. Not now is quiet and pays in three years, if at all.

The trouble is that everything producing long-term income security in this business sits in the not-now column. The National Association of Realtors’ 2026 member profile puts median gross income at $88,500 for agents with 16 years or more in the industry, and $8,000 for agents with two years or less.

The veterans report a median 49 percent of their business from repeat clients and another 32 percent from referrals. For the newest agents, both of those medians are zero.

Somebody will say that’s just arithmetic, that you need a past client before you can have a repeat one. That’s the point. The whole gap is 15 years of relationships, and not one hour of that work feels urgent on a Tuesday. This is a patient business being coached like an impatient one.

We do something else I think is worse. We coach in a permanent state of enthusiasm. Everything is fabulous; every market is an opportunity; you’re crushing it; this is your year. I call that toxic positivity, and it does real damage. You sit in a hard month with two deals coming apart, you hear all of it, and you quietly conclude the problem must be you.

What would help is unglamorous. This job burns through five things: prioritization, organization, time management, impulse control and emotional regulation. By Thursday of an ordinary week, most good agents are running low on at least two.

There’s nothing wrong with any of those people. Real support builds bumpers around those five, the same reason a bowling lane for kids has them. You don’t make the gutter disappear by concentrating harder.

That work means dealing with people as they are, for who they are. Not more, more, more. Not the next great thing. One thing, chosen for that person, small enough to start on a Thursday when everything else has gone sideways.

We haven’t served this business well on that, and I include myself. I’ve sold the four-week cycle. It’s a comfortable thing to sell, because Week 1 always works.

If you’re picking a program this fall, ask what gets cut. Anybody can hand you 15 things. The one worth paying is the person who tells you which one matters and which 14 you can skip.

We’re not in sales. We never were. Until the coaching in this business is built for that job, we’ll keep running very good people through programs that leave them feeling like the problem.

You aren’t the problem. This is still the best time there’s ever been to be a great agent. We just have to stop training you for somebody else’s job.

The views and opinions expressed here are those of the contributor and separate from the Inman newsroom.

Lance Pendleton is the founder of Reframe Lab, a coaching and consulting practice for real estate agents, and the former national head of agent development at Compass in Connecticut. Get connected on Instagram.
