#5490. Perez Hilton Returns to Miami Residence—After Hospitalization for At-Home Health Incident

Perez Hilton has returned to his Miami residence after a health incident left him hospitalized.

The 48-year-old was hospitalized in August following a distressing livestream that prompted several calls to police and requests for a welfare check.

Officers ultimately transported Hilton to a nearby hospital, while mental health professionals and the Crisis Response Unit offered support to his friends and family.

Hilton received treatment for multiple broken bones and significant blood loss. After undergoing surgery, he was transferred to an inpatient medical facility.

Now, his family has revealed that Hilton is “back with his family while continuing his recovery through an intensive outpatient program.”

They noted that he is getting "ongoing therapy" and "mental health support."

“Over the past few weeks, Perez has enjoyed several successful weekend visits with his mom and children. Being reunited with his loved ones has meant so much to everyone, especially after these past few difficult months. With Thanksgiving approaching, we’re looking forward to spending some much-needed quality time together as a family and enjoying a little peace and quiet during the holiday," the statement continued.

In September, his family shared an update on the situation as they begged fans to vacate his property.

The message revealed that before the livestream event, Hilton's "children, niece, and sister were inside the home."

"When it became clear that Perez was experiencing a severe mental health crisis and harming himself, they immediately fled to protect the children from witnessing any further trauma," the message continued.

Hilton's family previously revealed that he was receiving medical care and was "able to communicate."

The update came after Hilton opened about his move to Realtor.com®, reflecting on what he'll miss most about his property and his fond memories of Las Vegas.

“It is a beautiful home, and it served me well personally and professionally," he said. "I filmed tons of television segments and news interviews from this home, and produced two documentaries.

"I would film every day for my socials, and livestream as well, and I do a lot of talking head commentary work. I filmed tons of specials for different networks and streamers in my home and outdoors. It's just so beautiful,"

"All three of my favorite spaces in the home have one thing in common—they are all very healing for me. The primary bath has the biggest, most luxurious shower that I've ever had, and the closet is huge and has so much space. Also, I never had my own, dedicated office before, and I really loved that. It's just the perfect home for a family. Everybody has space," he added.

Speaking about the property's location, Hilton told Realtor.com, "It was important for me to be close to the Strip, but it’s equal distance to Summerlin and everywhere we needed to be. My children’s schools, doctors, and dentists were all just a few minutes away.”

Hilton was especially pleased with the fact that his mother had her own private living space. One of home designer Blue Heron's signature features is a "NexGen Suite," and, because he bought the home before it was finished, he got to customize elements of the layout to ensure they were perfect for his mom.

“This was perfect for me, because my mother is a huge part of my family,” said Hilton. “She’s both grandmother and co-parent to my children. To be able to give her the space that she deserves was important. She had her own entrance, her own living room and kitchenette area."

However, despite his love for Nevada, Hilton noted that he is confident in his decision.

"It just feels like the right move, the only move, to make at this time. I've loved Las Vegas, but it's time to be closer to family," he added.

The property is being sold with Kathryn Winterton of Las Vegas Sotheby’s real estate agency, who told Realtor.com, "This home was designed for the way people want to live and entertain today. The natural light, open spaces, and seamless connection to the backyard create an atmosphere that feels both sophisticated and welcoming."

The home spans 7,000 square feet and boasts several modern living spaces, as well as a resort-style pool.

As in so many family dwellings, Hilton says the kitchen is the heart of the home, with its premium appliances, sleek custom cabinetry and a massive dining and prep island.

The kitchen opens up to the high-ceiling living and dining areas, which feel expansive, welcoming and luxurious. Generous walls of glass provide abundant natural light create a light, airy atmosphere.

Outdoors on the acre lot there's a pool, spa, lush landscaping and multiple outdoor gathering spaces. Hilton said he did a lot of his production work outside, as there are a variety of luxurious backdrops ideal for his commentary.

Set in a chic, private gated neighborhood known as Prado, Hilton enjoyed the fact that the home is on a corner lot in a small community with fewer than 20 homes.

Hilton and his family enjoyed the home, the community and Las Vegas in general so much he says he feels a bit of guilt moving his family away. But "kids are adaptable," he says. He knows this from experience.

A little over three years ago, Hilton packed up his three children and his mother and moved to Las Vegas from Los Angeles, the city where he had infinite Hollywood connections and a luxe, six bedroom, five bath classic Spanish Colonial built in 1926.

Prior to that, Hilton and his family lived in New York City for several years.

Hilton took to Instagram to explain the reasoning behind his move from Las Vegas, where he has been living for the past 3.5 years.

"We’re moving permanently to Miami. I am so excited, not nervous. I know this is the right move for me and my children and my mother," he said at the beginning of the video.

Although Hilton insisted he has "nothing but wonderful memories" while calling Nevada home, he claimed that his decision to relocate to the Sunshine State came from a higher power.

“I need to move to Miami for many reasons. First, this is heaven-sent. God told me to move to Miami. ... The holy spirit made these words come out of my mouth: ‘Let’s move to Miami,'" he said.

The influencer noted that his "trauma" from growing up in The Magic City has since been "released."

“My entire family is in Miami. I still have friends from high school. Though I have not lived there in 30 years, it has always been my home. Once we move there, any second now, it will feel like home right away," he added.

Hilton, who has three children via surrogacy, said a large part of his decision to move was due to his difficult year, which was filled with several health scares, including a 21-day hospital stay and a blood clot.

"Even though it was really painful being in the hospital and so sick, I reconnected with my faith, and this move to Miami feels divine. I was just listening to God. I used to not have a great relationship with Miami when I was younger, but now things are different and Miami is different, and I'm excited to get to rediscover it as an adult," he told Realtor.com.

Speaking about his health woes, he said, "I know this move will be great for my family. Nearly dying this year twice and the experience here—you never think it’s going to happen, but it was just so hard not only for me but my mom, for the kids, for my sister who is in Los Angeles. Everybody else is in Miami. To a new beginning and thank you, God, for guiding me back to Florida where my family needs to be.”

#5488. Compass, MLSs Jockey Over Jurisdiction as Lawsuits Sprawl

In the ongoing legal battle between Compass and more than a dozen large MLSs across the country, both sides are maneuvering to control how and where the cases are tried, as the mega-brokerage seeks to spread the litigation as widely as possible.

The Arizona Regional MLS (ARMLS), one of 15 MLSs sued by Compass last week, filed a letter with the Southern District of New York on Nov. 18, arguing that Compass’s motion to “splinter one dispute across multiple courts” should be denied.

“Compass’s effort to scatter this dispute across multiple courts would create unnecessary complexity and expense without changing the fundamental issue at stake,” said Jeff Bosch, CEO of Arizona Regional Multiple Listing Service, in a statement shared with RISMedia. “We are defending cooperation rules that promote fair competition, give buyers broader access to available homes, and help sellers reach more potential buyers. We believe these rules are lawful and procompetitive, and we look forward to defending them in court.”

Simultaneously, Compass is grappling with court rules that require it to notify judges of related cases as it pursues a larger goal of maximizing pressure on each MLS, arguing that the lawsuits should proceed separately despite their many similarities.

“The overlap between the cases concerning the subject of the challenged rules and Compass’s phased-marketing program does not justify coordinating cases that involve different defendants, markets, witnesses, and damages,” Compass wrote in a letter filed in the Southern District of California.

The back-and-forth is the latest key maneuver as Compass and the MLSs battle over rules that prevent pre-marketed or off-MLS listings from being shown on the MLS.

As the mega-brokerage pursues a broad campaign to remake real estate, it has not shied away from using its significant size and resources to lean on MLSs that have stuck to their policies (specifically, restrictions on off-MLS marketing). In a September letter sent to the MLSs it would eventually sue, Compass explicitly pointed to the legal costs of defending a lawsuit, and promised to spend “millions of dollars to sue” MLSs that defied it.

In at least three of its lawsuits targeting MLSs, Compass informed federal judges of the other two-dozen lawsuits it has filed, while simultaneously arguing those lawsuits should not be consolidated or reassigned, claiming “each case turns on a distinct defendant, rule, and local market.”

Still, Compass acknowledged that the cases “overlap…in a limited respect,” but wrote in one letter it would not “concede…that consolidation, coordination, reassignment, or transfer would be appropriate.”

With around 350,000 federal civil lawsuits filed every year, judges are often highly motivated to find efficiencies and avoid redundancies in their caseloads. To that end, many districts require that attorneys notify the court of cases with similar factual elements or common parties filed in other districts, allowing judges to coordinate, consolidate or otherwise smooth out the litigation process.

In one of its letters, Compass cited this rule but said it was only informing the judge out of “an abundance of caution,” while still arguing the the other lawsuits “do not arise from the same or substantially identical transactions, happenings, or events.”

Forcing each MLS to defend a separate lawsuit will likely increase litigation costs overall, with Compass better able to bear that burden as a well-funded public company. At the same time, judges are also likely to consider geographic factors, as any consolidated case would force some MLSs to travel further for proceedings.

On November 12, Compass sued 15 MLSs in 15 separate actions in 11 districts, claiming their longstanding broker cooperation rules violated antitrust law. The en masse filing was preceded by a letter Compass sent to several MLSs in September, warning them to cease enforcement of their broker cooperation rules or face federal antitrust claims.

In response, six MLSs, later joined by one more, filed a lawsuit in New York seeking to prevent Compass from suing them along with a declaration that their cooperation rules are lawful under federal antitrust laws (and state-law analogues).

The MLSs have also sought to rally together, with at least two separate legal defense funds in the works—one by CRMLS, and another through the Council of Multiple Listing Services (which has not been named in the litigation, though many of the targeted MLSs are members).

In its November 13 motion, Compass claimed that the action filed by the MLSs should either be dismissed or handled individually in the jurisdictions where each MLS resides.

ARMLS counsel Gregory S. Skidmore argued in his letter that trying the cases individually would create “massive inefficiencies and duplication of effort.”

“The MLS Parties sued Compass where it is headquartered, and where Compass itself has chosen to litigate its own Cooperation Rules–related suit,” wrote Skidmore, referring to the brokerage’s injunction hearing against Zillow in November of 2025. “Compass has not shown any ‘indication that nonparty witnesses would refuse to appear’…and Compass’s executives reside in New York,” he continued. “Nor is any other district the locus of operative facts: Compass’s campaign originated at its New York headquarters and reached nationwide.”

Compass, in its separate letters, argued that each case is more about the local circumstances and specific rules of each MLS, and directly disputed that consolidation would create more efficiencies, and noted that potential damages will depend on sales prices in local real estate markets.

Skidmore, on the other hand, urged the SDNY court to to focus on “judicial economy” and claiming that Compass “bears the burden” of showing that severing the case is necessary.

“Transfer would create seven suits in five districts, each replicating Compass’s evidence,” he added. “Courts need not indulge an ‘onslaught of litigation.'”

Maria Patterson is the Executive Vice President and Jesse Williams is content director for RISMedia Premier.

#5487. What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

Taylor Swift, classical or silence? Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.

Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers. One is a carefully curated playlist, while the other is silence.

Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.

None could point to hard numbers showing a playlist moved a home faster or for more money. What they did offer was a clear set of rules from the agents who use music, and an equally firm argument from those who won’t touch it.

Ben Jacobs, co-founder of the Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman in New York City, thinks music raises more questions than it answers. He said he’s not a fan of playing music during showings.

“Buyers may wonder if the agent is trying to mask something, whether it’s street noise, construction nearby, sounds within the building or even a noisy appliance,” Jacobs told Inman. “You want buyers to experience the home as it actually is, without anything distracting from their ability to evaluate the space.”

His co-founder, Jessica Chestler, said music has its place. That place is just not a private showing.

“Music can be wonderful for setting a mood at a cocktail party, listing launch or special event, but during a showing, I think there’s something to be said for letting the property speak for itself,” Chestler said.

Megan Sullivan works at the same brokerage, and she uses music for the very reason Jacobs avoids it. Sullivan sells large estate homes across Fairfield and Westchester counties out of Douglas Elliman’s Greenwich, Connecticut, office. Some of those homes sit within earshot of things a seller can’t fix.

“I actually do like incorporating music into certain showings, particularly when a property is impacted by outside noise from planes, trains or automobiles,” Sullivan said. “Thoughtfully selected background music can help create a more welcoming atmosphere and soften those distractions, allowing buyers to focus on the overall experience of the home. I think it’s very property-specific.”

Jeffrey Hensel is a broker associate with North Coast Financial, a California hard money lender that funds fix-and-flip and probate deals. He looks at it from the investor side.

“Dead silence can amplify every creak, clank, and drip in an otherwise quiet home,” he said. “Background music masks these sounds and provides some white noise to help set a calm mood.”

Agents in the pro-music camp mostly aren’t trying to cover anything up. They simply want buyers to stay longer.

Sandra Daniels of Harry Norman, Realtors | Forbes Global Properties serves the East Cobb and Marietta area outside Atlanta. She’s currently listing a $3.9 million estate in The River Club in Suwanee, Georgia.

For those showings, she rotates light classical piano, The Macarons Project and a Spotify playlist called “Nora Ephron + Nancy Meyers Dinner Party.”

“Put a buyer in a home with a glass of Champagne or a cup of coffee and the right music playing, and that cozy, inviting atmosphere encourages people to stay, relax and feel at home,” Daniels told Inman.

Daniels also has a low-tech trick for vacant listings she expects to sell in the first week. She bought an old-school CD player and a few classical CDs. She leaves it on repeat through the first weekend of showings and stops by each evening to turn off the lights and music and lock up.

Natalia Bassova, founder and CEO of Resort Real Estate in Breckenridge, Colorado, saw the same effect at a luxury mountain listing. The home looked great, she said, but it showed cold.

“By adding some background instrumental music, it gave the buyers more time to spend in the home. They spent more time in the kitchen and great room areas,” Bassova said. “The property didn’t change, but the atmosphere did.”

For mountain and luxury homes, Bassova plays acoustic and piano music, including Ludovico Einaudi and The Piano Guys. For condos and new construction, she switches to soft contemporary instrumentals.

Agents who play music disagree on genre, but almost all agree on one thing: avoid lyrics.

“If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact,” Bassova said. Her never-play list covers anything with strong lyrics, politics, swearing or heavy bass.

Andrea Seeney is a global real estate advisor with Atlanta Fine Homes Sotheby’s International Realty and a trained opera singer and classical pianist. She compared lyrics to a seller’s personal effects.

“Acoustic performances are best because they set a tone and allow the buyer to fill in the blanks with their own thoughts,” Seeney said.

She leans toward jazz and usually plays Spotify’s Coffee House radio or its Ella Fitzgerald playlist. She says music works on buyers through memory: a song can take someone back to a time and place they enjoyed, “and that memory then reflects positively on the home.”

Hensel takes the lyrics rule a step further, to genre itself. If an agent plays hip-hop or country for a buyer who doesn’t listen to it, he says, that signals an assumption about who the buyer is. That can create friction neither side notices. His pick is quiet cocktail-lounge jazz like Miles Davis or Bill Evans, at a steady tempo and volume.

He also cited retail research by psychological scientists Adrian North and Lorraine Sheridan of Curtin University and Charles Areni of Macquarie University. It found that shoppers who heard classical music rated merchandise as higher quality and were willing to spend more.

Some agents ignore the rulebook completely.

Rachel Kilmer, an agent with ReeceNichols Real Estate in Kansas City, Missouri, plays Taylor Swift at nearly every open house. She swaps in country for more rural listings.

“In Kansas City, she’s a conversation starter,” Kilmer said. “People come in, and it’s, ‘Are you a Swiftie?’ ‘No, but I love the Chiefs!’ It really helps loosen up the conversation.”

She added, “I’m the one sitting there listening to it for two hours!”

Monica Shea, a broker with KW Aspire in Colorado Springs, Colorado, builds whole open houses around a theme, and the music follows.

She played the Eras Tour set list at a Taylor Swift–themed open house and the Frozen soundtrack at a hot cocoa bar event. A Halloween open house got not-too-spooky Halloween music. For regular showings, she has sellers put on a YouTube channel with seasonal background music and scenery.

Shea’s never-play list puts her directly at odds with a few other agents: smooth jazz. Shea says she never plays “anything that sounds like the Weather Channel.”

Marcel Finkelstein of Team BlackStar at eXp Realty hosts open houses every Sunday across Monmouth County, New Jersey. He sees music as more of an icebreaker than a staging tool.

His Apple Music rotation includes lounge instrumentals, vocal-free dance-pop and Bon Entendeur. It also has Afro house from DJ Alex Niyazov and the warm trumpet and sax of Fausto Papetti and Paul Mauriat.

He uses the same approach whether the listing is a $600,000 two-bedroom condo in Manalapan or a $2 million six-bedroom in Colts Neck.

“I want the atmosphere to feel calm, comfortable and welcoming, rather than like a sales presentation,” Finkelstein said.

Finkelstein added that his Instagram followers also know how much he loves music.

“Every week, I share new songs and incorporate music into my stories and posts about homes,” he said. “It’s a personal interest that carries through into how I present properties.”

On setup, agents who play music give similar advice. Keep the volume low enough that buyers can ask questions and the agent can hear their feedback. Use one good speaker rather than several.

Bassova puts hers in the middle of the home, and Seeney puts a small Bluetooth speaker in the kitchen. When sellers have a Sonos system, Daniels connects to it from her MacBook or iPad. Otherwise, she brings her own Bose speaker.

Kilmer runs her music from an iPad instead of her phone. “That way, incoming calls and texts don’t interrupt the music,” she said.

As for proof, none of the agents Inman spoke with track music as a performance metric. Bassova said she gets buyer feedback that certain homes feel relaxing, but nothing tied to days on market or offers.

So the evidence is anecdotal, and the playlists don’t agree. Agents can’t even settle on jazz. Both camps share one goal: the buyer should notice the home, not the soundtrack.

As Bassova said, “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact.”

#5486. Building Permit Woes Tip Leading Economic Indicators Negative

Leading economic indicators for the month of October took a slight downturn, as the latest Leading Economic Index (LEI) report from business research organization The Conference Board recorded a 0.3% drop to 99.3 from September.

The LEI is a predictive tool designed to anticipate the direction of the economy in the coming months. It is based on 10 component indicators, which, for example, include measures of average consumer expectations and the average weekly initial claims of unemployment insurance.

Justyna Zabinska-La Monica, senior manager of Business Cycle Indicators at The Conference Board, said that “The US LEI’s decline in October was mostly fueled by fewer building permits.”

Recent data on building permits has indeed been dismal. This month’s New Residential Construction report, for example, showed that permits were down 7.4% month-over-month and 8.7% year-over-year.

Zabinska-La Monica, for her part, emphasized that “(b)uilding permits data were at the weakest level since May 2020…Compared to September and one year ago, permits declined across all categories, including by type of dwelling and region. The only exception was the Midwest, where total permits were up slightly since September and 8.1% over the last 12 months.”

Zabinska-La Monica also singled out “consumer expectations for business conditions, average hours worked in manufacturing, and manufacturers’ new orders for nondefense capital goods” as “negative contributors” to October’s LEI. “Weakness in these components more than offset gains in others,” she explained.

The other two major indices in The Conference Board’s report, the Coincident Economic Index (CEI) and Lagging Economic Index (LAG), were both unchanged (apart from some minor September data revisions mentioned in the report).

The CEI, in contrast to the LEI, is considered a summary of indicators on the current state of the economy. The LAG serves as an after-the-fact confirmation of the state of the economy.

The overall outlook of The Conference Board, despite some disheartening October data, is still seemingly positive. Zabinska-La Monica noted that “the LEI’s six-month growth rate remained positive,” which “indicat(es) continued economic expansion ahead.” This economic expansion, however, will be “increasingly investment-led with softer household demand.”

Audrey Jiang is an editorial intern for RISMedia.

#5484. NAR’s latest data, must-have AI tools, Compass’ 15 new lawsuits

Congratulations, you’ve made it to Friday again this week. But before you head out for the weekend, we’re bringing you a quick catch-up on the biggest headlines and the most helpful how-tos for your business. So, Take 5 and peruse our top editor picks for this week and why they matter to your business.

P.S. Don’t miss The Download, our weekly column that breaks down one of the week’s top stories and equips you with what you’ll need to meet next Monday head-on.

Homeownership is slipping further out of reach for young Americans, according to the National Association of Realtors’ 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers. The report, released on Thursday, revealed that the share of first-time homebuyers rose 1 percent year over year to 22 percent. Despite the small gain, first-time buyer activity remains near historic lows (21 percent) and 18 percentage points below pre-2008 trends (40 percent). Same as last year, the median age of a first-time homebuyer was 40 — roughly a decade older than the typical median age in the 1980s.

Why it matters: This annual report gives you a pulse on national real estate trends and how you might want to pivot your strategies. For example, as noted above, the median age of the first-time homebuyer is 40, and the share of single women homeowners has risen to 20 percent. A longer nurture campaign might be in order (ahem, see below), and if you’re not already marketing toward single women, perhaps you should. Read the full report for more.

EXTRA: The buyer who can’t close for a year is your best asset in 2026

AI has been the topic of conversation for the past couple of years. And there’s a lot of talk. So how do you suss through the noise and find what works for your business? Jimmy Burgess has created a no-nonsense list of seven AI tools that are actually worth your time.

Why it matters: Burgess shares not only his top tools but also how to use them. These tools will help you turn prompts into better questions, find the questions your future clients are asking, remember the details that matter, evaluate your AI search visibility, turn one video into multiple pieces of content, make video editing easier and use AI as a strategist rather than a writing assistant. Don’t feel overwhelmed. You don’t have to use all of them at once.

Krystopher Benyamein recently sold a property in San Pedro where his team hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. They found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and they had to start again.

They eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when they shared the case study on Instagram, they didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing they’d done. They opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”

That opening puts the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, they explained how they responded, got the property back in front of buyers and ultimately closed.

Why it matters: In today’s market, there are many stories of buyers backing out of deals. This approach allows you to create content that keeps you top of mind, show sellers exactly how you work and reach a wider audience. Benyamein shows you how to do it and shares a FREE Canva template to help get the job done.

VA loans often get passed over for conventional loans. Inman’s Nick Pipitone spoke with Fathom Realty’s Lindsey Schmidt, an Army veteran who served in Iraq, about why VA financing still carries a stigma among sellers and listing agents, how she gets around it and why VA assumptions remain one of the most misunderstood tools in the market.

Why it matters: Military members often have to move. Understanding and busting myths about VA loans can help you get ahead of objections before making an offer, which will help you get more deals across the finish line and get more service members into homes.

Compass has been busy, creating and formalizing policy around employees in association leadership positions and how Compass brokerage agents cooperate on private listings.

The company announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it says can reach $15,000.

Why it matters: Compass International Holdings is currently in litigation with 16 total MLSs across 18 federal lawsuits. Not only is this big news that’s making waves throughout the industry, but its ripple effects could impact your MLS’s rules, if they haven’t already.

EXTRA: What Compass’ leadership ban signals for agents and associations

#5483. Agentic AI pushes the neocloud race beyond GPU counts toward global platforms

The neocloud boom is entering a sorting phase, and global cloud availability is emerging as the line between providers built for enterprise AI and those built to rent out racks of graphics processing units.

With agentic AI moving from pilots into production, buyers are looking past raw GPU counts toward integrated platforms they can build on. That shift is redrawing the competitive map for cloud AI infrastructure. Enterprise practitioners are now starting ambitious agentic AI agendas, and they need the full stack of services behind AI-native applications rather than standalone clusters, according to Kevin Cochrane (pictured, right), chief marketing officer of Vultr.

“There are those providers that are trusted platforms, that are global cloud platforms that have the totality of services that are required for real agentic AI deployments,” Cochrane said. “We’ll continue to see a separation of the pack and there’ll be those that are trusted platforms that enterprises can rely on and there’ll be those that aren’t.”

Cochrane and Duncan Ng (left), vice president of solutions engineering at Vultr, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed why agentic AI is reviving demand for central processing units, how Vultr builds data centers as integrated systems and which neocloud providers are likely to survive consolidation. (* Disclosure below.)

Calling a service an enterprise cloud takes more than racking accelerators. Vultr organizes its footprint into data center regions, each of which can control multiple facilities on one network. Developers get one application programming interface they can hook into a Terraform template, Cochrane explained. Many rivals, by contrast, stood up individual sites quickly to serve bespoke customer contracts.

“In traditional neoclouds, the data centers are actually islands. They’re not connected. It’s not one unified global network. It’s not one unified global platform,” Cochrane said. “These are like individual data centers stood up very quickly for bespoke customer contract. That is not a platform.”

Agentic AI is also reshaping the hardware mix inside those regions. Reasoning models now let agents chain dozens of steps, call tools and validate results in flight — work that leans heavily on CPUs, according to Ng. Vultr ran a cloud for more than a decade before the GPU rush and has used processors from Advanced Micro Devices Inc. as the backbone of its CPU fleet for several years, he added. The company has since extended that partnership to accelerators with a $1.2 billion order for AMD’s Helios rack-scale systems.

“This increased density, this increased usage — these are just new hosting companies,” Ng said. “This is just a new application that is 10 times more compute dense than the last that we’re trying to sell to.”

Enterprises are finally moving those workloads out of pilot and into production, Ng noted. One Big Four global systems integrator uses Vultr as the substrate for a risk management service. Vultr has been rolling out platform upgrades aimed at enterprise agentic AI to support that kind of deployment.

“What they’re doing is something that used to take consulting hours, people poring through spreadsheets and poring through invoices, poring through declarations,” he said. “They now are able to automate significant portions of this to serve a larger number of their customers and do a deeper dive into their risk supply chains.”

#5482. DSFederal Awarded USDA NIFA Grants Management and Reporting System Support Contract

WASHINGTON, Nov. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- DSFederal, Inc., a leading provider of digital transformation and IT solutions for Federal agencies, has been awarded a contract to provide Grants Management and Reporting System (GMRS) applications development and enhancement support for the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) National Institute of Food and Agriculture (NIFA).

Under the contract, DSFederal will provide application development, system enhancements, data management, and technical support to maintain and improve GMRS capabilities. Combining Agile DevSecOps methodologies with extensive experience in Federal grants management and data engineering, the team will strengthen system reliability, streamline workflows, and enhance data integration and reporting to support NIFA's grants management operations.

"As NIFA continues to modernize its grants management systems and expand its data and analytics capabilities, DSFederal is committed to delivering improvements that enhance efficiency, improve user experience, and better serve NIFA staff, grantees, and the broader research community," said Thiagarajan Prakash, Vice President of IT and NIFA GMRS Project Manager at DSFederal.

Through this engagement, DSFederal will help advance NIFA's mission of supporting agricultural research, education, and extension programs nationwide.

DSFederal is a woman-owned small business delivering innovative IT, data analytics, and management consulting solutions to Federal agencies. With nearly 20 years of experience supporting mission-critical government programs, DSFederal combines deep domain expertise, emerging technologies, and a commitment to excellence to help agencies modernize operations, improve decision-making, and achieve meaningful mission outcomes.

For more information, visit http://www.dsfederal.com/.

#5481. Palo Alto Networks agreed to buy AI startup Applied Compute for $4.5 billion

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The all-stock deal is aimed at securing open-weight AI models and is expected to close in the third quarter of fiscal 2027

Palo Alto Networks $PANW agreed to acquire Applied Compute, an artificial intelligence startup enabling companies to operate and tailor AI models of their own, in an all-stock transaction valued at $4.5 billion, Palo Alto Networks said on Wednesday. The combination is meant to help enterprises train, adapt and deploy open-source and open-weight AI models across public and sovereign clouds.

The transaction is subject to closing conditions, including regulatory clearance, the company said. The deal should be finalized during fiscal 2027's third quarter, according to Reuters.

"Every enterprise is going to run a mix of open and closed models, and every one of those models needs to be secured," Palo Alto Networks said in a statement.

Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora told CNBC the deal is a step toward a broader role in AI infrastructure. "Rather than being one player out of 10 in the industry serving compute, we want to be the one player with Palo Alto that delivers secure compute and security capability," he said.

Palo Alto Networks projects that, by fiscal 2029, the acquisition will contribute upwards of $1 billion of yearly recurring revenue to its next-generation security unit, according to CNBC.

Palo Alto Networks stock rose 6% on Thursday.

The company announced the acquisition alongside fiscal first-quarter results, with revenue up 39% from a year earlier. It raised its fiscal 2027 revenue forecast to a range of $14.52 billion to $14.57 billion.

"If it works, I think this will dwarf the ability that we have in cybersecurity," Arora said on the earnings call. "This could be bigger than what we do."

Open-weight models are artificial intelligence systems that developers release along with their learned parameters for anyone to access. They pose security risks such as unauthorized alteration, exposure of sensitive information and exploitation by malicious parties, according to Reuters.

#5480. NAR saved for his $541K exit; now it won’t pay, ex-CFO says

License under the Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 Generic license.

Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.

Pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005. To avoid booking the full expense when a senior vice president retired, NAR created a Compensation Reserve that let it steadily set aside funds throughout the executive’s tenure, which it would release at retirement. Pierpoint helped establish the reserve in 2005 at the direction of former NAR CEO Dale Stinton, court documents said.

Pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind. The former CFO said he was key in executing the buyer-broker commission settlement payout, which totaled $418 million. The first settlement payment, totaling roughly $200 million, was issued in February 2025, with subsequent payments of $72 million per year until the full $418 million is paid.

Pierpoint said he notified NAR of his impending retirement in late 2024 and requested his retirement payout. However, six days before his last day with NAR, Pierpoint alleged that a Grant Thornton auditor named White — there is no first name listed in the court documents — emailed him and said that “NAR had been ‘unable to locate any policy or verify any consistent practice’ concerning the Compensation Reserve or ‘the payout to executives of a full year of salary upon retirement.'”

White also allegedly said that the Compensation Reserve “was not used to fund” the exit packages of eight other senior vice presidents who retired before Pierpoint, which are listed in the court documents as L.J., F.S., B.M., D.H., J.G.,  J.B., D.G. and B.G. Real Estate News said L.J., D.G. and B.G. are likely former general counsel Laurie Janik, former SVP of talent development and resources Donna Gland, and former senior vice president and CEO Bob Goldberg.

As a result, Grant Thornton said it was “unable to approve the payout of a full year’s compensation without any concrete proof that such act is mandated by an employment agreement, policy or plan.”

Pierpoint claimed NAR had the funds to pay his retirement benefit and provided a ledger outlining what the Association allegedly reserved from December 2014 to December 2024. He also said the trial balances NAR provided to outside auditors, including Grant Thornton, included evidence of the Compensation Reserve’s existence and purpose.

“NAR carried its obligation to Pierpoint at approximately 97.6 cents on the dollar three months before it refused to pay him anything,” the complaint read. “The practice NAR now claims it cannot verify is documented in NAR’s own ledger, its own year-end schedules, its own payroll records and its own audit files, and was paid to every one of Pierpoint’s predecessors who retired. NAR did not stop believing in its obligation; it stopped wanting to pay it.”

Pierpoint’s counsel accused NAR of shirking its obligation to pay the former CFO due to its financial woes after the settlement. In December 2025, former NAR president Kevin Sears said the buyer-broker commission settlement saved the Association’s finances — the other option was to file an appeal and declare bankruptcy.

“John Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” said David Fish, an attorney with Workplace Law Partners, P.C., who represents Pierpoint. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives.”

“We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees,” he added.

Pierpoint’s counsel is requesting that NAR pay the $541,059 retirement payout, statutory damages of 5 percent of the unpaid amount for each month it remains unpaid, attorneys’ fees and costs, and prejudgment and post-judgment interest. They also seek a jury trial.

NAR denied Pierpoint’s claims, saying that the former CFO has “[mischaracterized] a varied set of individual arrangements with departing executives as a uniform and guaranteed retirement benefit.”

“Mr. Pierpoint was not entitled to the payment he now seeks, and NAR’s decision was unrelated to its antitrust settlement or its financial condition,” an NAR spokesperson told Inman in an emailed statement. “NAR is committed to appropriate financial controls and responsible stewardship of its members’ dues dollars. NAR pays compensation and benefits that are actually owed, not just because a former executive requests payment. No such obligation exists here, and we intend to vigorously defend against these claims through the appropriate legal process.”

#5478. Google workers are urging the company to let schools opt out of AI in Search

Free daily briefing on global business news.

More than 540 Google employees and contractors signed a letter to Sundar Pichai, according to the Alphabet Workers Union

Hundreds of Google $GOOGL employees signed a petition on Thursday asking the company to offer schools a version of Google Search that leaves out the AI features, according to Bloomberg.

The Alphabet Workers Union, the group behind the campaign, said the letter carries signatures from over 540 Google staff and contractors. It is addressed to Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai, Elizabeth Reid, vice president and head of search, and Chris Phillips, vice president and general manager of education.

"Cutting off access to Search for schools that don't wish to use AI will not help persuade our users, and will more likely result in them shutting out Google products altogether," the workers wrote. They also wrote that educators need "the freedom to choose how to implement" AI in their curriculum, according to Bloomberg.

Google said it would turn off Gemini and Search by default on K-12 student accounts until school administrators enable them. Administrators who enable Search must also take on the AI bundled into it, and Google offers no setting to disable those features separately. Google has said the changes are aimed at putting schools in charge of how AI gets used in their classrooms.

Senator Ed Markey, a Massachusetts Democrat, asked Alphabet on Nov. 9 to give schools a way to keep using Search while shutting out AI. His letter cited a lawsuit from a family alleging that their 13-year-old daughter confided suicidal thoughts to Google's AI on a school-issued Chromebook. Google said it is reviewing the allegations.

Google's Chrome operating system accounted for 58% of the laptops and tablets that went to U.S. K-12 schools last year, according to Bloomberg, citing research firm Futuresource Consulting.

Dan Carroll, co-founder of ed tech startup Clever, said schools that want to avoid AI face a hard choice, according to Bloomberg. Chromebooks are made to fit Google's software ecosystem, Search among it, and moving teachers and students to another search engine would cost both time and money, he said.

Carroll said Google may not want schools running a Search product that seems dated compared with the version most people now rely on. "Either Google listens to schools and gives students a version of search that's already feeling outdated compared to the market, or they alienate schools by requiring they use the new version," he said, according to Bloomberg.

The employees raised the same concern in their letter. "It is our job as Googlers to respect the user, and listen to them when they have concerns about our products," they wrote, according to Bloomberg.

#5476. MGMLS is merging into FMLS, what it means for central Georgia agents

Mid Georgia Multiple Listing Service will merge into First Multiple Listing Service, extending FMLS compulsory coverage into 12 central Georgia counties. The groups said the deal builds on a 6-year data-sharing partnership, with timing and terms not disclosed.  AI Summary

Mid Georgia Multiple Listing Service (MGMLS) has agreed to merge into First Multiple Listing Service (FMLS), expanding FMLS’s footprint into 12 additional compulsory counties in central Georgia and giving MGMLS members access to a larger technology, data and education platform, the organizations announced Thursday. Terms and an effective closing date were not disclosed.

“Our members are at the heart of every decision we make, and this opportunity is ultimately about creating even greater value for them,” said Laura Kostovetsky, president of the MGMLS board of directors. “We have built a strong organization and a strong community of real estate professionals and joining forces with FMLS gives us an opportunity to build on that success.”

MGMLS CEO Suzanne Beers said the combination expands services while keeping local expertise.

“This combination will give our members access to greater resources and capabilities while preserving the local knowledge and relationships they respect,” she said in a statement.

FMLS President and CEO Jeremy Crawford, a HousingWire Insider, added that the deal is designed to strengthen the regional “real estate ecosystem” and continue a broker-governed model focused on data integrity and cooperation.

For existing FMLS participants, the merger will extend the MLS’s compulsory coverage area deeper into middle Georgia, according to member communications. FMLS’s required-coverage footprint will grow to include Baldwin, Bibb, Butts, Crawford, Houston, Jasper, Jones, Monroe, Peach, Putnam, Twiggs and Wilkinson counties.

Those counties border areas where many FMLS brokers and agents already show and sell property under current data-sharing arrangements. With MGMLS folded in, FMLS will be the primary MLS serving that market, backed by local support.

#5475. 20 Amazon Black Friday deals, judged by how far each price beats past sales

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Amazon's 12-day Black Friday sale runs through Nov. 30. See 20 picks from CNN Underscored, judged by how they compare with past sale prices.

The Nano Charger Neo's sale price falls well below what the charger cost when it first went on sale this fall. Amazon $AMZN is selling the charger for $16 during Black Friday, down from a $26 list price, according to CNN Underscored. Notebookcheck reports that Anker launched the Neo in the U.S. in September at $25.99 on Amazon, so the crossed-out figure matches the launch price rather than an inflated tag. A charger this new has no long sale record to beat, which makes its launch price the benchmark. Still, Anker cut the price on a charger that was already cheap, not on a premium adapter, and that makes the hardware the next thing to judge.

Anker kept the price low by building a charger that does one job. The Neo is a USB-C wall adapter with a single port, according to Notebookcheck. It charges one device at a time and won't work as a hub for a desk full of gadgets. It also has no smart display, which means a buyer gets no screen showing charging status. Anker saved money on extras, not on basic function. Someone who tops up one phone at the bedside gives up nothing they would use, and that is the buyer this deal suits.

Amazon $AMZN's Black Friday price on the 512GB MacBook Neo is the lowest it has charged for Apple $AAPL's budget laptop since Prime Day in June. The Neo costs $649 at Amazon, according to CNN Underscored. Other earlier sales took only around $10 off, a cut most buyers would barely notice at checkout. A shopper who skipped the June sale has not had a lower price at Amazon since then. CNBC reports that Apple's advertised starting price covers the 256GB base model, not the 512GB version. A shopper comparing prices should make sure both figures refer to the same storage size.

Stepping up to the 13-inch MacBook Air means spending far more, with that model starting at $1,099, according to CNBC. Apple gave the Neo an A18 Pro chip rather than the M-series chips in the Air and Pro, so the buyer gives up some power in exchange for the lower price. Apple also rates the Neo for up to 16 hours on a charge, enough to get through a workday away from an outlet. The deal suits someone who wants macOS for everyday work and has no need for the Air's extra power.

Sony $SONY’s ULT Field 1 is at its lowest price ever in several colors, according to CNN Underscored, starting at $68 at Amazon $AMZN for the cheapest one. Prices vary by color, so check the exact shade you want, including Smoke Blue, the newest of the speaker’s five colors, according to SoundGuys.

The ULT Field 1 isn’t a new release. Smoke Blue is just a new finish, and the speaker itself is unchanged, SoundGuys reports. “For the past few years, the Ult Field 1 has been the portable speaker that I’ve relied on the most,” Altland said.

The money buys a speaker built to go outdoors rather than to anchor a party. SoundGuys reports that it carries an IP67 water and dust rating and that it is the entry-level model in Sony's lineup. An owner can take it into rain and dirt without much worry. A buyer who pays the $68 starting price gets the most basic speaker in that lineup, with durability as its main strength.

Anyone who wants a tough speaker to toss in a bag should buy it in one of the record-low colors, while anyone hosting a crowd should look further up Sony's lineup.

Amazon $AMZN is selling the pan for $116, 22% below its $149 list price and its best price ever, according to CNN Underscored. That’s a real low, but $116 is still a lot for one pan.

The deal makes the most sense for a cook who already needs a new pan or has been planning to buy a HexClad. If your current pan still works, the discount alone isn’t a reason to replace it.

For a cook who was already shopping for a pan, this is the lowest it has ever been.

Amazon $AMZN has cut $52 off this Cuisinart knife block set, bringing it to $78, according to CNN Underscored. That’s a big markdown, but few buyers ever pay the full list price.

Against earlier sales, the real saving is smaller. Past markdowns put the set around $90, so $78 is about $12 lower, but it’s still the lowest price it has had.

The stronger case for the set is how much of it a cook can actually use. Twelve of the 15 pieces are knives, so most of the $78 pays for blades rather than for extras. For someone stocking a first kitchen or replacing a drawer of mismatched knives, this is a complete block at a little under its usual sale price, and that matters more than the size of the markdown.

Rubbermaid’s nine-piece Brilliance glass set is $50 at Amazon $AMZN, its lowest price since 2023, according to CNN Underscored. Anyone who started watching it after 2023 has never seen it this cheap.

It’s also $15 lower than Amazon’s July offer. “We hardly ever see glass food storage containers from Rubbermaid go on sale,” Altland said. If you need new containers, it’s worth buying now rather than waiting.

Amazon $AMZN is selling the Aquarius for $50, matching its lowest Amazon price since 2019, according to CNN Underscored. For a product most people buy once and use daily for years, that’s the price a patient buyer waits for.

The saving is narrower than it looks, though. Against the $100 list price it seems dramatic, but it’s only $5 below recent sale prices. If you’ve been meaning to buy one, now is a good time. If you’re only curious, there’s no rush.

The Dyson V9 Motorbar is $270 at Amazon $AMZN for Black Friday, 55% off its list price, according to CNN Underscored. That matches its lowest price ever, which has happened only twice this year, and puts a Dyson stick vacuum under $300.

The deal is only at Amazon. If you already want a Dyson stick vacuum, it’s worth a close look while the event lasts. If you don’t care about the brand, compare it with the cordless models you were already considering.

For a Dyson under $300, this is the deal to check.

Amazon $AMZN is selling the Qrevo S Pro for less than it has charged at any earlier sale. The robot vacuum and mop costs $380 at Amazon for Black Friday, $70 below its earlier markdowns, according to CNN Underscored. A shopper who held out through those sales now pays less for having waited. Anyone who passed on this machine before has a new reason to look again, because this is a lower price, not the same deal coming back.

Most colors of Samsonite’s Freeform hardside carry-on are at least 51% off at Amazon $AMZN, according to CNN Underscored, at $108. A cut that deep across most of the range makes this a good time to buy if you need a new carry-on.

Price varies by color. Some sell for as little as $103, while a few shades don’t get the full discount, so check your preferred color before buying.

Before checking out, confirm the price shown for the color in the cart.

Black Friday is no longer a single morning of doorbusters. Amazon $AMZN now holds it as a sale that lasts well beyond one day, and that gives shoppers time to check a price before they buy instead of grabbing a deal on impulse. Through that whole stretch, nearly every product page shows a list price with a line through it and a percentage off, so almost everything looks like a bargain at first glance. The percentage tells a shopper little on its own. What separates a good deal from a routine one is how much less an item costs today than the last time it was on sale. Among this year's picks, that difference is a few dollars for some items and the lowest price in years for others. The useful question is how much lower an item costs than before, not how much it is marked down.

Price history matters most for new tech. A markdown on a product launched this year lowers the price of something that hasn’t been discounted much yet, while a cut on older stock may only match an earlier sale. The strongest deals here tend to be new gear at a first or record-low price. The weakest are items that already sold for about the same at earlier sales.

CNN Underscored set out to find Amazon's strongest Black Friday discounts across tech, kitchen, beauty, home and travel, from Apple $AAPL's new earbuds and a budget MacBook to a drip coffee maker, a robot vacuum and a Samsonite carry-on. Amazon is holding the sale for 12 days, which leaves room to weigh each of these prices against its own history before the event ends. The picks include everything from a phone charger to a laptop, so no single size of discount can tell a reader which deals are worth acting on. The slides that follow judge each deal on two things: how its price compares with what the item has sold for at earlier sales, and what a buyer gets for the money.

A watch released this fall has only a short sale record, so a Black Friday price on it can be judged against just a few weeks of history. Apple $AAPL unveiled the Series 12 on Sept. 9, 2026, according to CNBC. CNN Underscored reports that the watch has had only one price cut since then, and Amazon $AMZN's Black Friday price, from $329, is $20 below that earlier sale. That makes this the least the new watch has cost, but only by a small step. A shopper who skipped the first sale hasn't missed a deeper cut, and nobody buying now is getting a once-in-years bargain.

The $399 list price that Amazon crosses out is a real price. Apple set the watch at that price and did not raise it this year, according to CNBC. That means the $70 markdown is a true cut, not a discount off an inflated reference figure.

Part of what Apple promoted the watch for had not arrived when Apple unveiled it. Audio Intelligence, a feature Apple announced for the Series 12, had not shipped at the time of the event, and Apple expected health coaching for Apple Watch to launch later this year, according to CNBC. A buyer paying $329 is paying for the hardware plus software Apple promised. Before counting either feature as part of the value, it makes sense to confirm that it is available on the watch.

The deal suits a buyer who wants this year's watch now, at the lowest price it has had, but it gives no reason to rush for features that may still be on the way.

Anker dropped the extras without dropping the power. The Neo carries a 45W rating and can reach 65W, Notebookcheck reports, and Apple $AAPL's 40W Dynamic Power Adapter with 60W Max sold for $34.99 on Amazon around the time the Neo launched. At the sale price, a buyer pays far less for the Neo than for Apple's adapter and gets a higher rating at both its base and its peak. Anker also says the Neo charges the iPhone 18 Pro Max quickly, but those speed figures come from the company's own official tests.

The case for buying rests on what a shopper can check: a price well under the launch price and a power rating above Apple's.

For earbuds this popular, the size of the markdown matters less than whether a shopper can expect a lower price later. Amazon $AMZN is charging $179 for the AirPods Pro 3, no more than $10 above the cheapest they have ever been, according to CNN Underscored. Past sales have gone only a little lower, so a shopper who waits has limited room to save, though nothing guarantees that $179 is the floor. The open question is what $179 buys.

The earbuds have a strong reputation among iPhone owners, and their heart-rate sensor holds up. Rikka Altland, CNN Underscored’s senior deals editor, ranks them above any other wireless earbuds for iPhone users. In a study published in PLOS Digital Health, researchers at University College Dublin found the earbuds were off by 2.08 beats per minute on average. For someone who already runs with earbuds in, that can replace a separate fitness tracker for everyday workouts.

Accuracy on average does not mean accuracy at any given moment. Most single readings landed somewhere between 10.27 beats per minute too low and 10.22 too high, according to PLOS Digital Health. A miss that size is enough to put a runner in the wrong training zone. The earbuds are better for following trends over weeks than for pacing a hard interval. The people tested were 18 to 37 years old, so the study does not show how the sensor performs for older users.

For listening and casual fitness tracking, this near-record price is worth taking. Anyone who needs precise heart-rate zones should still budget for a chest strap.

The 512GB model is the step-up version, so the sale gets a buyer double the base storage for less. For a laptop kept for years, that extra room matters more than extra speed.

With no lower Amazon price since June, Black Friday is a reasonable time to buy.

Beats released the 360 over-ear headphones at the end of summer, and Amazon $AMZN is already selling them for $249 under a “First-Time Deal” label, according to CNN Underscored. Because this is the model’s first sale, there’s no earlier discount to compare it with yet.

Amazon is taking $101 off, which is real money on headphones this new. The trade-off is that there’s no sale history yet to show whether the price will drop further.

The headphones also give a buyer more years of use for the money. Their ear pads are swappable, so an owner can replace the part that touches the head when the padding wears out instead of replacing the whole pair. That makes the $249 purchase last longer than the original pads do.

For a buyer who wants this year's Beats over-ears, an early discount on headphones built to be kept going is reason enough not to wait.

UGreen’s Nexode power bank goes on sale often, so its list price says little. Amazon $AMZN’s Black Friday price of $60 is $10 below an earlier markdown, according to CNN Underscored. That’s a real but modest improvement: a reason to buy if you need a large power bank, not a drop you have to rush to catch.

The pack is worth $60 mainly to someone who charges a laptop and a phone on the road or at a desk. The 145W in its name is its maximum output. With two devices plugged in, the pack reached as much as 100W on one port and 45W on the other, according to Creative Bloq. That’s enough to charge a laptop and a phone at the same time. “The Nexode Power Bank 25000mAh 145W is a very capable power bank that knows its target market and delivers what most people want,” said Paul Hatton, a reviewer at Creative Bloq. For anyone who wants a battery that fits in a pocket, he suggests Anker’s lighter Nano 5K Power Bank instead.

For a traveler who works off a laptop, this is a well-timed buy below an earlier sale price, but anyone who only tops up a phone would be paying for more battery than they need.

The Technivorm Moccamaster KBGV costs $248 at Amazon $AMZN for Black Friday, the second-lowest price on its record, according to CNN Underscored. Discounts on this machine are uncommon, so this is close to its best price, though not quite at it.

The silver model sold for $239 on Prime Day in June 2026, according to Gear Patrol. Prices vary by color, so check the finish you want before deciding this is a low.

Spending close to $250 on a drip coffee maker makes sense only if the buyer plans to keep the machine for many years. Technivorm backs each unit with a five-year warranty, Gear Patrol reports, and its workers build the machines by hand in Amerongen, Netherlands. Those years of covered use are a better test of the price than the list price.

For a machine meant to last, this is a fair time to buy, and a shopper who passes on it could sit through several more sales before another markdown comes along.

For anyone who needs a full knife set, this is the lowest price it has had.

Even a dish rack is worth buying at the right moment, and for KitchenAid's full-size model that moment is this sale. Amazon $AMZN is selling the rack for $50, less than it has cost at any point in 2026, according to CNN Underscored, and $20 under its price at the most recent sale. A shopper who has been putting off replacing a worn rack has a real reason to buy now. That reason is the drop below the last sale price, not the struck-through list price.

The rack also has an independent test behind it. Bob Vila chose this KitchenAid after testing several racks, with testing by trained chef and reviewer Lizzy Briskin. That review dates to February 2024, before Amazon listed the rack under its “Rust-Resistant” name.

The rack's design keeps water off the counter and lets the owner clean the part that collects grime. Its base is angled so water drains into the sink, and Bob Vila reports that the drainage board can be removed for cleaning. The drainage works from one side only, so the rack suits a kitchen with a fixed spot beside the sink, where that side can sit over the basin. It also takes real counter space, measuring 7 by 20 by 15 inches, so anyone with a small kitchen should measure before buying.

For a household with a set place by the sink, $50 is the least this rack has cost in 2026, and the rack had a strong record before the sale began.

Amazon $AMZN has cut the Philips Sonicare 7300 to $100 for Black Friday, 50% off for the first time and $70 below its summer markdown, according to CNN Underscored. The kit also includes a travel case.

An electric toothbrush keeps costing money after checkout because the brush heads wear out. The 7300 tracks when a head needs replacing, and this kit includes two spare heads, so a new owner won’t need replacements for a while. Since the 50% markdown covers the whole kit, a buyer saves on both the handle and the first replacement heads.

Someone who needs a new toothbrush pays half the list price for the handle and its first replacement heads.

Amazon $AMZN has the Supersonic Nural at $349 for Black Friday, at least $100 off, according to CNN Underscored. It’s still a premium price, but the cut is big enough to matter on a single beauty tool.

Buyers don't have to trade taste for price, because Amazon has cut the price on three colors rather than on one leftover finish. A shopper can pick the color they want instead of settling for whichever one happens to be discounted. That choice helps most when the dryer is a gift and the buyer has to match someone else's taste.

For someone already set on a Dyson dryer, this is a good time to buy one.

Shark's TurboBlade Cool + Heat Tower Fan looks like a standout bargain at half price, but the size of its markdown is the weakest part of the case for buying it. Amazon $AMZN has cut the fan's price by 50%, to $200, according to CNN Underscored. Even at half price, that is a lot of money to spend on a fan. A shopper should judge the deal by more than the percentage on the tag. The question that matters is how $200 compares with what the fan has sold for earlier this year.

This is the second time in 2026 the fan has sold for $200, the best price of the year, and it’s $35 below the markdown earlier this fall, according to CNN Underscored. Shoppers who passed on that fall sale come out ahead.

The stronger reason to buy now is what the fan does in cold weather. Shark sells the TurboBlade as a Cool + Heat unit, so a November purchase is not a fan bought out of season. A household can use the one appliance to cool a room in summer and warm it in winter. A buyer spends $200 on two seasonal jobs rather than one.

The fan’s usefulness in both summer and winter, together with its best price of the year, makes a better case for buying than the size of the cut.

At $380, the Qrevo S Pro may also belong among robot cleaners it usually costs too much to rival. "The new Qrevo S Pro is normally a bit too expensive to earn a spot on our list of the best autonomous floor cleaners, but now that there are $320 in savings attached, that hierarchy of power might be able to change,” Altland said. She doesn’t say the machine has earned that spot, only that it could. At this price, the robot is a contender rather than a proven winner. A buyer should compare it with the robot cleaners that already rank highly before choosing it over them.

A shopper gets a cleaner that usually costs too much to rank among the best, now priced low enough to be in the running.

Amazon $AMZN is selling Sony $SONY’s WH-1000XM6 over-ear headphones for $348, $112 off and the lowest price they’ve had, according to CNN Underscored. A record low means the deal holds up against what the headphones have actually sold for, not just the list price.

Shoppers who’ve been waiting for the right moment have no earlier, lower price to hold out for. Anyone passing on this price is betting a later sale will go lower, and nothing in the sale history so far points that way.

#5474. Xi calls for inclusive regional cooperation based on solidarity, openness, innovation

BEIJING, Nov. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The following article was published today by China Daily.

President Xi Jinping outlined economy and trade, connectivity, innovation and development as four pillars for building an Asia-Pacific community and opening up new prospects for regional cooperation, as he chaired the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, on Thursday.

The gathering marked the third time that China has hosted the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders' meeting, following those held in Shanghai in 2001 and Beijing in 2014.

"Today, momentous changes not seen in a century are accelerating across the globe," Xi told the leaders and representatives of APEC economies and heads of international organizations attending the meeting.

APEC's 21 member economies are home to more than one-third of the world's population and account for over 60 percent of global GDP.

Xi called for efforts to build an Asia-Pacific community characterized by solidarity and mutual assistance, openness and integration, enterprise and innovation, as well as inclusive development.

Members of APEC are like passengers riding the same ship, he noted, adding that "to navigate the waves of the Pacific, we must unite as one and look out for each other".

"We must expand our shared interests, meet the difficulties and challenges together, and steadily build a shared sense of community," he said.

He called for upholding openness and integration, advancing economic integration and championing free and open trade and investment. Development should benefit everyone, he said, while taking into account the different needs of Asia-Pacific economies.

Xi said that China, an advocate, promoter and forerunner of Asia-Pacific economic cooperation, is ready to work with all parties to strengthen the pillar of economy and trade, upgrade the pillar of connectivity, foster the pillar of innovation and enhance the pillar of development.

On trade, Xi said the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific is a shared vision of APEC members, and he called for steady progress in realizing this vision and setting a higher standard for openness.

He urged efforts to align regional economic and trade agreements, boost trade and investment facilitation and digitalization, reduce barriers to trade and investment, and help economies build the capacity to participate in high-standard economic and trade arrangements.

Regarding connectivity, he called for stronger infrastructure networks, closer coordination of policies and regulations, and easier travel for business and tourism. Cultural and people-to-people exchanges should also be promoted to foster mutual understanding, he said.

On innovation, Xi described the digital economy and artificial intelligence as engines of innovation-driven growth.

"We should build an open ecosystem for innovation, encourage the broad application of AI, and promote the innovation-driven transformation and upgrading of industries," he said.

On development, he emphasized the need to promote regional cooperation on energy and food security, deepen anti-corruption governance across borders, and expand green and low-carbon cooperation to achieve sustainable economic growth.

He also called for improving livelihoods and investing in people to tap into the full potential of talent across the Asia-Pacific.

"China is rooted in the Asia-Pacific and will continue to support Asia-Pacific cooperation," Xi said.

He announced that China will provide $20 million to support APEC's practical cooperation, and will establish a Center for Asia-Pacific Community Studies in Shenzhen to conduct policy research and exchanges.

China will also set up cooperation institutions in areas including digital technology, cross-border data flows, clean energy and the development of small and medium-sized enterprises, he said.

Leaders and representatives of member economies delivered remarks in turn. All parties spoke highly of the fruitful outcomes of the APEC China Year, thanked China for its excellent work, and made positive responses to the major initiatives and measures put forward by Xi.

Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the International Monetary Fund, who was invited to brief the meeting on the state of the global economy, said that AI has had a material impact on global growth this year, helping counterbalance the economic effects of an energy supply shock.

Describing AI as a significant factor in medium-term competitiveness, productivity and growth, she called on economies to develop digital infrastructure, prepare workers for the technology, and address risks to financial stability and cybersecurity.

She also underscored the importance of dialogue and cooperation through forums such as APEC, saying that working together can help advance shared prosperity and peace.

After listening to the other participants' remarks, Xi called for turning the consensus on building an Asia-Pacific community into action, maintaining a clear direction for cooperation and delivering solid results to continuously achieve tangible and accessible outcomes.

At the conclusion of the meeting, leaders adopted the 2026 APEC Leaders' Declaration, which puts forward the Shenzhen Outlook on building an Asia-Pacific community, as well as three outcome documents covering trade, connectivity and innovation.

Vietnamese President To Lam, whose country will host APEC in 2027, welcomed leaders and representatives to attend next year's meeting.

With China's leadership and the positive contributions of its members, APEC 2026 has achieved important accomplishments, adding momentum to economic integration and development in the Asia-Pacific, he said.

#5473. China-based AI robotics biotech firm MegaRobo raises $200M to accelerate scientific discovery

Chinese biotech robotics firm MegaRobo Co. Ltd. today announced it has raised $200 million in new funding to invest in its core technology and expand its automated life sciences infrastructure for increasingly complex physical systems.

Founded in 2016, MegaRobo builds robotic systems that let artificial intelligence software run physical experiments, alongside precision measurement and inspection tools for manufacturers.

Investors joining the round included Oman Investment Authority, Asia Investment Capital, Granite Asia, Sinovation Ventures and CMB International. The company raised $600 million to date across multiple funding rounds, including nearly $300 million in Series C during 2022.

“The first generation of AI learned from humanity’s accumulated knowledge. The next generation will increasingly learn by acting in the physical world — through experiments, production and continuous feedback,” said founder and Chief Executive Daniel Huang. “That shift changes AI from a system that interprets the world into one that can help create new knowledge, materials, processes and products.”

The company’s two most prominently marketed offerings are Megalaxy Lab, an AI-connected experimental platform and CellVue T2000, its automated cell-imaging instrument. Both appear on the company’s English-language homepage. MegaRobo also sells more specialized lab equipment, including the Auflo sample-preparation workstation and the Seloris cell culturing automation system.

The key distinction is that Megalaxy Lab is the public face for the company’s AI-for-science strategy, while CellVue and other systems represent concrete examples of the instruments it builds for the industry.

The company said through Megalaxy it is making real-world experimentation programmable and accessible. Researchers and AI agents can configure experiments, route them through automated laboratory systems, track execution, receive structured, machine-readable results, and feed them directly into the next cycle of scientific reasoning. This includes virtual large data readouts that can be amplified as digital twins representing the scientific data, protein design, biochemistry and other properties.

MegaRobo said it’s working together with industry partners, including Tencent Cloud and Twist Bioscience, to expand its capability in the AI Science community with the launch of Poreva Open, a global AI protein design challenge open to all models and technical approaches. Megalaxy will provide wet-lab validation for more than 10,000 protein design sequences, creating an opportunity to test models against real experimental data.

The company is also developing the One Intelligence Stack as a common technology foundation for instruments, machines, materials processes and real-world feedback. It’s not just a collection of isolated AI applications and products, but a chain infrastructure that enables AI to act, learn and observe across complex physical environments.
