#5472. 10M transactions show off-MLS private listings discount

A 10M-transaction review found coming soon listings that later hit the MLS sold for higher prices than comparable MLS-only listings. Listings kept private and off the MLS sold for less, with larger discounts reported in majority non-white and Hispanic neighborhoods.  AI Summary

Compass wants buyers to see it first. A study of more than 10 million home sales suggests some sellers would do better if everyone saw it at once. The gap between the marketing and the money is the real story.

On September 22, Compass launched “See It First,” the centerpiece of its largest Compass.com redesign in a decade, pulling coming-soon and private exclusive listings from its nine brands into one early-access showcase. “With See It First, we’re giving consumers the opportunity to discover more homes earlier,” Julie Keef, Compass’s head of consumer search, told HousingWire. Compass cited 56% year-over-year traffic growth on its site in August and a multimillion-dollar ad campaign behind the launch.

The timing was awkward. The day after the redesign, HousingWire reported on a study from the Association of Real Estate License Law Officials (ARELLO) that reviewed more than 10 million residential transactions between January 2024 and June 2026. The numbers complicate the private-listing story.

The study drew a line most consumers never hear. Coming-soon listings, the kind that get pre-marketed and then hit the MLS, sold for about $9,200 more than comparable MLS listings in the mid-market and close to $17,000 more at the top. Listings that stayed private and off the MLS did the opposite, coming in roughly $5,000 below MLS in the mid-range and about $3,500 below at the high end.

Powerfact: The premium belongs to exposure, not exclusivity. Pre-marketing plus full MLS reach won. Staying hidden lost.

The trend lines tell the same story. Coming-soon volume climbed 13 percent in the year ending June 2026. Private listings fell 3 percent over the same stretch. The market is quietly voting with its feet, even as the marketing points the other way.

Then there is the finding no fiduciary should skim past. The private-listing discount landed hardest in non-white neighborhoods. Private listings sold about 0.88% below MLS in majority-white areas, 2.21% below in majority non-white areas, and 3.33% below in majority-Hispanic areas. ARELLO stressed the gaps “do not establish causation or unlawful discrimination” but warrant “further examination.”

Powerfact: A smaller audience is a smaller check, and the sellers with the least room to lose lost the most.

Compass CEO Robert Reffkin has made no secret of where he stands. He has called the Clear Cooperation Policy “anti-competitive and anti-consumer” and said Compass “has not and will not adhere” to it. He has a fair point that the industry defends old rules on autopilot. But this study is not an association talking point. It is transaction data, and it says the gated model Compass is now marketing at scale tends to cost the person who owns the house.

Give Compass its due. It built a genuine consumer destination, kept the listing agent’s name and photo front and center instead of selling leads back to them, and made pre-marketing easy. The coming-soon half of the strategy is exactly what the data rewards. The gated half is where sellers should slow down.

Lead with the numbers, not the logo. Before you take a listing, walk the seller through both roads in dollars. Pre-market to build demand, then open the home to the full market through the MLS. That combination is what the study rewards.

If a seller wants to stay private, document it. Put the estimated cost of reduced exposure in writing and let them decide with eyes open. That single habit protects your client and protects you.

And sharpen your language. “Coming soon” is a launch runway. “Private” is a closed door. Selling them as the same thing is how good sellers quietly lose money.

Portals will keep spending to own the first click. Your job sits at the other end of the deal, on the seller’s final number. The agents who thrive from here will be the ones who can explain exposure, price it honestly, and prove the point with data instead of a slogan. The tools are changing fast. The fiduciary duty underneath them has not moved an inch.

Darryl Davis, CSP, is a national speaker, real estate coach, and the bestselling author of How to Become a Power Agent® in Real Estate. Learn more at darrylspeaks.com.

#5471. Bitcoin Price Holds $64K Ahead of Nvidia Earnings: AI Bubble Finally Pops?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin price is struggling to find direction just below $65,000 as we brace for Nvidia earnings report. BTC USD has recovered from its weekend low near $62,000, but remains down 13% over seven days. Its modest rebound comes as technology stocks face yet another selling pressure.

This timing puts the Bitcoin price in an uncomfortable position. Nvidia’s results could determine if investors return to risk assets or abandon another crowded trade. With market sentiment still deep in extreme fear, we still have little conviction that the worst is over.

Meanwhile, Michael Burry is increasing his bearish bets against technology stocks. The investor made famous by The Big Short is targeting the Nasdaq-100 and semiconductor sector. His positioning raises an ugly question: Is the AI boom approaching its own dot-com moment?

Burry doubled his Nasdaq-100 put position on November 12, targeting early 2027 options 20% below the index’s market level. He also bought back part of his previously reduced bearish position in the VanEck Semiconductor ETF.

His argument goes beyond stretched stock valuations. Burry believes conventional accounting earnings can exaggerate technology companies’ underlying profitability. Depreciation schedules, particularly across expensive data-center infrastructure, sit at the center of his concerns.

Consider a hyperscaler investing billions in GPUs and AI infrastructure. Those purchases become capital assets rather than immediate operating expenses. Companies subsequently recognize depreciation across their estimated useful lives.

This accounting treatment can make current earnings look stronger than the underlying cash economics. If hardware becomes obsolete faster than expected, reported profitability could overstate actual investment returns.

The concern becomes significant when companies must continuously replace expensive accelerators. Their infrastructure spending needs to generate sufficient revenue before the equipment loses economic value.

Burry isn’t alone in questioning the investment cycle. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman previously acknowledged excessive enthusiasm surrounding artificial intelligence.

“Are we in a phase where investors as a whole are overexcited about AI? My opinion is yes,” Altman said.

Jeff Bezos offered another interpretation, describing the spending cycle as an “industrial bubble.” He argued that excessive investment could still produce valuable infrastructure, even when individual investors lose money.

Nvidia’s own Jensen Huang previously defended the industry’s economics. According to him, the AI infrastructure was already generating productive revenue, rather than merely attracting speculative capital.

The disagreement exposes the central tension surrounding the AI bubble. Demand can be genuine while valuations and infrastructure commitments become unsustainable.

The dot-com crash offers an important historical comparison. The Nasdaq Composite lost 78% between March 2000 and October 2002. Internet technology survived, but countless businesses and investors did not.

Today’s AI infrastructure market has similarities, particularly aggressive capital expenditure and expectations of exponential demand. However, established hyperscalers now finance much of the expansion through enormous operating businesses.

Now, can future AI revenue justify today’s investment?

Bitcoin once traded with relatively little correlation to traditional equities. That relationship changed dramatically as institutional participation expanded.

CME Group’s historical correlation research illustrates the shift. Between 2014 and 2016, Bitcoin’s correlation with the S&P 500 stood near -0.01. Its correlation with the Nasdaq-100 was effectively zero. Between 2020 and 2022, those correlations climbed to 0.40 and 0.42, respectively. They remained positive through April 2025, reaching 0.30 against both indices.

The shift matters because institutional investors increasingly treat Bitcoin as another liquid risk asset. Portfolio rebalancing, leveraged positions, and macroeconomic conditions can influence its price alongside technology stocks.

An AI sell-off could create another liquidity shock across crypto. Investors facing losses elsewhere might sell Bitcoin to raise cash or reduce overall exposure. But an AI correction doesn’t automatically invalidate Bitcoin’s monetary thesis. A technology valuation reset could eventually redirect capital toward alternative assets.

The gap lies between an isolated technology correction and a financial liquidity crisis. Bitcoin could eventually decouple from semiconductor stocks under the first scenario. The second could pressure both markets simultaneously. For now, Bitcoin price remains exposed to the same risk appetite driving technology shares.

Nvidia’s third-quarter fiscal 2027 results arrive at a particularly sensitive moment. Wall Street expects $109 billion in revenue and $2.47 in adjusted earnings per share.

Investors will focus heavily on Data Center revenue, gross margins, and forward guidance. The company’s Vera Rubin platform also faces scrutiny as customers expand their AI infrastructure commitments.

A headline earnings beat might not satisfy investors demanding another acceleration in growth. Strong revenue accompanied by cautious guidance could trigger another sell-the-news reaction.

The opposite scenario could restore confidence across technology stocks. Strong guidance would reinforce expectations that hyperscaler spending remains sustainable. Bitcoin could benefit if investors regain their appetite for speculative assets.

Technically, Bitcoin needs to stabilize above its recent $62,000 weekend low. A break below that level would expose the psychologically important $60,000 threshold.

A stronger recovery would put $68,000 back into view as an important technical resistance area. Reclaiming that level could help establish if buyers are returning.

Bitcoin price now faces a test extending beyond crypto markets. Nvidia must demonstrate that AI infrastructure spending can translate into durable earnings growth.

Burry is betting that expectations have run too far ahead. Huang’s former company built the infrastructure powering the AI revolution, but investors now need proof of its economic returns.

If the AI bubble starts deflating, Bitcoin must answer another question: Can it survive without Wall Street’s appetite for technology risk?

#5469. Covius rolls out capital markets dashboard for bulk title reviews

Covius expanded high-volume batch title processing and launched Loanscape CM for capital markets. The dashboard pairs bulk title searches with rule validation across 100-plus attributes to flag loans that may need additional review.  AI Summary

Covius announced on Thursday that it has expanded its high-volume title capabilities and launched a new dashboard designed to help capital markets clients review property information and identify potential risks in large loan portfolios.

The company said its Covius Settlement Services (CSS) business unit has enhanced its batch title processing capabilities and introduced Loanscape CM (Capital Markets), a dashboard that provides greater visibility into title-related risks and helps streamline portfolio reviews.

Capital markets investors and due-diligence providers rely on large volumes of property reports for portfolio acquisitions, risk monitoring and loan reviews. Following its integration of Title365 operations earlier this year, Covius said it has increased its capacity to process and analyze property information while reducing turnaround times.

The new dashboard combines high-volume title searches with automated business rule validation to identify loans that may require additional review.

The company’s automated workflow evaluates more than 100 attributes in a standard title report to identify potential risks or conditions that warrant further investigation, said Joe Chappell, president of Covius Settlement Services.

“On bulk orders of any size, our new dashboard is able to isolate the loans that require further internal review prior to delivery, as well as identify the risk elements necessary for our clients’ review, creating significant efficiencies for large scale transactions,” he added.

Loanscape CM is the latest addition to the company’s Loanscape Decisioning Framework, a suite of title decisioning tools. The suite also includes Loanscape HE (Home Equity), which provides underwriter-approved title clearance for home equity originations, and Loanscape LM (Loss Mitigation), which identifies title-related information and potential loss-mitigation options in a single view.

The Loanscape framework integrates with major point-of-sale, origination, servicing and default systems, as well as multiple order management platforms, to automate processes and streamline operations.

Covius acquired Title365’s operations earlier this year and integrated them with its existing title business. The combined operations now operate under the Covius Settlement Services name.

#5468. OCLC and Ecole Solutions partner to bring EZproxy services to libraries across India

Ecole Solutions is now OCLC's distributor for hosted EZproxy and EZproxyAnalytics, providing local sales, training, and support for Indian institutions

DUBLIN, Ohio and BANGALORE, India, Nov. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- OCLC and Ecole Solutions, the Bangalore-based provider of technology solutions for libraries and academic institutions, today announced a distribution partnership to make OCLC's hosted EZproxy and EZproxy Analytics available to academic and research libraries in India.

Ecole Solutions will market and sell both services and provide local customer support, including implementation, training, and technical assistance. The distribution agreement covers much of the Indian subcontinent, including India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Bhutan.

OCLC and Ecole Solutions are partnering to make OCLC's EZproxy available to academic and research libraries in India

"We're delighted to welcome Ecole Solutions as our partner in India," said Eric van Lubeek, Managing Director, OCLC EMEA/Asia Pacific. "Ecole Solutions' local knowledge and technical expertise will help libraries quickly implement and realize the benefits of EZproxy services. This partnership reflects our long-term commitment to supporting the Indian library community."

India's One Nation One Subscription (ONOS) initiative expands access to scholarly research publications across the country. At the same time, libraries continue to invest in databases, e-books, and other digital resources and need reliable information to assess their use and value.

"EZproxy works with virtually any publisher and alongside the national federations and institutional logins libraries already use, giving researchers one way into their collection, from anywhere," said L. S. Venkatesh, Director, Ecole Solutions. "Librarians gain the usage evidence they need for collection decisions and quality reviews. OCLC hosts the service, and our team provides local support."

OCLC and Ecole Solutions leaders will introduce the new partnership and meet with library leaders at the PLANNER 2026 Convention in Guwahati, India, 25-27 November.

Libraries in India interested in learning more can visit https://www.ecoleglobal.com/.

More about EZproxy is on the OCLC website.

Ecole Solutions is an India-based technology services provider specializing in digital transformation for educational institutions. It delivers advanced plagiarism and AI-detection software, alongside e-learning and campus management solutions. These tools empower universities nationwide to enforce strict academic integrity and optimize operations.

OCLC is a nonprofit global library organization that provides shared technology services, original research, and community programs so that libraries can better fuel learning, research, and innovation. Through OCLC, member libraries cooperatively produce and maintain WorldCat, the most comprehensive global network of data about library collections and services. Libraries gain efficiencies through OCLC's WorldShare, a complete set of library management applications and services built on an open, cloud-based platform. It is through collaboration and sharing of the world's collected knowledge that libraries can help people find answers they need to solve problems. Together as OCLC, member libraries, staff, and partners make breakthroughs possible.

#5467. Anthropic's CFO says IPO will fund continued compute and R&D spending

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Krishna Rao said the IPO gives the company access to cheaper capital as Anthropic stock opened at $111.50 on Nasdaq

Anthropic Chief Financial Officer Krishna Rao said on Thursday that the company's initial public offering will let it keep investing to stay at the frontier of AI development, according to Bloomberg.

“Building at the frontier is a capital-intensive endeavor, and we are going to make the investments to continue to be at the frontier,” Rao told Bloomberg Television before the stock’s opening trade. Rao said the offering gives Anthropic access to cheaper capital.

Anthropic priced its initial public offering at $83 a share on Wednesday. Anthropic stock began trading on the Nasdaq $NDAQ Global Select Market on Thursday under the symbol ANT and opened at $111.50, according to Bloomberg. The offering is expected to close on Nov. 20, and the company granted underwriters a 30-day option to buy up to 147 million more shares of Class A common stock.

Anthropic puts roughly three-quarters of its compute toward R&D work, according to Bloomberg. The company has pledged roughly $901 billion toward compute and infrastructure, with payments stretching across almost two decades, according to Bloomberg, citing a November securities filing.

Rao said Anthropic must work through a "cone of uncertainty" while weighing the revenue it expects against how much compute and infrastructure it will require. He said the company intends to be "forward-leaning" in securing compute, yet cautious about how much it spends. "We have the best compute efficiency in the world, we believe," Rao said.

Rao said computing deals with companies including Alphabet $GOOGL's Google and SpaceX give Anthropic "a tremendous amount of flexibility." "We have a lot of options when we buy compute, and we can pick the best ones relative to our overall portfolio," he said.

Anthropic is the first developer of cutting-edge AI models to list its shares publicly, according to Bloomberg. The company’s price topped the $70 to $78 range it had guided for the offering, which puts its fully diluted valuation at roughly $1.5 trillion, Bloomberg said.

#5466. Rocket, Mr. Cooper to pay $6.75M over cybersecurity lapses in New York

Rocket Mortgage and Mr. Cooper Group agreed to pay $6.75 million to the New York State Department of Financial Services to settle alleged violations of the state’s cybersecurity regulations.  AI Summary

Rocket Mortgage and Mr. Cooper Group have agreed to pay a combined $6.75 million to the New York State Department of Financial Services (NYDFS) to resolve allegations of cybersecurity violations tied to data protection, risk assessments and incident reporting, the parties announced Thursday.

Rocket will pay $2 million to settle NYDFS claims that the company failed to report cybersecurity incidents in a timely manner, did not implement multifactor authentication, and lacked sufficient policies and procedures to safeguard customers’ nonpublic information. Mr. Cooper, meanwhile, will pay $4.75 million related to a November 2023 cyberattack that exposed sensitive borrower data and disrupted online operations.

In a statement given to HousingWire, a Rocket spokesperson said the company “has strengthened our information security program, adopted a formal data disposal policy, enhanced monitoring, team member training and testing.”

“Rocket Mortgage today entered two separate consent orders with the New York State Department of Financial Services,” the statement read. “One concerns a 2023 cybersecurity incident at Mr. Cooper, two years before Rocket’s acquisition. Rocket, as Mr. Cooper’s successor, will adhere to the required information security controls and audits. The second consent order concerns a 2021 on-site examination that identified gaps in Rocket Mortgage’s processes and procedures related to multi-factor authentication, secure data disposal and incident notification.”

NYDFS found that Rocket Mortgage failed to notify the department of cybersecurity incidents within the required 72 hours on seven occasions between December 2019 and August 2021. In six of the seven cases, NYDFS only learned of the incidents after examiners uncovered them during a 2021 on-site examination.

That exam also identified gaps in Rocket’s processes and procedures related to multifactor authentication, secure data disposal and incident notification, according to the consent order.

The NYDFS action against Mr. Cooper stems from a widely reported cybersecurity incident in November 2023 that forced the company to lock down certain technology systems, including access to its online payment portal.

According to the consent order, hackers impersonated employees on phone calls to the IT help desk to fraudulently obtain temporary passwords. They then used the credentials to gain access to company systems and bypass multifactor authentication controls.

NYDFS said Mr. Cooper had not completed a comprehensive cybersecurity risk assessment for almost four years leading up to the attack, leaving the servicer unprepared for the threat.

The department found that Mr. Cooper’s failure to protect nonpublic information stored within its systems resulted in the exposure of millions of individuals’ Social Security numbers, dates of birth and other nonpublic information, including data affecting hundreds of thousands of New York residents.

The incident also disrupted Mr. Cooper’s online business operations for five days, temporarily cutting off many customers from access to their accounts.

“New York’s cybersecurity regulation requires covered entities to maintain strong safeguards to protect consumer data, understand evolving risks, and report cybersecurity incidents to regulators,” NYDFS Acting Superintendent Kaitlin Asrow said in a statement. “The Department is committed to rigorous oversight to ensure regulated institutions protect consumers and adapt their cybersecurity programs to evolving risks.” Beyond the monetary penalty, Rocket is expected to strengthen its controls to protect its information systems and consumers’ private information.

#5464. Hitachi Vantara bets smarter storage can close AI’s pilot-to-production gap

Enterprises pushing AI from pilot to production are learning that data, not GPUs, is the hardest part, and open table formats such as Apache Iceberg are part of the answer. Demand for AI infrastructure shows few signs of slowing, but much of the information companies need is still scattered, ungoverned and out of reach.

That pressure is turning storage into an active layer that classifies, governs and serves data to models. Unstructured files such as logs and medical images hold intelligence AI can now extract, according to Arun Prasad Raman (pictured, left), vice president of hybrid cloud and AI infrastructure at Hitachi Vantara Corp.

“Storage is not seen as just storing the data,” Raman said. “You need to bring in more intelligence natively rather than moving the data to another replication and bringing it back for, say, indexing. If it can do it natively, that’s where the value add is.”

Raman and Jeff Lundberg (right), principal product and solutions manager at Hitachi Vantara, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed AI’s pilot-to-production gap, Apache Iceberg and how Hitachi Vantara is adding intelligence to storage. (* Disclosure below.)

Reference architectures for AI factories and data platforms are largely settled. Most projects stall because data is spread across on-premises systems, software-as-a-service applications and the cloud, while access control, governance and shifting regulations add friction, according to Lundberg. Hitachi Vantara is responding with industry-specific solutions built on its Hitachi iQ stack and its sister businesses’ rail and energy experience, he explained.

“It’s about the outcome more so than the technology that we’re trying to put into place,” Lundberg said. “That’s an enabler to get you to the solution you’re trying to get to.”

Much of that work now happens in storage. Last week, Hitachi Vantara expanded its VSP One platform with new object storage and data lakehouse capabilities. A service in its object store flags files containing personal information, such as Social Security numbers. Data scientists can then keep that data out of specific models or block its replication to another country, Raman explained.

“That’s the intelligence we are adding into the storage itself,” Raman said. “So that’s where the evolution of storage is making it more intelligent.”

Analytics follow the same logic. CT scan metadata can be stored in Apache Iceberg format on the company’s object store and queried directly. An application could list every abdominal scan from the past year without a separate extract, transform and load or ETL process or database, Raman noted.

“Whether it’s a backup or it’s 10 years old, it still carries some intelligence,” Raman said. “As long as it carries intelligence, it becomes important to AI.”

#5462. Dow dives 748 points as stocks hit session lows the moment Anthropic starts trading

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Anthropic stock opened at $111.50, up 34% from its IPO price, as the S&P 500 fell 1% and the Nasdaq dropped 0.9%

Anthropic stock opened at $111.50 on the Nasdaq $NDAQ on Thursday, 34% above its $83 IPO price, and the major U.S. stock indexes fell to session lows as trading began.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 748 points, or 1.5%. The S&P 500 slipped 1%, and the Nasdaq fell 0.9% after having climbed by as much as 2% at its peak. Anthropic trades under the ticker ANT and opened before noon.

Anthropic set its share price higher than the $70 to $78 band it had signaled to investors and enlarged the deal, according to The Wall Street Journal. The offering is the largest on record. Semiconductor shares and other artificial-intelligence names had rallied earlier in the morning once the pricing was announced.

At one stage, Anthropic stock dropped over 10% from where it opened, but it later recovered to a 20% gain, near $100 a share.

Nvidia $NVDA, Micron $MU Technology and Meta $META Platforms gave up their gains. Advanced Micro Devices stock fell over 8% after Hunterbrook Capital revealed it was betting against the shares, citing possible violations of U.S. export controls tied to China, according to CNBC.

Steve Sosnick, chief strategist at Interactive Brokers, described the decline as part of a pattern, according to CNBC. "It seems to be merely the latest round of 'sell the rally' behavior that has pervaded market activity this month," Sosnick said. "The drop was quick, stunning, and meaningful. It appears that traders were waiting for the deal to begin trading to unleash another bout of selling, and once SPX broke through its recent support, that led to another round of sharp declines."

Not everyone on Wall Street viewed the drop as a concern. “Today doesn’t matter,” Ted Mortonson, a tech strategist at Baird, told CNBC. “It’s a blink of an eye of their journey. It’s an important event, but how they navigate the next three years that will determine valuation.”

Investors have grown warier of AI lately, questioning if the massive outlays to construct the technology's infrastructure will eventually deliver substantial returns, according to CNBC.

#5461. ADP Acquires ZenBusiness

Transaction extends ADP's offerings to include formation solutions and added compliance capabilities; expands ability to serve entrepreneurs and small businesses from startup through scale

ROSELAND, N.J., Nov. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- ADPÂ® (Nasdaq: ADP), a global leader in HR and payroll solutions, today announced that it has acquired ZenBusiness, a formation and compliance services business with an AI-powered platform that has helped over one million entrepreneurs begin their small business journey.  With this acquisition, ADP can now support small businesses across all aspects of starting a business and scaling it, including business formation, insurance, payroll, compliance, HR and workforce management.

"For more than 77 years, ADP has helped small businesses and entrepreneurs navigate complex regulatory environments and achieve their dreams with confidence," said Maria Black, president and CEO, ADP. "The ZenBusiness team shares in this vision and we are excited to welcome them to ADP.  For many small business owners, ADP is the trusted name they turn to for payroll, compliance and HR. Together, we will support the millions of entrepreneurs who start a new business each year with the tools they need to build and manage their business and workforce, from day one."

Founded in 2015 and based in Austin, Texas, ZenBusiness provides business entity formation, compliance services, and strategic guidance.  ADP supports more than 980,000 small business clients in managing their payroll, tax, insurance and HR needs compliantly and with confidence. With this acquisition, ZenBusiness' AI-powered technology and digital customer engagement capabilities will build on ADP's scale and deep domain expertise to create an unmatched, integrated solution that will help entrepreneurs and small business owners manage their business compliantly from day one through scaling their workforce.

"For more than a decade, our mission at ZenBusiness has been to champion the dreams of entrepreneurs with the critical formation and compliance solutions they need to start and grow a business," said Ross Buhrdorf, CEO of ZenBusiness.  "The ZenBusiness team is excited to join ADP and leverage our collective expertise to support small businesses throughout the entire business lifecycle. I can't imagine a better home for our team, our clients and our mission."

About ADPADP has been shaping the world of work with innovation and expertise for more than 75 years. As a global leader in HR and payroll solutions, ADP continuously works to solve business challenges for our clients and their workers, from simple, easy-to-use tools for small businesses to fully integrated platforms for global enterprises â and everything in between. Always Designing for People means we're focused on just that â people. We use our unmatched AI-driven insights and proven expertise to design innovative solutions that help people achieve greater success at work. More than 1.1 million clients across 140+ countries rely on ADP's exceptional service to support their people and drive their business forward. HR, Talent, Time Management, Benefits, Compliance, and Payroll. Learn more at ADP.com

#5460. Exclusive: ICE Mortgage Technology appoints AI strategy, product leaders

ICE Mortgage Technology appointed Kiran Sahota as vice president of AI strategy and Leslie Peeler as vice president of product.  AI Summary

ICE Mortgage Technology has appointed Kiran Sahota as vice president of AI strategy and Leslie Peeler as vice president of product, the company announced Thursday.

The two executives will help guide how ICE applies artificial intelligence, automation and other technology across its mortgage platforms, including origination, servicing, and data and analytics. The leadership moves come as lenders and servicers face persistent pressure to reduce costs while managing rising compliance and performance requirements.

“Kiran and Leslie have been at the forefront of major technology and operational change in our industry,” Bob Hart, president of ICE Mortgage Technology, said in a statement. “They have applied emerging technologies to some of the toughest challenges facing lenders and servicers, and their expertise will be instrumental as we continue investing in technology that helps our customers succeed.”Peeler joins ICE from mortgage subservicer Cenlar, where she most recently served as executive vice president and chief operating officer. Cenlar is in the process of being acquired by Pennymac. Her background also includes senior leadership roles at IBM and a stint as senior vice president of credit portfolio management at Fannie Mae.

At ICE, Peeler will oversee servicing product development, including the MSP loan servicing system.

“Mortgage servicing is no longer just about administering loans. It’s about helping clients adapt to changing market conditions, operate more intelligently and build stronger relationships with homeowners,” Peeler said.Sahota will lead the application of AI and intelligent automation across ICE’s mortgage technology business. Her role will focus on identifying high-impact use cases where AI can address operational and customer experience challenges for lenders and servicers.

She previously served as chief information officer at Freedom Mortgage and later as president of Xpanse, a mortgage technology company launched by the founders of Freedom. Earlier in her career, Sahota held vice president roles at Rocket Mortgage and Rock Ventures.

“Having worked on the lender and servicer side has given me a deep understanding of the challenges they face every day,” Sahota said. “The question shouldn’t be where we can add AI, but what problems matter most and whether AI is the best way to solve them.”

#5458. Alphabet is raising at least C$5 billion in a new Canadian bond sale

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The offering includes floating- and fixed-rate notes maturing in three to 40 years, Alphabet's second Canadian dollar deal

Alphabet $GOOGL, the parent of Google, is offering five series of Canadian dollar notes in a bond sale that aims to raise at least C$5 billion ($3.5 billion), according to Bloomberg.

The offering includes one series of floating rate notes and four series of fixed rate notes, according to Alphabet's preliminary prospectus supplement dated Thursday. The document leaves the amounts, interest rates and maturity dates blank. The floating rate notes will pay interest quarterly at Daily Compounded CORRA plus a margin to be set.

Maturities will run from three years out to 40 years, and early talk puts the longest piece roughly 190 basis points over comparable sovereign bonds, according to Bloomberg.

The notes will be senior unsecured obligations that rank equally with Alphabet's other unsecured and unsubordinated debt, the company said. They will be structurally subordinated to debt and other obligations of its subsidiaries. The notes will not be listed on a securities exchange, and no public trading market exists for any series.

RBC Capital Markets, Scotiabank and TD Securities are the joint book-running managers. The underwriters expect to deliver the notes through CDS Clearing and Depository Services on the third business day after pricing, the company said.

Alphabet sold its first Canadian dollar notes six months ago, according to Bloomberg. That May offering raised C$8.5 billion across four parts and formed part of a multi-market sale that brought in about $17 billion. Amazon $AMZN.com followed a month later with C$14 billion in high-grade bonds denominated in Canadian dollars, and each transaction set a record as the largest Canadian corporate-bond sale up to that point.

Alphabet has also tapped other currencies. It had brought in €6 billion ($6.73 billion) by issuing euro-denominated notes by early November. Bloomberg reports that the company has raised money in euros, pounds and Australian dollars.

Technology companies have borrowed heavily since last year, taking on several hundred billion dollars to pay for server farms and semiconductor acquisitions, according to Bloomberg.

#5457. Zoning reform is remaking parking lots into a housing paradise

Parking lot redevelopment is gaining momentum as zoning reforms expand by-right and ministerial approvals on commercial land. The tradeoffs include labor and affordability rules, tighter lending, and continued lawsuits over eligibility and process.  AI Summary

Developers across the country paved over paradise to put up a parking lot. But changes to zoning laws to increase housing supply now have developers paving over parking lots to create a housing paradise.

In California, a series of state laws has made that easier. Florida lawmakers have gone after the same land. San Diego suburb National City took matters into its own hands. Because of its high housing costs, California has been the leading model for how reforms can work. But the Golden State is also a model for how neighborhood advocates and cities fight the reforms, often rendering them worth less than the paper they’re written on.

Much of the zoning reform push across the country focuses on where ground-up developers could build residential density, particularly infill in urban areas. The pressure is on land.

Underused parking lots are one option. The median share of downtown land used only for parking is about 26% in U.S. cities with more than 500,000 people, according to the U.S. Department of Transportation.

California’s Assembly Bill 2011 created a ministerial approval path, exempt from environmental review, for apartments on sites where office, retail or parking is a principal use. AB 2243 expanded those tools for commercially zoned property when it took effect last year.

Florida’s Live Local Act requires cities and counties to allow multifamily rentals by right on commercial, industrial and mixed-use land when a share of the units is affordable. Lawmakers have amended the law multiple times, including this year, since enactment in 2023.

National City shows how the local action can work. The city loosened height limits in its mixed-use zones last year, making underused lots more workable for housing.

National City Investment Group has broken ground on Market View, a 120-unit workforce housing project that will replace a parking lot beside Manolo Farmers Market in National City. This small grocery chain has locations in San Diego, where leaders have instituted reforms that have faced neighborhood challenges and lawsuits that new state law quashes.

Opponents still turn to the courts, even though reforms were meant to curtail or preclude lawsuits. And they are getting more inventive.

In San Francisco, neighbors are suing over an 848-unit project at 15 Marina Blvd. The towers would replace the Safeway’s parking lot and rise above a newly built store. They say the city wrongly ruled it eligible for AB 2011 and denied them a hearing.

To get the case into federal court, local opponents invoked an 1871 law, commonly known as the Ku Klux Klan Act. The developer wants the federal court to dismiss the case.

In Los Angeles, the fight is over habitat. Planners rejected 398 homes at the Woodland Hills Country Club in August, citing mountain lions. The state Department of Housing and Community Development said the city violated AB 2011. Pro-housing groups have sued the city while the developer threatens its own lawsuit for damages that could exceed $20 million.

Under AB 2011, a qualifying project gets ministerial approval, which means municipal staff checks it against objective standards and no hearing is required. Residents lose the chance to comment on the project or its environmental effects, said Sheri Bonstelle, a land-use attorney at Greenberg Lusker who represents developers, told HousingWire TBD.

“Neighbors are really upset that they no longer have a voice at all,” Bonstelle said.

Developers will also pay for the faster path. AB 2011 projects must meet labor standards, including prevailing wage. Bonstelle said that can add roughly 30% to construction costs, which developers weigh against discretionary review and the risk of a lawsuit under the California Environmental Quality Act.

“It’s literally a monetary analysis,” Bonstelle said.

The math has worked for some of her clients, she said. They’ll trade off higher costs for the elimination of entitlement risk and confidence that a project can be built. Bonstelle said lenders also favor the ministerial path. That’s especially crucial now, given the tight lending environment.

How much access neighbors get depends on the city. Los Angeles has a detailed AB 2011 application, Bonstelle said, so developers must file substantial information that neighbors can request and review. The city knew these projects were coming and was thorough about what had to be filed. Smaller cities are the bigger problem, she said.

“It’s more of an issue with the smaller cities that haven’t had the projects come through yet,” Bonstelle said.

Some cities hand developers a checklist meant for a building permit, she said. Her firm then goes through item by item with city attorneys to explain that most of those materials are not due at the planning stage of ministerial review.

Other cities believe state law should not apply to them and decline to process applications, Bonstelle said. In one case, her firm is working with a small city that has been “incredibly difficult.” The firm is asking the state Department of Housing and Community Development for a technical assistance letter explaining what the law requires.

Florida’s Live Local Act addresses similar commercial land. Cities and counties must approve multifamily rentals administratively on commercial, industrial and mixed-use land, with no rezoning or public hearing, if at least 40% of units are affordable for 30 years. Lawmakers have amended the law three times since 2023, most recently in 2026.

The law covers parking lots zoned for those uses, Patrick Chopson, an Atlanta architect and co-founder of Cove, told HousingWire TBD. “That’s a big deal,” Chopson said. Cove, which has a proprietary AI platform, recently acquired Deerfield Beach, Fla., architectural firm Gallo Herbert Architects. The firm has done a lot of work statewide in affordable housing.

The act also funds projects. In St. Petersburg, Nashville-based Elmington Capital Group plans Skyway Flats, a 174-unit affordable apartment building on surface parking next to an assisted living facility in the city’s Skyway Marina District.

The five-story building will have 28 one-bedroom, 100 two-bedroom and 46 three-bedroom apartments. All will target households earning 30% to 80% of the area median income, and 18 will go to young adults aging out of foster care.

Pinellas County commissioners unanimously approved $6 million in March to buy the land. The county will require affordability for 99 years. The $77 million project also draws on federal tax credit equity, tax-exempt bonds and a state loan through the Live Local Act.

Skyway Flats is in predevelopment. Elmington expects financial closing and a construction start in early 2027.

Similar to Pinellas County officials, National City planners acted on their own. They changed zoning to allow more density on parking lots. The change fits within the California law context. San Diego County alone needs more than 171,000 homes, regional officials say.

The city’s planning commission began reforming the code in July 2025 to allow four stories. Previously, the code capped buildings at three.

That cap limited how many units a project could hold, Andrew Regenberg of Gafcon, the firm working with the owner, told the commission in a public hearing. Chris Dallo, who heads the investment group, backed the change.

“We believe that more housing means more opportunity not just for our market, but for local businesses,” Dallo told the commission.

Market View is scheduled for completion in the first quarter of 2028. It will have three buildings, mostly studios, one-bedrooms and two-bedrooms, linked by open space and the market. RDC designed it, and R.D. Olson Construction is the general contractor.

Councilmember Ditas Yamane, who represents the district, said the groundbreaking followed a long review.

“This milestone is the result of a long, thoughtful process and extensive due diligence to bring this vision to life,” Yamane said.
